# Financial Regulation, Climate Change, and Climate-related Risk Disclosure

Last updated:

June 1, 2026

Actions

Slated for Rollback

![Rolled up US currency.](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/dollar-1362244_640.jpg)

## Current Status

In May 2026, the [SEC released a proposed rescission](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/proposed/2026/33-11421.pdf "https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/proposed/2026/33-11421.pdf") of the climate-related risk disclosure rules finalized under the Biden administration. While federal disclosure efforts were stalled in litigation and now will likely be dismantled through the proposed rescission, the state of California is working to implement new climate disclosure laws and litigation challenging those state laws is ongoing.

## Why It Matters

Climate change impacts pose enormous risks to the US financial system. These risks can be physical, such as damaged infrastructure and transportation networks due to increasingly severe weather events, wildfires, and sea-level rise, or transitional, such as investment values changing with underlying shifts in energy and climate policy or consumer demand. These climate-related risks result in financial risk for businesses and investors. At the same time, a growing number of companies are setting net-zero goals and other greenhouse gas emissions targets, but their reporting is too fragmented and inconsistent to be useful to investors and regulators. Financial regulators, most notably the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), are taking steps to inform people about how climate risks can affect companies, investors, and financial markets.

## Key Resources

* **Legal Analysis**: [Climate Disclosure Regimes Offer Insights for Future US Policy](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/climate-disclosure-regimes-offer-insights-for-future-us-policy/)
* **Legal Analysis**: [The Securities and Exchange Commission Finalizes a Narrower Climate-Related Risk Disclosure Rule](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/the-securities-and-exchange-commission-finalizes-a-narrower-climate-related-risk-disclosure-rule/)
* **Quick Take**: [SEC Climate-Related Risk Disclosure Rule Compliance Timeline](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/sec-climate-related-risk-disclosure-rule-compliance-timeline/)​
* **Legal Analysis**: [Litigation Updates on California’s New Climate Disclosure Laws](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/litigation-updates-on-californias-new-climate-disclosure-laws/)
* **Legal Analysis**: [The Implementation and Legal Risks of California’s New Climate Disclosure Laws](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/the-implementation-and-legal-risks-of-californias-new-climate-disclosure-laws/)
* **Quick Take**: [Global Climate Disclosure Regimes](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/global-climate-disclosure-regimes/)
* **Quick Take**: [The SEC’s Proposed ESG Rules Aim to Provide Better Information to Investors](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/the-secs-proposed-esg-rules-aim-to-provide-better-information-to-investors/)
* **Legal Analysis**: [What to know about the SEC Proposed Climate Risk Disclosure Rule](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/what-to-know-about-the-sec-proposed-climate-risk-disclosure-rule/)
* **Legal Analysis**: [Entering a New Era in Climate-Related Disclosure and Financial Risk Management in the U.S.](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Vizcarra-ALI2021-ClimateFinanceRiskOutlook.pdf)

## Timeline

[Trump Administration II](#)

**June 1, 2026** The SEC informed the Eighth Circuit that it issued a proposed rescission of the climate-related risk rule and stated that it will submit a separate status report by August 31, 2026. *State of Iowa, et al v. SEC*, Docket No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.)

**May 29, 2026** The [SEC released a proposed rescission](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/proposed/2026/33-11421.pdf) of the climate-related risk disclosure rules finalized under the Biden administration, arguing that “[t]he Final Rules were a dramatic overreach of the Commission’s statutory authority and, independently, unsound as a matter of policy.” Comments will be due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

**May 21, 2026** An Eighth Circuit judge denied the motion to lift abeyance in the case challenging the SEC’s never-implemented climate-related risk disclosure rule. A group of states led by Iowa asked the Court to lift the abeyance and vacate the rule. *State of Iowa, et al v. SEC*, Docket No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.)

**May 4, 2026** The SEC submitted its proposed [Rescission of Climate-Related Disclosure Rules](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/jsp/EO/eoDashboard.myjsp) to OIRA for review. Once approved by OIRA, the Commission is expected to vote on the rescission.

**Feb. 26, 2026** The California Air Resources Board approved adoption of the [California Greenhouse Gas Reporting and Climate Financial Risk Disclosure Initial Regulation](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/news/carb-approves-climate-transparency-regulation-entities-doing-business-california), which implements SB 253 and SB 261.Companies will have to meet a reporting deadline of Aug. 1, 2026 for GHG scopes 1 and 2 emissions reporting.

**Dec. 9, 2025** CARB [released draft rules](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/200s%20initial%20regulation_staff%20report.pdf?source=email) for corporate GHG disclosure requirements consistent with SB 253. Under the proposal, companies with $1 billion of annual revenue or more will disclose their Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by August 2026. CARB delayed supply chain reporting until 2027 and will not penalize incomplete data in the first year of reporting. A 45-day comment period is now open and CARB will hold a hearing on **Feb. 26, 2026**.

**Nov. 18, 2025** The Ninth Circuit granted a motion for injunction pending appeal of California’s climate risk reporting rule, slated to go into effect in January 2026, at the request of the US Chamber of Commerce. The court did not pause implementation of the GHG reporting rule, which CARB announced has a first reporting deadline in August 2026. Oral argument for both statutes is set for **Jan. 9, 2026**. Appellants withdrew their application to the Supreme Court for an injunction pending appeal. *Chamber of Com. of the U.S. v. Sanchez*, No. 25-5327 (9th Cir.).

**Oct. 29, 2025** In a case challenging California’s climate disclosure laws, the appeals court denied the portion of the appellants’ emergency motion requesting that the merits panel rule by Nov. 3, 2025 on their pending motion for injunction pending appeal. The court placed the case, which has been fully briefed, on the calendar for Jan. 2026. On Nov. 10, 2025, appellants [filed an emergency application](https://admin.climatecasechart.com/wp-content/uploads/case-documents/2025/20251112_docket-25-5327_notice.pdf) to the Supreme Court. *Chamber of Com. of the U.S. v. Sanchez*, No. 25-5327 (9th Cir.).

**Oct. 24, 2025** Exxon Mobil [filed suit](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/71751076/exxon-mobil-corporation-v-sanchez/) against California in the Eastern District of California challenging the state’s climate disclosure laws and arguing that they would unlawfully compel speech and require the company to use a flawed GHG methodology. *Exxon Mobil Corporation v. Sanchez*, 2:25-at-01462, (E.D. Cal.)

**Sept. 12, 2025** The Eighth Circuit announced in litigation over the SEC’s climate risk disclosure rule that the case will be held in abeyance “until such time as the Securities and Exchange Commission reconsiders the challenged Final Rules by notice-and- comment rulemaking or renews its defense of the Final Rule.” The court explains, “It is the agency’s responsibility to determine whether its Final Rules will be rescinded, repealed, modified, or defended in litigation.” *State of Iowa, et al v. SEC*, Docket No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.).

**Sept. 11, 2025** In a case challenging California’s climate disclosure laws, the judge denied industry plaintiffs’ motion for an injunction pending appeal. The judge also stayed all proceedings pending resolution of the plaintiffs’ appeal over the denial of a preliminary injunction to pause the implementation of the laws on First Amendment grounds. *Chamber of Com. of the U.S. v. Calif. Air Res. Bd.*, C.D. Cal., No. 2:24-cv-00801.

**Aug. 13, 2025** In the case challenging California’s climate disclosure laws, the judge denied industry plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction to pause the implementation of the laws on First Amendment grounds. *Chamber of Com. of the U.S. v. Calif. Air Res. Bd.*, C.D. Cal., No. 2:24-cv-00801.

**July 23, 2025** The SEC filed a status report in *State of Iowa, et al v. SEC*, Docket No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.) telling the court the commission did not intend to “review or reconsider the rules” and “respectfully request[ed] that the Court terminate the abeyance, continue considering the parties’ arguments, and exercise its jurisdiction to decide the case.”

**April 24, 2025** [The Eighth Circuit granted](https://www.bloomberglaw.com/product/blaw/document/X6ORBT962209T9BO5MJ0NVSHPB9) intervenor states’ [April 4 request](https://climatecasechart.com/wp-content/uploads/case-documents/2025/20250404_docket-24-1522-24-1623-24-1624-24-1626-24-1627-24-1628-24-1631-24-1633-24-1634-24-1685_motion.pdf) to hold litigation in abeyance “pending further order of the court.” The court directed the SEC to file a status report within 90 days “advising whether the Commission intends to review or reconsider the rules at issue in this case. If the Commission has determined to take no action, then the status report should address whether the Commission will adhere to the rules if the petitions for review are denied and, if not, why the Commission will not review or reconsider the rules at this time.” *State of Iowa, et al v. SEC*, Docket No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.).

**Mar. 27, 2025** The SEC [voted to end its legal defense of the climate-related risk disclosure rule](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025-58) and [the SEC Solicitor notified the Eighth Circuit](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/State-of-Iowa-et-al-v.-SEC-Entry-null.pdf) that it would not defend the rule in court, noting that “[b]ecause Commission counsel is no longer authorized to advance the arguments presented in the Commission’s response brief, the Commission yields any oral argument time back to the Court or to other parties as the Court determines.” [*State of Iowa, et al v. SEC*, Docket No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.)](https://www.bloomberglaw.com/ms/product/blaw/document/XL4MS46BFJ9Q398JDBJ5RSV03N)

**Feb. 11, 2025** [The SEC notified the Eighth Circuit](https://www.bloomberglaw.com/product/blaw/document/X48V7NKJ51B9K0OP1LOTP0PLHV5) that the recent change in composition of the commission and the president’s recent memorandum on a regulatory freeze “bear on the conduct of this litigation”  and that the commission will “promptly notify the Court of its determination about its positions in the litigation” and submit a status report within 45 days. The commission asked the court not to schedule oral argument prior to this forthcoming status report. *Iowa v. SEC*, Case No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.).

[Biden Administration](#)

**Jan. 2024**The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) released a report “[Assessing the Impacts of Climate Change: Federal Budgetary Risks, Adaptation Planning, and the Climate Benefits of Federal Investments](https://perma.cc/D2ZT-9HAR).”

**Jan. 13, 2024** The Defense Department, General Services Administration, and NASA withdrew its proposed regulation, [Federal Acquisition Regulation: Disclosure of Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Climate-Related Financial Risk](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/13/2024-30621/federal-acquisition-regulation-disclosure-of-greenhouse-gas-emissions-and-climate-related-financial).

**Oct. 1, 2024** Intervenors (18 states and the District of Columbia) in support of SEC’s climate-related disclosure rule filed their[final brief](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/68335607/00805102814/state-of-iowa-v-sec/). *Iowa v. SEC*, Case No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.)*.*

**Oct. 1, 2024** The Securities and Exchange Commission filed their [final brief](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/68335607/00805102776/state-of-iowa-v-sec/) in response to petitioners and in support of their final rule on climate-related disclosures. *Iowa v. SEC*, Case No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.)*.*

**Sept. 17, 2024** Petitioners filed their reply brief in the consolidated challenge to the SEC’s climate-related risk disclosure rule in the Eighth Circuit. *Iowa v. SEC*, Case No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.).

**Aug. 15, 2024** Intervenors and amici filed briefs in support of the SEC’s climate-related risk disclosure rule, including [Intervenor states](https://climatecasechart.com/wp-content/uploads/case-documents/2024/20240816_docket-24-1522-24-1623-24-1624-24-1626-24-1627-24-1628-24-1631-24-1633-24-1634-24-1685_brief.pdf), [Legal scholars](https://climatecasechart.com/wp-content/uploads/case-documents/2024/20240816_docket-24-1522-24-1623-24-1624-24-1626-24-1627-24-1628-24-1631-24-1633-24-1634-24-1685_amicus-brief.pdf), [Institutional investors](https://climatecasechart.com/wp-content/uploads/case-documents/2024/20240815_docket-24-1522-24-1623-24-1624-24-1626-24-1627-24-1628-24-1631-24-1633-24-1634-24-1685_amicus-brief.pdf), [Environmental NGOs](https://climatecasechart.com/wp-content/uploads/case-documents/2024/20240815_docket-24-1522-24-1623-24-1624-24-1626-24-1627-24-1628-24-1631-24-1633-24-1634-24-1685_amicus-brief-8.pdf), and [First Amendment experts](https://climatecasechart.com/wp-content/uploads/case-documents/2024/20240815_docket-24-1522-24-1623-24-1624-24-1626-24-1627-24-1628-24-1631-24-1633-24-1634-24-1685_amicus-brief-9.pdf). *Iowa v. SEC*, Case No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.).

**Aug. 6, 2024** The [SEC filed its respondent brief](https://www.bloomberglaw.com/product/blaw/document/X3G6FSKUAJ79SR816HC8AGCV5A5) defending the rule in the consolidated challenge to the SEC’s climate-related risk disclosure rule in the Eighth Circuit. *Iowa v. SEC*, Case No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.).

**June 24, 2024** Amici submitted their briefs in support of petitioners in the consolidated challenge to the SEC’s climate risk disclosure rule in the Eighth Circuit. *Iowa v. SEC*, Case No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.).

**June 21, 2024** Petitioners submitted their briefs in the consolidated challenge to the SEC’s climate risk disclosure rule in the Eighth Circuit, including[state petitioners](https://www.bloomberglaw.com/product/blaw/document/X7HDDB88M0B91691G61FS3EGENK),[Chamber of Commerce and other industry petitioners](https://aboutblaw.com/beuL), and[energy producers](https://aboutblaw.com/beuQ). *Iowa v. SEC*, Case No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.).

**May 9, 2024** [The Federal Reserve released the results of the first Climate Scenario Analysis](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/csa-exercise-summary-20240509.pdf) conducted by the six biggest investment banks.

**April 4, 2024** After an onslaught of [litigation challenging the rules](https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/us-appeals-court-temporarily-pauses-sec-climate-disclosure-rules-2024-03-15/), the SEC[issued an administrative stay](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/other/2024/33-11280.pdf) of the final rules pending judicial review of the consolidated Eighth Circuit petitions.

**March 21, 2024** The Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation selected the Eighth Circuit via lottery to hear a case consolidating nine circuit court challenges to the SEC’s climate-related risk disclosure rule. *Iowa v. SEC*, Case No. 24-01522 (8th Cir.).

**March 15, 2024** The Fifth Circuit granted an administrative stay putting the rule on hold at the request of energy companies. *Liberty Energy v. SEC*, Docket No. 24-60109 (5th Cir.).

**March 6, 2024** The SEC narrowly voted to release its long-awaited [final climate-related risk disclosure rule](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/final/2024/33-11275.pdf), which requires public companies to report on material climate-related risks that affect the business and, for some large companies, greenhouse gas emissions, if material. The [rule will be effective 60 days after publication in the Federal Register](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/sec-climate-related-risk-disclosure-rule-compliance-timeline/). A number of lawsuits were filed by states, industry, and environmental groups following the release of the final rule. [Read our analysis](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/the-securities-and-exchange-commission-finalizes-a-narrower-climate-related-risk-disclosure-rule/).

**Jan. 30, 2024** [A lawsuit was filed challenging two new California climate disclosure and financial reporting laws](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/in-house-counsel/business-groups-sue-over-new-california-emissions-reporting-law#) for requiring disclosure by qualifying public and privately-held businesses of GHG emissions and climate-related risks throughout their value chain. The plaintiffs allege SB 253 and 261 violate constitutional rights by compelling companies to engage in nonfactual, costly speech on climate change. They seek to enjoin the California Air Resources Board from taking any action to enforce the two laws. [*Chamber of Com. of the U.S. v. Calif. Air Res. Bd.*](https://www.bloomberglaw.com/public/document/ChamberofCommerceoftheUnitedStatesofAmericaetalvCaliforniaAirReso?doc_id=X1Q6OLN3NU82), C.D. Cal., No. 2:24-cv-00801.

**Dec. 4, 2023** The CFTC released [proposed guidance for voluntary carbon credit derivative contract trading](https://www.cftc.gov/sites/default/files/2023/12/2023-28532a.pdf) intended to outline factors that may provide greater transparency in the carbon credit market.

**Oct. 4, 2023** The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) filed a [notice with the SEC proposing to amend the NYSE Listed Company Manual to adopt a new listing standard Natural Asset Companies (NACs)](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/10/04/2023-22041/self-regulatory-organizations-new-york-stock-exchange-llc-notice-of-filing-of-proposed-rule-change). NACs are a new class of corporations that hold the rights to the ecological performance produced by natural or working areas, such as large-scale farmlands, and have the authority to manage the areas for conservation, restoration, or sustainable management.

**Sept. 20, 2023** [The SEC adopted amendments to the Investment Company Act “Names Rule”](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/10/11/2023-20793/investment-company-names) that will require fund names to more accurately reflect their portfolio. Specifically, the changes will require more funds with names that suggest particular areas of focus, including Environmental, Social, or Governance factors, to follow the 80 percent investment policy, which requires those funds to invest at least 80 percent of fund value in the specified area of investment focus.

**Sept. 19, 2023** Treasury released [Principles for Net-Zero Financing & Investment](https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/136/NetZeroPrinciples.pdf), a document designed to promote consistency and credibility and encourage greater adoption of best practices related to financial institutions’ net zero commitments, with a focus on Scope 3 emissions.

**Sep. 14, 2023** California’s legislature passed two climate disclosure bills. Th e[Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB253) (SB-253) would require companies that do business in California with total annual revenues over $1 billion to disclose their scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions. The [Greenhouse Gases: Climate-Related Financial Risk Act](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB261) (SB-261) would require companies that do business in California with total annual revenues over $500 million to disclose their climate-related financial risk.

**June 27, 2023** [The Federal Insurance Office released a report](https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/136/FIO-June-2023-Insurance-Supervision-and-Regulation-of-Climate-Related-Risks.pdf) assessing climate-related risk in the insurance industry. The report assesses climate-related challenges in supervision and regulation of insurers and makes a series of recommendations for strengthening state oversight, improving climate risk-related tools, and more.

**March 29, 2023** [The SEC announced a $55.9 million agreement with a Brazilian mining company](https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2023-63) to settle charges related to false statements that the company had made in its sustainability reports about the safety of its dams prior to a 2019 dam collapse.

**March 7, 2023** Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen [delivered opening remarks at the first meeting of the Climate-related Financial Risk Advisory Committee (CFRAC)](https://perma.cc/327K-AWW6), emphasizing that “taking climate change into account is prudent risk management.” The CFRAC, [established in October, 2022](https://perma.cc/2XQ5-G7WH), as an external advisory committee to the Treasury Department’s Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC), is [tasked with advising the FSOC on climate-related risks to the financial system](https://perma.cc/93WT-6X8Z).

**Jan. 26, 2022** 25 states with Republican attorneys general[sued the U.S. Department of Labor](https://perma.cc/QQS8-L5QA) in U.S. District Court, seeking an injunction to block the [rule](https://perma.cc/LH5G-ANS9) scheduled to go into effect on Jan. 30, 2023, to allow 401(k) managers to consider ESG factors in making investment decisions.

**Dec. 21, 2022** The New York Department of Financial Services [released a proposed rule to govern how banks and insurers “identify, measure, monitor, and control climate-related financial risks.”](https://perma.cc/LXQ3-2RA5)

**Jan. 17, 2023** The[Federal Reserve released its first climate scenario exercise](http://federalreserve.gov/publications/files/csa-instructions-20230117.pdf) for the six largest US banks. The banks will explore the physical risks and transition risks from a large hurricane event in the Northeastern US.

**Dec. 14, 2022** [The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) voted to start a regulatory review of its Green Guides](https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/GreenGuides-FRN-11-5-22.pdf), which are designed to help companies avoid making misleading or deceptive environmental claims.

**Dec. 5, 2022** [The Federal Reserve released draft principles](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/files/other20221202b1.pdf) for a high-level framework for management of climate-related financial risk for financial institutions with over $100 billion in assets. The proposed guidance is “substantially similar” to guidance released by OCC and FDIC.

**Nov. 22, 2022** The Department of Labor [released](https://perma.cc/62TC-FRJ6) a [final rule allowing 401(k) managers to consider ESG factors in making investment decisions](https://perma.cc/LH5G-ANS9), providing for the rule to take effect on Jan. 30, 2023.

**Nov. 14, 2022** Three federal agencies, including the Department of Defense, [proposed a rule that would require major federal government contractors and suppliers to publicly disclose their greenhouse gas emissions and climate-related risks and set emissions-reduction targets](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/11/14/2022-24569/federal-acquisition-regulation-disclosure-of-greenhouse-gas-emissions-and-climate-related-financial).

**Nov. 2, 2022** The SEC adopted a [final rule requiring mutual funds and other investment funds to provide more information about the proxy votes they cast on ESG](https://www.sec.gov/rules/final/2022/33-11131.pdf) and other issues. The rule directed fund managers to group each proxy vote they cast within a subject-matter category such as “Environment or climate” or “Corporate governance,” among other measures aimed at increasing investor access to information about proxy voting behavior.

**Oct. 19, 2022** The Treasury’s Federal Insurance Office (FIO) [announced plans to request information from property & casualty (P&C) insurers](https://perma.cc/U8BA-433Y) regarding their underwriting data on homeowners’ insurance. The FIO intends for the information to aid its “assessment of climate-related exposures and their effects on insurance availability.”

**Oct. 19, 2022** [Nineteen state attorneys general subpoenaed six major American banks](https://perma.cc/5ED6-BXKE) for documents regarding their involvement with the Net Zero Banking Alliance, a consortium of financial institutions convened by the United Nations to further net-zero goals.

**Oct. 3, 2022** The Financial Stability Oversight Council, part of the U.S. Department of the Treasury, [established the Climate-related Financial Risk Advisory Committee (CFRAC)](https://perma.cc/2XQ5-G7WH), which is intended to further the goals of “identifying, assessing, and responding to the risks climate change poses to the financial system.”

**Sept. 29, 2022** [The Federal Reserve announced that six of the largest US banks will participate in a pilot climate scenario analysis exercise](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/other20220929a.htm) to assess climate-related risks. The pilot, designed to improve firms’ ability to measure and manage climate risks, will launch in early 2023.

**Sept. 21, 2022** The [SEC Investor Advisory Committee](https://www.sec.gov/spotlight/investor-advisory-committee-2012/20220914-draft-climate-related-disclosure-recommendation.pdf) endorsed the SEC’s proposed climate risk disclosure rule and specifically its proposal to require companies to disclose greenhouse gas emissions, including Scope 3 emissions from indirect sources such as supply chains.

**July 28, 2022** [Treasury’s Office of Financial Research unveiled its new Climate Data and Analytics Hub pilot](https://www.financialresearch.gov/press-releases/files/OFR_Climate_data_and_analytics_hub_fact_sheet.pdf), a tool designed to help financial regulators assess climate-related financial risks. During the pilot phase, the Federal Reserve Board of Governors and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York will have access to the tool, with the goal of providing wider access in the future.

**June 30, 2022** The Treasury Department’s [Federal Insurance Office](https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-markets-financial-institutions-and-fiscal-service/federal-insurance-office) requested information about property insurance availability in disaster prone areas as well as the financial risk that climate change poses to the insurance industry.

**June 15, 2022** [The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, in which the US participates, proposed a global approach](https://www.bis.org/bcbs/publ/d532.htm) for how banks should manage climate-related financial risk.

**June 2, 2022** The CFTC hosted a [Voluntary Carbon Convening](https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/PressReleases/8525-22) to discuss supply and demand for high quality carbon offsets, including data and standardization issues.

**June 2, 2022** The CFTC voted unanimously to release a [Request for Information for public comment on climate-related financial risk](https://www.cftc.gov/LawRegulation/FederalRegister/final-rules/2022-12302.html) with respect to the derivative market and the underlying commodities market.

**May-June 2022** The SEC sent letters to at least six companies questioning the “more expansive disclosure” on ESG issues that the company included in their corporate sustainability report than their 10-Ks. The SEC asked the companies whether they considered providing the same type of climate-related disclosure in both reports.

**May 31, 2022** The Governmental Accounting Standards Board issued guidance to states and cities on the [Intersection of Environmental, Social, and Governance Matters with Governmental Accounting Standards.](https://www.gasb.org/Page/ShowPdf?path=ESG%20Memo%20FINAL%2005312022.pdf&title=May%2031,%202022%E2%80%94Intersection%20of%20Environmental,%20Social,%20and%20Governance%20Matters%20with%20Governmental%20Accounting%20Standards) The guidance reviews existing accounting standards that intersect with ESG issues to help government accountants think about how to address and report on ESG-related questions.

**May 25, 2022** The [SEC announced proposed amendments to Rule 35d-1 under the Investment Company Act of 1940, the fund “Names Rule](https://www.sec.gov/rules/proposed/2022/ic-34593.pdf),” to enhance transparency and avoid misleading investors. The SEC would update the 80 percent investment policy requirement, which requires funds with certain names to invest 80 percent of their assets in investments reflected in the fund name, to include funds with particular characteristics, including ESG investments. The proposed changes [would not permit funds that consider ESG as one of many non-determinative factors to use ESG or similar terminology in their name](https://www.sec.gov/files/ic-34593-fact-sheet.pdf), and doing so could be considered materially deceptive or misleading. The proposing release will be published in the Federal Register and open for comment for 60 days.

**May 25, 2022** [The SEC announced proposed amendments to rules and reporting forms to facilitate “consistent, comparable, and reliable information” for investors about environment, social, and governance (ESG) strategies](https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2022-92). Under the proposed amendments, funds claiming ESG impacts would need to provide more information to show their approach and impact. For example, [funds with a focus on environmental impact would need to disclose the greenhouse gas emissions of the portfolio investments](https://www.sec.gov/files/ia-6034-fact-sheet.pdf).

**May 23, 2022** [The SEC charged an investment management firm for “misstatements and omissions” about environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in investment decisions](https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2022-86?utm_medium=email&utm_source=govdelivery) for some of the mutual funds it managed.

**May 18, 2022** [The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the SEC’s use of in-house administrative law judges is unconstitutional](https://aboutblaw.com/24J), holding that (1) the use of in-house SEC judges violates the petitioners’ Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial, (2) the delegated legislative authority does not “provide an intelligible principle by which the SEC would exercise the delegated power,” (3) the removal process for in-house judges violates the Article II Take Care Clause.[*Jarkesy v. SEC*](https://aboutblaw.com/24J)*,* 5th Cir., No. 20-61007.

**April 28, 2022** [The SEC announced a lawsuit against a company](https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2022-72) for making false and misleading claims about the safety of a mine ahead of its deadly collapse in 2019. It is one of the commission’s first enforcement actions related to ESG since the launch of its Climate and ESG Task Force. According to the SEC, the company misled investors and others, including through its environment, social and governance (ESG) disclosures.

**April 8, 2022** The National Association of Insurance Commissioners [approved new climate-change related risk disclosure requirements](https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/inline-files/2022ProposedClimateRiskSurvey_0.pdf?msclkid=e24cf6f2b47211eca09ac1c752e22857) for a number of state insurance regulators.

**April 4, 2022** The Office of Management and Budget [released a report](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/ap_21_climate_risk_fy2023.pdf) on the federal budget’s exposure to climate risk. The report highlights six climate-related financial risks that could reduce federal revenue annually by up to 7.1 percent: disaster relief, flood insurance, crop insurance, healthcare expenditures, wildland fire suppression spending, and flood risk at Federal facilities.

**April 5, 2022** The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) [requested comment on draft principles to provide a framework for managing climate-related financial risks for banks](https://www.fdic.gov/news/board-matters/2022/2022-03-29-notational-fr.pdf) with over $100 billion in consolidated assets.

**Mar. 21, 2022** The [SEC proposed a new rule with requirements for publicly traded companies to disclose climate-related information in registration statements and periodic reports](https://www.sec.gov/rules/proposed/2022/33-11042.pdf?utm_medium=email&utm_source=govdelivery), including information regarding climate risks (such as how extreme weather and energy transitions might affect their business), and certain climate-related financial statement metrics. The regulation would also require registrants in certain cases to disclose direct greenhouse gas emissions associated with their customers and suppliers, as well as emissions associated with purchased electricity. Additionally, the proposal would require companies that advertise emissions reduction goals to detail how they plan to achieve these goals, their reliance on carbon offsets, and their progress so far.

**Dec. 6, 2021** [Correspondence between the SEC and Honda](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000715153/000119312521348261/filename1.htm) reflected a[growing trend of SEC comment letters to filing companies](https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/eenews/2022/05/12/sec-gets-aggressive-in-demanding-climate-data-00031955) asking for additional disclosure related to climate change-related risks and in some cases asking companies to justify claims that certain information is immaterial to investors. Companies receiving comment letters related to climate risk disclosure include Honda, Phillips, Amazon, Comcast, and Target and more.

**Oct. 21, 2021** In response to Biden’s E.O. 14030 on climate-related financial risk, the Financial Stability Oversight Council, chaired by the secretary of the Treasury, [published a report](https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/261/FSOC-Climate-Report.pdf) stating that climate change is a threat to financial markets. The report included recommendations for member agencies to assess climate-related risks, build capacity and expertise, and enhance climate-related disclosures and data.

**Oct. 14, 2021** The [Department of Labor’s Employee Benefits Security Administration released its proposed rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/10/14/2021-22263/prudence-and-loyalty-in-selecting-plan-investments-and-exercising-shareholder-rights), “Prudence and Loyalty in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights,” amending the Investment Duties regulation under ERISA. It clarifies how ERISA fiduciaries can consider climate change and ESG in their investment decisions. This rule responds to changes made by EBSA to these regulations in 2020 that were seen as hostile to ESG factors.

**Sept. 2021** Researchers at the New York Federal Reserve Bank [developed a stress testing procedure](https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/staff_reports/sr977.html) to measure financial institutions’ resilience to climate-related risks. The procedure, titled Staff Report Number 977, introduced a measure of systemic climate risk called CRISK that quantifies institutions’ expected capital shortfall in a climate stress scenario.

**Sept. 22, 2021** The [SEC’s Division of Corporate Finance released a guidance document focused on climate-related disclosure under existing rules and standards](https://www.sec.gov/corpfin/sample-letter-climate-change-disclosures?utm_medium=email&utm_source=govdelivery&source=email#_ftnref3). The guidance documents include a sample letter demonstrating how the agency may communicate with companies on disclosure requirements, as well as some clarifying points and additional questions.

**Aug. 31, 2021** The Treasury’s Federal Insurance Office [issued a Request for Information](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/08/31/2021-18713/federal-insurance-office-request-for-information-on-the-insurance-sector-and-climate-related) in response to the May 20 executive order on Climate-Related Financial Risk. The office seeks comments on best methods for monitoring and assessing the climate-related risks to the insurance and financial sectors. Additionally, the office seeks input on three climate-related insurance priorities: supervision and regulation, market resilience and mitigation, and sector engagement.

**May 20, 2021** [President Biden issued Executive Order 14030 requesting a Climate-Related Financial Risk Strategy](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/05/20/executive-order-on-climate-related-financial-risk/), an Assessment of Climate-Related Financial Risk by Financial Regulators, and directing the Department of Labor to consider proposing a rule to suspend, revise, or rescind two rules. These rules are the “Financial Factors in Selecting Plan Investments” and “Fiduciary Duties Regarding Proxy Voting and Shareholder Rights” which the agency had earlier decided not to enforce.

**Apr. 19, 2021** The Department of Treasury announced a coordinated climate policy strategy focused on three prongs: climate transition finance, climate-related economic and tax policy, and climate-related financial risks. To implement this strategy, [Treasury created a Climate Hub and appointed a Climate Counselor to coordinate these efforts](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy0134).

**Apr. 14, 2021** [The Senate confirmed President Biden’s SEC Chair nominee, Gary Gensler](https://www.sec.gov/news/public-statement/gensler-confirmation), who spoke about climate risk and the importance of climate-related financial disclosures during his hearing.

**Apr. 9, 2021** The [SEC’s Division of Examinations issued a Risk Alert that notes the risk presented by lack of standardization in the rapidly growing field of ESG products](https://www.sec.gov/files/esg-risk-alert.pdf). In its examinations of investment advisers, funds, and effective practices, the division has observed deficiencies and internal control weaknesses that should be addressed.

**Mar. 23, 2021** Lael Brainard, a governor of the Fed, [announced the creation of the Financial Stability Climate Committee (FSCC)](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/brainard20210323a.htm) in a speech at a Ceres conference. The FSCC is a systemwide committee charged with developing and implementing a program to assess and address climate-related financial risks, and to complement the work of the SCC in this area.

**Mar. 17, 2021** The[Commodity Futures Trading Commission announced the creation of the Climate Risk Unit (CRU)](https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/PressReleases/8368-21), which supports the CFTC’s mission by focusing on the role of derivatives in assessing climate-related risk and facilitating a transition to a low-carbon economy.

**Mar. 15, 2021** The SEC[requested comments to help assess the materiality of climate-related disclosures as well as the costs and benefits of different regulatory approaches to climate disclosure](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/lee-climate-change-disclosures).

**Mar. 10, 2021** [The US Department of Labor released a statement on enforcement of its final rule on Financial Factors in Selecting Plan Investments and Fiduciary Duties Regarding Proxy Voting and Shareholder Rights](https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/releases/ebsa/ebsa20210310), announcing that it will not enforce the rules’ disincentivization of ESG investing.

**Mar. 4, 2021** The [SEC Division of Enforcement announced the creation of the Climate and ESG Task Force](https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2021-42?utm_medium=email&utm_source=govdelivery) to develop initiatives to identify ESG-related misconduct. The initial focus will be to identify any material gaps or misstatements in issuers’ disclosure of climate risks under existing rules.

**Mar. 3, 2021** The [SEC Division of Examinations announced its 2021 Examination Priorities](https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2021-39), highlighting plans to integrate climate and ESG considerations into the agency’s broader regulatory framework.

**Feb. 26, 2021** The [SEC issued an Investor Alert & Bulletin titled “Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Funds – Investor Bulletin”](https://www.sec.gov/oiea/investor-alerts-and-bulletins/environmental-social-and-governance-esg-funds-investor-bulletin) noting recent increases in popularity for ESG funds and providing educational information for investors.

**Feb. 24, 2021** [SEC commissioner Allison Lee directed the Division of Corporation Finance](https://www.sec.gov/news/public-statement/lee-statement-review-climate-related-disclosure) to enhance its focus on climate-related disclosure in public company filings, including updating the 2010 guidance and assessing existing compliance.

**Jan. 2021**The Federal Reserve formed the Supervision Climate Committee, a system-wide group bringing together senior staff across the Federal Reserve Board and Reserve Banks. The SCC will build the Federal Reserve’s capacity to understand the potential implications of climate change for financial institutions, infrastructure, and markets.

[Trump Administration I](#)

**Jan. 14, 2021** The [Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) finalized a rule designed to prevent banks from refusing to finance categories of projects or companies](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2021/nr-occ-2021-8a.pdf), requiring them to undergo individual risk assessments to support their decision to deny services to any particular potential customer.

**Nov. 13, 2020** The EBSA’s [final rule on Financial Factors in Selecting Plan Investments](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2020/11/13/2020-24515/financial-factors-in-selecting-plan-investments) cautioned against considering ESG factors in ERISA-covered plan investments, emphasizing financial outcomes over other considerations, and restricted fiduciaries from offering ESG-themed funds as default options.

**Nov. 9, 2020** The Fed [discussed climate change and microprudential risks in the November 2020 Supervision and Regulation Report](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/202011-supervision-and-regulation-report.pdf), pointing to chronic flooding, wildfires, severe weather, and energy transitions as potential risks, and recommends adapting governance and disclosures to better account for climate-related risks.

**Nov. 4, 2020** [The SEC published a final rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2020/11/04/2020-21580/procedural-requirements-and-resubmission-thresholds-under-exchange-act-rule-14a-8) that amends procedural requirements, as well as a provision relating to resubmitted proposals under the shareholder-proposal rule, Rule 14a-8, which protects a shareholder’s rights to exercise governance rights, such as electing board directors, via proxy voting. The rule protects shareholders’ proxy voting rights by requiring certain companies to include shareholder proposals in their proxy statements. 

**Nov. 1, 2020** The [Federal Reserve’s Financial Stability Report includes climate change](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/financial-stability-report-20201109.pdf) for the first time in a section titled “The Implications of Climate Change for Financial Stability.”

**Jan. 30, 2020** [SEC chairman Jay Clayton issued a statement](https://www.sec.gov/news/public-statement/clayton-mda-2020-01-30) supporting the agency’s current approach to ESG disclosures and encouraging “market participants to continue to engage” with the SEC on the topic.

**Jan. 7, 2020** [The Office of Compliance Inspections and Examinations of the SEC announced their examination priorities for fiscal year 2020](https://www.sec.gov/about/offices/ocie/national-examination-program-priorities-2020.pdf), including the “accuracy and adequacy” of registered investment advisors’ ESG disclosures.

**June 15, 2017** [The Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures published a report establishing recommendations for a climate reporting framework](https://assets.bbhub.io/company/sites/60/2020/10/FINAL-2017-TCFD-Report-11052018.pdf) that provides clear, comparable, and consistent information to investors about the risks and opportunities presented by climate change.

[Obama Administration](#)

**April 22, 2016** [The SEC published a concept release](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2016/04/22/2016-09056/business-and-financial-disclosure-required-by-regulation-s-k) seeking public comment on modernizing disclosure requirements. The publication includes requests for comment on considering climate-related and environmental, social and governance (ESG) information in disclosure requirements.

**Feb. 8, 2010** The SEC’s climate related disclosure guidance goes into effect, and the SEC [publishes an interpretive release](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2010/02/08/2010-2602/commission-guidance-regarding-disclosure-related-to-climate-change) regarding existing disclosure requirements’ application to climate change.

**Jan. 27, 2010** The Securities Exchange Commission [voted to publish “Commission Guidance Regarding Disclosure Related to Climate Change](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/interp/2010/33-9106.pdf),” which details how existing SEC disclosure rules applicable to certain mandatory financial filings for publicly traded companies should apply to risks associated with anthropogenic climate change.

args.summary:
This webpage from Harvard Law School's Environmental & Energy Law Program (EELP) serves as a regulatory tracker for financial regulation, climate change, and climate-related risk disclosure. The page tracks federal and state actions on climate-related financial disclosure requirements.

CURRENT STATUS: In May 2026, the SEC released a proposed rescission of the climate-related risk disclosure rules finalized under the Biden administration, arguing the Final Rules were "a dramatic overreach of the Commission's statutory authority and, independently, unsound as a matter of policy." While federal disclosure efforts were stalled in litigation and now will likely be dismantled through the proposed rescission, California is working to implement new climate disclosure laws (SB 253 and SB 261), with litigation challenging those state laws ongoing.

WHY IT MATTERS: Climate change impacts pose enormous risks to the US financial system, including physical risks (damaged infrastructure, severe weather, wildfires, sea-level rise) and transitional risks (changing investment values due to shifts in energy/climate policy or consumer demand). A growing number of companies are setting net-zero goals and GHG emissions targets, but their reporting is too fragmented and inconsistent to be useful to investors and regulators. The SEC has been taking steps to inform people about how climate risks can affect companies, investors, and financial markets.

KEY TIMELINE EVENTS (reverse chronological):
- June 1, 2026: SEC informed Eighth Circuit it issued proposed rescission of climate risk rule; will submit status report by Aug. 31, 2026 (State of Iowa v. SEC, No. 24-01522)
- May 29, 2026: SEC released proposed rescission of climate-related risk disclosure rules; comments due 60 days after Federal Register publication
- Feb. 26, 2026: California Air Resources Board approved adoption of the California Greenhouse Gas Reporting and Climate Financial Risk Disclosure Initial Regulation implementing SB 253 and SB 261; first reporting deadline Aug. 1, 2026 for GHG scopes 1 and 2
- Nov. 18, 2025: Ninth Circuit granted injunction pending appeal of California's climate risk reporting rule; GHG reporting rule (Aug. 2026 deadline) not paused; oral argument set for Jan. 9, 2026 (Chamber of Commerce v. Sanchez, No. 25-5327)
- Oct. 24, 2025: Exxon Mobil filed suit against California challenging climate disclosure laws (Exxon Mobil v. Sanchez, E.D. Cal.)
- Mar. 27, 2025: SEC voted to end its legal defense of the climate-related risk disclosure rule
- March 6, 2024: SEC narrowly voted to release its final climate-related risk disclosure rule requiring public companies to report material climate-related risks and, for some large companies, GHG emissions if material; multiple lawsuits followed
- March 21, 2024: Eighth Circuit selected via lottery to hear consolidated challenges to the SEC rule
- Sept. 14, 2023: California passed SB-253 (requires companies with $1B+ annual revenue doing business in CA to disclose scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions) and SB-261 (requires companies with $500M+ annual revenue to disclose climate-related financial risk)
- May 20, 2021: Biden issued Executive Order 14030 requesting a Climate-Related Financial Risk Strategy
- Prior administration actions include the Federal Reserve's climate scenario exercises, Treasury's Climate-related Financial Risk Advisory Committee (CFRAC), CFTC's Climate Risk Unit, SEC's Climate and ESG Task Force, and various proposed and final rules from 2020-2024

KEY CALIFORNIA LAWS: SB-253 (Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act) requires companies doing business in California with over $1 billion annual revenues to disclose scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions. SB-261 (Greenhouse Gases: Climate-Related Financial Risk Act) requires companies with over $500 million annual revenues to disclose climate-related financial risk.

KEY RESOURCES: The page links to multiple legal analyses including coverage of the SEC's final climate disclosure rule, California's climate disclosure laws and related litigation, global climate disclosure regimes, ESG rules, and compliance timelines. The EELP expert for this topic is Sara Dewey (Administrative Law, Corporate Climate Risk, Inflation Reduction Act, Methane Emissions, Natural Resources Law, Power Sector).

This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
![Gibson Dunn](https://www.gibsondunn.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05b/logo-gibson-dunn.svg)

Mobile Navigation

# SEC Proposes Rescission of Climate-Related Disclosure Rules

Client Alert  |  June 3, 2026

***It will be important to the comment process for commenters to submit their views on the Proposal. A well-developed administrative record—including from those who support the Proposal—helps inform the Commission’s deliberations and supports the durability of any final action.***

***Background***  
  
On May 29, 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC or Commission) formally [proposed](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/proposed/2026/33-11421.pdf) (the Proposal) to rescind the Commission’s climate-related disclosure rules adopted in March 2024, the Enhancement and Standardization of Climate-Related Disclosures for Investors (the Climate Rules or the Final Rules).[[1]](#_ftn1) The Climate Rules were among the Gensler Commission’s most consequential rulemakings, both in terms of their breadth and the litigation they generated.  
  
The Climate Rules were first proposed on March 21, 2022 and finalized on March 6, 2024.[[2]](#_ftn2) As adopted, the Climate Rules established a climate-related disclosure framework for registration statements and annual reports, including disclosures regarding climate-related risks, governance and oversight, and risk-management processes, as well as financial statement requirements for recording the effects of severe weather events and other natural conditions.[[3]](#_ftn3)  
  
The Climate Rules have been highly contentious and have generated significant litigation.[[4]](#_ftn4) Litigation challenging the validity of the Climate Rules began almost immediately following their adoption, and in April 2024, the Commission stayed the effectiveness of the rules pending completion of consolidated litigation in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit.[[5]](#_ftn5) In March 2025, the Commission voted to abandon its defense of the rules. The Eighth Circuit then issued an order holding the case in abeyance until the SEC either “reconsider[ed] the challenged [rules] by notice-and-comment rulemaking or renew[ed] its defense of the [rules].”[[6]](#_ftn6) On May 7, 2026, the SEC notified the Eighth Circuit of its decision to propose rescission of the Climate Rules by notice-and-comment rulemaking.[[7]](#_ftn7)  
  
The Proposal itself does not terminate the Climate Rules. Instead, since the Proposal is subject to the Administrative Procedure Act’s notice-and-comment requirements, the Proposal initiates a comment process through which the Commission will consider public input on whether to rescind the Climate Rules in the manner proposed by the Commission. The Proposal was published in the Federal Register on June 3, 2026, and comments are due on or before August 3, 2026.[[8]](#_ftn8)

This Gibson Dunn client alert (June 3, 2026) reports on the SEC's formal proposal, issued May 29, 2026, to rescind its climate-related disclosure rules (the "Climate Rules") adopted in March 2024 under the Gensler Commission. The Climate Rules established a climate-related disclosure framework for registration statements and annual reports, covering climate-related risks, governance, risk-management processes, and financial statement requirements for severe weather events. The rules generated significant litigation immediately after adoption, and in April 2024 the SEC stayed their effectiveness pending consolidated litigation in the Eighth Circuit. In March 2025, the SEC voted to abandon its defense of the rules, and in May 2026 notified the Eighth Circuit of its decision to propose rescission through notice-and-comment rulemaking.

Key details: The Proposal was published in the Federal Register on June 3, 2026, with comments due by August 3, 2026. The Proposal does not itself terminate the Climate Rules—it initiates an APA notice-and-comment process. The SEC estimates annualized cost savings from rescission of approximately $4.9 billion per year over 10 years across all affected registrants. The Proposal cites concerns raised by commenters and litigants, and notes the court has not made any decision on the merits. Gibson Dunn advises that commenters should submit views addressing practical, legal, and economic implications, particularly quantitative and qualitative data on the effects of the Climate Rules, to build a well-developed administrative record supporting the durability of any final action. The alert was prepared by Gibson Dunn lawyers including Mellissa Campbell Duru, Elizabeth Ising, Thomas J. Kim, Ronald O. Mueller, Lori Zyskowski, and Jack Strachan.

# SEC’s Recission of Climate-Related Disclosure Rules

**What:** On June 3, 2026, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC or Commission) published a proposed withdrawal of its climate-related disclosure rule that required registrants and public companies to provide standardized, detailed information about climate-related risks, governance, and certain greenhouse gas emissions in SEC filings. This action would eliminate the pending disclosure framework rather than replacing it with an alternative set of climate-specific reporting requirements, reverting issuers to existing, principles-based disclosure obligations.

**Why:** The Commission is proposing to rescind the climate-related disclosure adopted in 2024 because the final rules were, in the Commission’s view, an overreach of statutory authority and unsound policy. The SEC further states it is rolling back the climate disclosure rules, considering legal challenges and questions about whether the rule imposed disproportionate compliance costs relative to investor-protection benefits. The Commission also points to the need to reassess its regulatory agenda and avoid duplicative or overlapping mandates where climate-related information may already be captured under existing materiality-based disclosure standards and other regulatory or market-driven Environmental Social Governance frameworks.

The Office of Advocacy previously commented on the proposed rule in 2022, encouraging the SEC to publish a supplemental initial regulatory flexibility analysis and to reconsider the breadth of its Scope 3 Greenhouse Gas (GHG) disclosure rules.

**Action:** Read the withdrawal of the final rules and submit comments by the **August 3, 2026**, deadline.

This webpage is from the SBA Office of Advocacy (advocacy.sba.gov), which serves as a voice for small businesses. The main content is a regulatory alert regarding the SEC's proposed rescission of its climate-related disclosure rules.

**Key Details:**
- On June 3, 2026, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) published a proposed withdrawal of its 2024 climate-related disclosure rule that required registrants and public companies to provide standardized information about climate-related risks, governance, and certain greenhouse gas emissions in SEC filings.
- The rescission would eliminate the pending disclosure framework rather than replace it with an alternative, reverting issuers to existing principles-based disclosure obligations.
- The SEC's rationale includes: the final rules were deemed an overreach of statutory authority and unsound policy, disproportionate compliance costs relative to investor-protection benefits, ongoing legal challenges, the need to reassess its regulatory agenda, and the view that climate-related information may already be captured under existing materiality-based disclosure standards and other regulatory or market-driven ESG frameworks.
- The Office of Advocacy previously commented on the proposed rule in 2022, encouraging the SEC to publish a supplemental initial regulatory flexibility analysis and to reconsider the breadth of its Scope 3 Greenhouse Gas (GHG) disclosure rules.
- The comment deadline for the withdrawal of the final rules is August 3, 2026.
- Contact: John Vatian at john.vatian@sba.gov.

The page also lists recent regulatory alerts including topics such as FDA Substances Generally Recognized as Safe, FDA Drug Registration and Listing, EPA Construction General Permit comments, DoD CMMC Reform Task Force, HUD's definition of "Manufactured Home," NOAA Vessel Speed Rule, and EPA risk evaluation for dichlorobenzene. # Formal Rescission of the U.S. SEC Climate Disclosure Rules Has Begun

May 19, 2026

* ## Author

   [Charles R. Berry](/people/charles-r-berry/)

On May 4, 2026, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) submitted a proposed rulemaking titled [*Rescission of Climate‑Related Disclosure Rules*](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eoDetails?rrid=1364512) to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs for review. This submission marks the SEC’s first formal step toward potential rescission, through notice-and-comment rulemaking, of its rules requiring disclosure of climate-related risks and greenhouse gas emissions (the “Rules”), over two years after their adoption.

## **History of the Climate-Related Disclosure Rules**

The Rules, proposed in 2022, were adopted on March 6, 2024 by a 3-2 vote of the SEC, after an extended comment period during which over 14,000 comments were received. The Rules immediately faced a series of legal challenges from all sides, with nine court petitions filed in several federal courts within 10 days, including: (a) a lawsuit filed by 25 Republican state attorneys general arguing that the SEC exceeded its authority in adopting the Rules; (b) an action filed by the Sierra Club claiming that the rules did not go far enough; and (c) a court filing requesting a stay of the Rules led by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

The petitions were subsequently consolidated and assigned by lottery to the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals. In April 2024, the SEC announced that it would pause the implementation of the Rules pending resolution of the legal challenges. The SEC emphasized that this stay did not stay any other existing rules or guidance, including the long-standing Commission Guidance Regarding Disclosure Related to Climate Change, Release Nos. 33-9106; 34-61469 (Feb. 2, 2010) (the “2010 Guidance”).

Following the 2024 election, changes in the makeup of the SEC eliminated virtually all support for the Rules within the SEC, which voted to end its defense of the Rules on [March 27, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025-58).

## **Defense of the Rules**

The SEC initially attempted to avoid the notice-and-comment procedure for rescission by requesting that the court issue a ruling on the legality of the Rules, after the SEC had withdrawn its defense of the Rules in the consolidated litigation before the Eighth Circuit. The court denied the SEC’s request in September 2025 and ordered the SEC to either reconsider the regulation through ordinary rulemaking procedures or to renew its defense of the Rules in court.

On May 7, 2026, the SEC sent a letter to the court, informing the court that the SEC “does not intend to renew its defense of the Rules” and confirming that it had started the process to formally rescind the Rules. In its letter to the court, the SEC stated its rationale for reconsidering the Rules, emphasizing its “concerns that the Rules exceed the Commission’s statutory authority and the costs of the Rules outweigh their benefits.”

The notice-and-comment rulemaking procedure could potentially be a lengthy process (as noted above, initial approval of the Rules took over two years). The procedure involves publishing the proposal along with explanations and legal authority justifying the proposed repeal, as well as holding a public comment period, with agency staff required to consider and respond to significant issues raised in the comments. Final rescission of the Rules is expected to be subject to legal challenge. However, given the already consolidated litigation in the Eighth Circuit, any legal challenges to rescission would likely be expedited.

## **What to Do About** **Climate-Related Disclosures Now**

Companies evaluating whether and how to make disclosures about climate-related issues and greenhouse gas emissions may examine their disclosure obligations, including how to navigate consistency where different requirements apply across different jurisdictions. Under federal securities law, such disclosures remain governed by traditional considerations of financial materiality, and the SEC’s 2010 Guidance remains instructive. However, the evolving European Union framework, including via the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (“CSRD”), incorporates the concept of “double materiality” (i.e., how sustainability issues might create financial risks for the company (financial materiality) and how the company itself impacts people and the environment (impact materiality)). Further complicating the disclosure landscape are state-specific laws that have extraterritorial reach and that apply to both public and private companies, such as California’s SB 200s (SB 253 and SB 261), which currently face their own legal challenges, and New York’s anticipated Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act.

Companies may continue to monitor these developments and work with counsel to assess applicability and develop resilient governance and disclosure practices that hold up in the face of continuing uncertainty and fragmentation of frameworks.
