<webpage_content>
# CSDDD | Updates, Compliance

  

**What is the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)?**

The CSDDD introduces the obligation for companies to conduct appropriate **human rights and environmental due diligence** with respect to their operations, operations of their subsidiaries, and operations of their business partners in companies’ chains of activities.

The due diligence process set out in the CSDDD covers the **six steps** defined by the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Business Conduct:

**(1)** integrating due diligence into policies and management systems,

**(2)** identifying and assessing adverse human rights and environmental impacts,

**(3)** preventing, ceasing or minimising actual and potential adverse human rights, and environmental impacts,

**(4)** assessing the effectiveness of measures,

**(5)** communicating,

**(6)** providing remediation.

---

**June 22, 2026 - Development regarding the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive | Opinion, legal intelligence**

Throughout May and June 2026, discussions increasingly shifted from compliance to competitiveness.

The European institutions justified the amendments as a way to reduce administrative burdens and improve EU competitiveness. The Council repeatedly presented the Omnibus package as a simplification measure intended to reduce reporting and due diligence obligations, and limit burden on smaller firms.

At the same time, sustainability specialists criticized the dilution of due diligence obligations, and argued that fewer companies would now be subject to mandatory human rights and environmental due diligence.

This political debate became one of the dominant themes during May and June. The second dominant theme was the Omnibus amendments on CSDDD provisions requiring companies to adopt and implement  **climate transition plans.**

In Article 22 of the CSDDD we read:

  
   
 ![](Article_22_CSDDD.jpg)   
   

In recital 47 of Directive 2026/470 (also known as the Omnibus I Directive) of 24 February 2026 amending Directives 2006/43/EC, 2013/34/EU, (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards certain corporate sustainability reporting requirements and certain corporate sustainability due diligence requirements, we read:

![](Article_22_CSDDD_2.jpg)   
   

The legal framework continues to exist. The CSDDD was not repealed, but the February 2026 amendments fundamentally changed its practical reach. May and June 2026 was largely the period during which companies, regulators, investors, and advisers were recalibrating their expectations around that new reality. The Omnibus reforms have changed who must comply, when they must comply, and what due diligence will actually be required.

---

**May 14, 2026 - Important 2026 development regarding the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive | Opinion, legal intelligence**

The most important 2026 development regarding the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive is the **substantial political and legislative recalibration** of the existing one through the Omnibus simplification package. The central issue in 2026 is how much of its original ambition will survive the competitiveness driven reform process now underway inside the European Union.

The Omnibus simplification package was formally adopted at EU level after intense political negotiations. The package significantly amends both the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and the CSDDD. The Council of the European Union confirmed in February 2026 that the objective was **explicitly linked to boosting EU competitiveness,** reducing administrative burden, and limiting indirect obligations imposed on smaller entities through supply chains.

Implementation timelines have been materially delayed. One of the most important practical consequences is that the transposition deadline for Member States has effectively been pushed back, and the operational application date for many companies has moved toward 2029. Several analyses note that the earlier staggered implementation structure has been replaced or simplified.

The scope has been narrowed considerably. The political compromise **reduced the number of companies** falling directly within scope by increasing thresholds and limiting trickle down compliance effects on SMEs and smaller suppliers.

The **political climate surrounding ESG regulation** in Europe has changed dramatically. The language of competitiveness, strategic autonomy, simplification, and debureaucratization is now dominating the legislative discussion. Critics argue that the EU is retreating from global sustainability leadership under pressure from economic slowdown, geopolitical fragmentation, and growing divergence with the United States. Supporters of the reforms argue that the original framework created disproportionate compliance costs and threatened European industrial competitiveness.

In practical terms, many multinational groups, especially U.S. based companies with EU exposure, are now reassessing whether the long-term direction of the EU remains toward expansive ESG governance or toward a more selective and economically defensive model.

Another very important 2026 development is the **increasing intersection between sustainability law and AI governance.** Academic and policy discussions are now examining whether the CSDDD, CSRD, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, and emerging cloud and data infrastructure regulation can collectively govern the environmental footprint of AI systems, hyperscale data centers, semiconductor supply chains, and digital infrastructure expansion.

From a risk management perspective, the most important unresolved issue in 2026 is **uncertainty itself.** Companies are struggling with **three variables.** The legal text already adopted, the Omnibus-driven simplification amendments, and the broader political direction of the EU under competitiveness pressure. That combination creates what could fairly be described as **regulatory transition risk,**  a situation where firms must invest in governance systems while the governing architecture itself is still being politically renegotiated.

  

**Legal, risk and compliance experts are increasingly asking:**

**1. Is the Omnibus simplification a temporary recalibration, or the beginning of a structural retreat from expansive ESG regulation?** The answer affects long term governance investments, contractual structures, supplier onboarding procedures, and sustainability assurance programs. The central legal intelligence question is therefore whether the EU intends merely to simplify implementation mechanics or whether it is fundamentally redefining the balance between sustainability obligations and economic competitiveness.

**2. Which is the future interpretation of “appropriate measures” and “best efforts” obligations under the due diligence framework?** Legal teams are attempting to assess how aggressively supervisory authorities and courts may interpret the standard of care. The unresolved issue is whether companies will effectively be judged against a traditional procedural compliance standard or against a quasi substantive expectation to prevent adverse human rights and environmental outcomes. This distinction is enormously important because it determines whether legal exposure is manageable through governance evidence, or whether firms face near open ended liability tied to downstream events outside their direct operational control.

**3. What is next with the civil liability evolution?** Although political compromise efforts have attempted to moderate liability exposure, legal teams remain concerned that creative litigation strategies may emerge through national tort law, consumer protection law, directors’ duties, securities disclosure obligations, unfair competition law, and fiduciary duty challenges. Many legal departments are therefore analyzing whether the practical litigation risk may remain high even if the formal text of the Directive is softened.

This discussion increasingly intersects with U.S.- style litigation dynamics. European legal teams are examining whether activist litigation funds, NGO-supported proceedings, shareholder actions, or collective redress mechanisms may gradually transform ESG due diligence obligations into a new category of strategic litigation risk. The question is whether sustainability governance becomes a permanent source of multidimensional legal exposure.

---

**Did the Donald Trump administration trigger Europe’s CSDDD Delay? | Opinion, legal intelligence**

We must break this question into two separate inquiries that distinguish between direct and indirect influence.

**1. Did the Donald Trump administration directly trigger Europe’s CSDDD delay?**

No. The U.S. government under Donald Trump did not take action, including formal diplomatic intervention, legal threat, or policy demand, that caused the EU institutions to delay the CSDDD. The delay was enacted entirely through internal EU legislative processes, formalized in the EU’s own amending directive, and justified on competitiveness and simplification grounds in EU institutional communications.

**2. Did the Donald Trump administration indirectly influence Europe’s decision to delay the CSDDD?**

While Donald Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025 did not cause the delay, it indirectly influenced the political atmosphere in Europe. His administration openly rejected ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) regulation and signaled a rollback of sustainability policies in the United States. This development strengthened the arguments of EU political factions and industry groups who were already opposed to sustainability legislation, including the CSDDD.

Trump’s policy stance did not change EU law, but it  **reinforced narratives** within Europe such as:

a. Europe risks losing global competitiveness if it overregulates while the U.S. deregulates.

b. EU companies will be disadvantaged against American competitors that have no ESG obligations.

c. We should pause or simplify sustainability regulations until we understand the new U.S. economic strategy.

**Legal causality** examines whether a decision can be attributed to a legally identifiable act or instrument. It requires evidence that shows one actor caused another to act. It is grounded in verifiable documents and institutional records. For the CSDDD delay, there is no legal record anywhere in EU legislative files, Council minutes, Commission communications, or Official Journal publications that attributes the delay to the Donald Trump administration. In legal causality terms, the Trump administration did not directly cause the delay.

**Political causality** deals with influence. It examines how external events, political narratives, or power shifts shape the decisions of governments and institutions, even when those influences are not formally documented in law. Political causation does not require direct evidence of an order or agreement, only a plausible and observable impact on decision-making behavior. For the CSDDD delay, the return of the Trump administration in January 2025 created a political climate in which certain factions inside the EU argued more aggressively for slowing down EU sustainability legislation. Trump’s anti-ESG approach provided political ammunition for these actors. Even if he never asked the EU to delay CSDDD, his policies indirectly strengthened the case of those who wanted a delay.

In early 2025, the Trump administration announced suspension and review of ESG-related SEC rules, particularly those connected to climate disclosures and supply-chain transparency. This rollback was interpreted by EU industry groups as a **strategic deregulatory agenda designed to stimulate domestic business competitiveness.** They claimed that if Europe continued expanding sustainability obligations while the U.S. reversed them, global investors will reallocate capital away from the EU. This argument was used repeatedly in European policy discussions to justify slowing down, or reconsidering, the timing of CSDDD implementation.

  
 ![](WSJ1.jpg)   
   
   
 ![](WSJ2.jpg)   

These are important developments. The EU exports rules through market access regulation, while the U.S. responds through trade policy leverage. The CSDDD debate is a case study in regulatory geopolitics.

The European Union exercises what scholars frequently call the “Brussels Effect.” Under this model, the EU conditions access to the EU internal market on compliance with EU regulatory standards, even where the regulated entities are established outside the Union.

The CSDDD extends obligations to non-EU companies that generate substantial turnover within the Union. Such entities are required to conduct human rights and environmental due diligence across their global supply chains as a condition for operating within the EU market.

The United States responds to foreign regulatory measures primarily through trade policy mechanisms. The relevant instruments typically include trade negotiations, tariff and non-tariff countermeasures, trade investigations under domestic statutes, and dispute settlement proceedings within the World Trade Organization framework.

U.S. policymakers argue that regulatory regimes with extraterritorial effects, such as supply-chain due diligence requirements, constitute non-tariff barriers to trade or measures inconsistent with obligations under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.

Under the current political environment, particularly during the second administration of Donald Trump, the United States is far less likely to rely on the dispute settlement mechanisms of the World Trade Organization. This represents a significant departure from earlier U.S. trade strategy.

**DISCLAIMER:**  The analysis presented here is provided for informational and educational purposes only. It does not express support for, or opposition to, any government, regulatory authority, political position, or policy approach. The objective is to assist risk, compliance, legal, and governance professionals in understanding evolving regulatory, legal, and geopolitical developments that may affect their professional responsibilities.

This content is intended to facilitate informed decision making by highlighting structural trends, regulatory interactions, and potential areas of operational impact. It does not constitute legal advice, policy advocacy, or an endorsement of any particular regulatory framework or political position. The perspectives discussed reflect an analytical assessment of publicly available information, and should be interpreted in the context of risk awareness, compliance preparedness, and strategic foresight only.

---

**24 February 2026 - DIRECTIVE (EU) 2026/470 amending Directives 2006/43/EC, 2013/34/EU, (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards certain corporate sustainability reporting requirements and certain corporate sustainability due diligence requirements.**

In its communication of 11 February 2025 entitled ‘A simpler and faster Europe: Communication on implementation and simplification’, the Commission set out a vision for an implementation and simplification agenda that delivers fast and visible improvements for people and business on the ground. That requires more than an incremental approach, and it is necessary for the Union to take bold action to achieve that goal. The Commission, the European Parliament, the Council, Member States’ authorities at all levels and stakeholders need to work together to streamline and simplify Union, national and regional rules and implement policies more effectively.

[DIRECTIVE (EU) 2026/470 of 24 February 2026, amending Directives 2006/43/EC, 2013/34/EU, (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards certain corporate sustainability reporting requirements and certain corporate sustainability due diligence requirements.](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202600470&utm)

---

**Strategic interpretation of DIRECTIVE (EU) 2026/470 for risk and compliance professionals - Opinion, legal intelligence**

DIRECTIVE (EU) 2026/470e signals a shift.

Phase 1, regulatory expansion (2020–2024).

Phase 2, competitiveness recalibration (2025–2026). EU adjusts rules to reduce costs, maintain global competitiveness, and respond to geopolitical and trade pressures.

---

**Council signs off simplification of sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements.**

The CS3D’s scope is narrowed by raising its thresholds to companies with more than 5,000 employees and above €1.5 billion net turnover, considering that such large companies have the biggest influence on their value chain and are best equipped to make a positive impact and absorb the costs and burdens of due diligence processes.

On the identification and assessment of adverse impacts, companies can focus on the areas of their chains of activities where actual and potential adverse impacts are most likely to occur. To provide companies with flexibility, when a company has identified adverse impacts equally likely or equally severe in several areas, this company is given the ability to prioritise assessing adverse impacts which involve direct business partners. Companies are also supposed to base their efforts on reasonably available information, which will reduce the trickle-down effect of information requests on smaller business partners.

To provide for a significant burden relief, the obligation for companies to adopt a transition plan for climate change mitigation under the CS3D has been removed.

The updated rules also remove the EU harmonised liability regime and the requirement for member states to ensure that the liability rules are of overriding mandatory application in cases where the applicable law is not the national law of the member state.

When it comes to penalties, businesses will be liable at a national level for failure to apply the rules correctly. The new directive provides for a maximum cap of 3% of the company’s net worldwide turnover, with the Commission issuing the necessary guidelines in this regard.

Finally, the amending directive postpones the CS3D’s transposition deadline by member states into national law by another year, to 26 July 2028. Companies will have to comply with the new measures by July 2029.

[24 February 2026 - Council signs off simplification of sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements.](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/02/24/council-signs-off-simplification-of-sustainability-reporting-and-due-diligence-requirements-to-boost-eu-competitiveness/)

---

**9 December 2025 - Council and Parliament strike a deal to simplify sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements.**

The Council’s presidency and European Parliament’s negotiators reached a provisional agreement to simplify sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements to boost EU competitiveness. The agreement simplifies the directives on corporate sustainability reporting (CSRD) and corporate sustainability due diligence (CS3D) by reducing the reporting burden and limiting the trickle-down effect of obligations on smaller companies.

While the CS3D’s scope was not covered by the Commission’s proposal, the provisional agreement increases the thresholds to 5,000 employees and €1.5 billion net turnover. The co-legislators considered that such large companies have the biggest influence on their value chain and are best equipped to make a positive impact and absorb the costs and burdens of due diligence processes.

**NEXT STEP:** The provisional agreement must be now endorsed by the Council and the European Parliament. before it is formally adopted by the two institutions.

[9 December 2025 - Council and Parliament strike a deal to simplify sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2025/12/09/council-and-parliament-strike-a-deal-to-simplify-sustainability-reporting-and-due-diligence-requirements-and-boost-eu-competitiveness/)

---

**16 April 2025 - Directive (EU) 2025/794 was published in the Official Journal of the European Union, implementation timelines changed for the CSDDD.**

The official name: Directive (EU) 2025/794 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 April 2025 amending Directives (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards the dates from which Member States are to apply certain corporate sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements.

**Article 2, Amendment to Directive (EU) 2024/1760 (Note: The CSDDD)**

In Article 37(1) of Directive (EU) 2024/1760, the first and second subparagraphs are **replaced** by the following:

‘1. Member States shall adopt and publish, **by 26 July 2027,** the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive. They shall forthwith communicate the text of those measures to the Commission.

They shall apply those measures:

(a) **from 26 July 2028** as regards companies referred to in Article 2(1), points (a) and (b), which are formed in accordance with the legislation of the Member State and that had more than 3 000 employees on average and generated a net worldwide turnover of more than EUR 900 000 000 in the last financial year preceding 26 July 2028 for which annual financial statements have been or should have been adopted, with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies **for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2029;**

(b) **from 26 July 2028** as regards companies referred to in Article 2(2), points (a) and (b), which are formed in accordance with the legislation of a third country and that generated a net turnover of more than EUR 900 000 000 in the Union, in the financial year preceding the last financial year preceding 26 July 2028, with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies **for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2029;**

(c) **from 26 July 2029** as regards all other companies referred to in Article 2(1), points (a) and (b), and Article 2(2), points (a) and (b), and companies referred to in Article 2(1), point (c), and Article 2(2), point (c), with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies **for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2030.’.**

[16 April 2025 - Directive (EU) 2025/794 was published in the Official Journal of the European Union, implementation timelines changed for the CSDDD.](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202500794)

---

**3 April 2025 - European Parliament, Amending Directives (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards the dates from which Member States are to apply certain corporate sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements**

In the context of the Commission’s commitment to **reducing reporting burdens and to enhancing competitiveness,** it is necessary to introduce targeted amendments to Directive (EU) 2024/1760 in order to achieve those objectives.

The date from which Member States are to apply Directive (EU) 2024/1760 **should be postponed** by one year for the first set of companies that fall within the scope of that Directive in order to give companies more time to prepare for the requirements of that Directive and to provide them with the opportunity to take into account the guidelines to be issued by the Commission on how they should fulfil their due diligence obligations in a practical manner.

Furthermore, the application date of 1 January 2029 for the measures necessary to comply with the reporting obligation pursuant to Article 16 of Directive (EU) 2024/1760 regarding the third set of companies that fall within the scope of that Directive **should be amended** in order to ensure coherence with the respective application dates for the other sets of companies.

Moreover, in the light of a parallel legislative proposal which aims to simplify the sustainability framework and reduce the burden on companies, the deadline for the Member States to transpose Directive (EU) 2024/1760 should be **extended by one year** in order to take into account possible delays in their ongoing transposition efforts due to possible amendments to that Directive.

[3 April 2025 - European Parliament, Amending Directives (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards the dates from which Member States are to apply certain corporate sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-10-2025-0064_EN.html)

---

**26.2.2025 - Proposal for a DIRECTIVE amending Directives 2006/43/EC, 2013/34/EU, (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards certain corporate sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements**

Article 4 amends Directive (EU) 2024/1760 (Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive ‘CSDDD’).

[26.2.2025 - Proposal for a DIRECTIVE amending Directives 2006/43/EC, 2013/34/EU, (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards certain corporate sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements](https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/1d14a487-f042-476f-997f-adf7c3e14950_en?filename=CSDDD%20Omnibus%20proposal.pdf)

---

**26.2.2025 - Proposal for a DIRECTIVE amending Directives (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards the dates from which Member States are to apply certain corporate sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements**

In its Communication of 11 February 2025 entitled **‘A simpler and faster Europe: Communication on implementation and simplification’,** the Commission set out a vision for an implementation and simplification agenda that delivers fast and visible improvements for people and business on the ground. That requires more than an incremental approach and the Union is to take bold action to achieve that goal. The Commission, the European Parliament, the Council, Member States’ authorities at all levels and stakeholders need to work together to **streamline and simplify** Union, national and regional rules and implement policies more effectively.

In Article 37(1) of Directive (EU) 2024/1760, the first and second subparagraphs are **replaced by the following:** ‘Member States shall adopt and publish, by **26 July 2027,** the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive. They shall forthwith communicate the text of those measures to the Commission.

They shall apply those measures:

(a) **from 26 July 2028** as regards companies referred to in Article 2(1), points (a) and (b), which are formed in accordance with the legislation of the Member State and that had more than 3 000 employees on average and generated a net worldwide turnover of more than EUR 900 000 000 in the last financial year preceding 26 July 2028 for which annual financial statements have been or should have been adopted, with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2029;

(b) **from 26 July 2028** as regards companies referred to in Article 2(2), points (a) and (b), which are formed in accordance with the legislation of a third country and that generated a net turnover of more than EUR 900 000 000 in the Union, in the financial year preceding the last financial year preceding 26 July 2028, with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2029;

(c) **from 26 July 2029** as regards all other companies referred to in Article 2(1), points (a) and (b), and Article 2(2), points (a) and (b), and companies referred to in Article 2(1), point (c), and Article 2(2), point (c), with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2030.’.

[26.2.2025 - Proposal for a DIRECTIVE amending Directives (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards the dates from which Member States are to apply certain corporate sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements](https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/71ca40f4-7929-42fc-922c-8a0073b0660f_en?filename=CSDDD%20Omnibus%20proposal_0.pdf)

---

**July 29, 2024 - European Commission, Frequently Asked Questions about the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)**

**1.1. What is the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive?**

• The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (the Directive) sets out a corporate due diligence duty for large companies to identify and address adverse human rights impacts (such as child labour) and environmental impacts (such as pollution) in their own operations, those of their subsidiaries and in their “chain(s) of activities”.

• In addition, the Directive sets out an obligation for large companies to adopt and put into effect a transition plan for climate change mitigation which aims to ensure, through best efforts, that the business model and strategy of the company are compatible with the transition to a sustainable economy and with the limiting of global warming to 1,5° C in line with the Paris Agreement and the objective of achieving climate neutrality as established in Regulation (EU) 2021/1119, including its intermediate and 2050 climate neutrality targets.

  

**1.2. What are the basic due diligence duties for companies?**

The core due diligence duties for companies in the scope of the Directive include the following actions:

• Integrating due diligence into the corporate policies and risk management systems.

• Identifying adverse human rights and environmental impacts in the company’s operations as well as those of its subsidiaries and of its business partners in the chain of activities; and prioritising them according to their severity and likelihood.

• Addressing negative impacts that have been, or should have been, identified, where necessary in the order of prioritisation. Companies have to prevent and/or mitigate potential impacts and, when negative impacts have already occurred, bring them to an end or, if not immediately possible, at least minimize their extent. Companies also have to provide remedies if they caused the adverse impact or contributed to it through acts or omissions.

• As a measure of “last resort” when all other actions have failed, and where severe impacts are at stake and only where these impacts outweigh the foreseeable negative consequences of disengagement, companies are required to suspend or terminate a business relationship.

**Companies are also required to:**

• engage with stakeholders, i.e. consult them at certain stages of the due diligence process (in particular during the identification of impacts), based on meaningful information (i.e. of sufficient quality and level of detail to allow them to fully participate) provided to stakeholders; companies may do so through industry or multi-stakeholder initiatives (except for the consultation of their own employees and their representatives);

• establish and maintain a complaints and notification procedure;

• monitor the effectiveness of due diligence measures;

• communicate publicly on due diligence according to the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (with some exceptions).

  

[July 29, 2024 - European Commission, Frequently Asked Questions about the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)](https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/7a3e9980-5fda-4760-8f25-bc5571806033_en?filename=240719_CSDD_FAQ_final.pdf)

---

**July 5, 2024 - The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) was published in the Official Journal of the European Union**

According to Article 37 (Transposition), Member States shall adopt and publish, by 26 July 2026, the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive. They shall apply those measures:

**(a) from 26 July 2027** as regards companies referred to in Article 2(1), points (a) and (b), which are formed in accordance with the legislation of the Member State and that had **more than 5 000 employees on average and generated a net worldwide turnover of more than EUR 1 500 000 000** in the last financial year preceding 26 July 2027 for which annual financial statements have been or should have been adopted, with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2028;

**(b) from 26 July 2028** as regards companies referred to in Article 2(1), points (a) and (b), which are formed in accordance with the legislation of the Member State and that had **more than 3 000 employees on average and generated a net worldwide turnover of more than EUR 900 000 000** in the last financial year preceding 26 July 2028 for which annual financial statements have been or should have been adopted, with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2029;

**(c) from 26 July 2027** as regards companies referred to in Article 2(2), points (a) and (b), which are formed in accordance with the legislation of a **third country** and that generated a net turnover of **more than EUR 1 500 000 000 in the Union,** in the financial year preceding the last financial year preceding 26 July 2027, with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2028;

**(d) from 26 July 2028** as regards companies referred to in Article 2(2), points (a) and (b), which are formed in accordance with the legislation of a third country and that generated a net turnover of **more than EUR 900 000 000 in the Union,** in the financial year preceding the last financial year preceding 26 July 2028, with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2029;

**(e) from 26 July 2029** as regards all other companies referred to in Article 2(1), points (a) and (b), and Article 2(2), points (a) and (b), and companies referred to in Article 2(1), point (c), and Article 2(2), point (c), with the exception of the measures necessary to comply with Article 16, which Member States shall apply to those companies for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2029.

  

**In order to understand the deadlines, we need Article 2 of the CSDDD**

**Article 2, Scope.**

1. This Directive shall apply to companies which are formed in accordance with the legislation of a Member State and which fulfil one of the following conditions:

  

(a) the company had **more than 1 000 employees on average and had a net worldwide turnover of more than EUR 450 000 000** in the last financial year for which annual financial statements have been or should have been adopted;

  

(b) the company did not reach the thresholds as referred to in point (a) but is **the ultimate parent company** of a group that reached those thresholds in the last financial year for which consolidated annual financial statements have been or should have been adopted;

  

(c) the company entered into or is the ultimate parent company of a group that entered into **franchising or licensing agreements in the Union** in return for royalties with independent third-party companies, where those agreements ensure a common identity, a common business concept and the application of uniform business methods, and where those **royalties amounted to more than EUR 22 500 000 in the last financial year** for which annual financial statements have been or should have been adopted, and provided that the company had or is the ultimate parent company of a group that had a **net worldwide turnover of more than EUR 80 000 000 in the last financial year** for which annual financial statements have been or should have been adopted.

  

2. This Directive shall also apply to companies which are formed in accordance with the legislation of a **third country** and fulfil one of the following conditions:

  

(a) the company generated a **net turnover of more than EUR 450 000 000 in the Union** in the financial year preceding the last financial year;

  

(b) the company did not reach the threshold as referred to in point (a) but is the **ultimate parent company** of a group that on a consolidated basis reached that threshold in the financial year preceding the last financial year;

  

(c) the company entered into or is the ultimate parent company of a group that entered into **franchising or licensing agreements in the Union** in return for royalties with independent third-party companies, where those agreements ensure a common identity, a common business concept and the application of uniform business methods, and where those royalties amounted to **more than EUR 22 500 000 in the Union** in the financial year preceding the last financial year; and provided that the company generated, or is the ultimate parent company of a group that generated, a **net turnover of more than EUR 80 000 000 in the Union** in the financial year preceding the last financial year.

  

3. Where the **ultimate parent** company has as its main activity the holding of shares in operational subsidiaries and does not engage in taking management, operational or financial decisions affecting the group or one or more of its subsidiaries, it may be exempted from carrying out the obligations under this Directive. That exemption is subject to the condition that one of the ultimate parent company’s subsidiaries established in the Union is designated to fulfil the obligations set out in Articles 6 to 16 and Article 22 on behalf of the ultimate parent company, including the obligations of the ultimate parent company with respect to the activities of its subsidiaries. In such a case, the designated subsidiary is given all the necessary means and legal authority to fulfil those obligations in an effective manner, in particular to ensure that the designated subsidiary obtains from the companies of the group the relevant information and documents to fulfil the obligations of the ultimate parent company under this Directive.

  

The **ultimate parent** company shall apply for the exemption referred to in the first subparagraph of this paragraph to the competent supervisory authority, in accordance with Article 24, to assess whether the conditions referred to in the first subparagraph of this paragraph are met. Where the conditions are met, the competent supervisory authority shall grant the exemption. Where applicable, such authority shall duly inform the competent supervisory authority of the Member State where the designated subsidiary is established of the application and then of its decision.

  

The **ultimate parent** company shall remain jointly liable with the designated subsidiary for a failure of the latter to comply with its obligations in accordance with the first subparagraph of this paragraph.

  

4. For the purposes of paragraph 1, the number of **part-time employees** shall be calculated on a full-time equivalent basis. Temporary agency workers and other workers in non-standard forms of employment, provided that they fulfil the criteria for determining the status of worker as established by the Court of Justice of the European Union, shall be included in the calculation of the number of employees in the same way as if they were workers employed directly for the same period of time by the company.

  

5. Where a company meets the conditions laid down in paragraph 1 or 2, this Directive shall only apply if those conditions are met in **two consecutive financial years.** This Directive shall no longer apply to a company referred to in paragraph 1 or 2 where the conditions laid down in paragraph 1 or 2 cease to be met for each of the last two relevant financial years.

  

6. As regards the companies referred to in paragraph 1, the Member State competent to regulate matters covered by this Directive shall be the Member State in which the company has its registered office.

  

7. As regards a company as referred to in paragraph 2, the Member State competent to regulate matters covered by this Directive shall be the Member State in which that company has a branch. If a company does not have a branch in any Member State, or has branches located in different Member States, the Member State competent to regulate matters covered by this Directive shall be that in which that company generated the highest net turnover in the Union in the financial year preceding the last financial year.

  

8. This Directive shall not apply to AIFs, as defined in Article 4(1), point (a), of Directive 2011/61/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council or to undertakings for collective investment in transferable securities (UCITS) within the meaning of Article 1(2) of Directive 2009/65/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council.

  
 

---

**Understanding the due diligence obligation in the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)**

The due diligence **policy** should contain a description of the company’s approach, including in the long term, to due diligence, a code of conduct describing the rules and principles to be followed by the company’s employees and subsidiaries, and, where relevant, the company’s direct or indirect business partners, and a description of the processes put in place to implement due diligence, including the measures taken to verify compliance with the code of conduct and to extend its application to business partners.

The **code of conduct** should apply in all relevant corporate functions and operations, including procurement and purchasing decisions.

Companies should also update their due diligence policy without undue delay after a **significant change** occurs, but at least every 24 months. A significant change should be understood as such a change to the status quo of the company’s own operations, the operations of its subsidiaries or business partners, the legal or business environment or any other substantial shift from the situation of the company that the company could be reasonably expected to react to it and update the policy.

**Examples** of a significant change could be the cases when the company operates in a new economic sector or geographical area, starts producing new products or changes the way of producing the existing products using technology with potentially higher adverse impacts, or changes its corporate structure via restructuring or mergers or acquisitions.

Incorporating due diligence into **risk management systems** must be understood in line with the relevant international framework to ensure that the due diligence obligations are put in place and being overseen. In order to fulfil this obligation, companies should be allowed to internally organise according to their needs, for example by using existing management systems, setting up a risk management system of the company or creating a human rights and environment officer.

---

**24 May 2024 - The Council of the European Union gave the final approval to the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)**

The CSDDD introduces a  **new corporate due diligence obligation**  for businesses operating in the EU. The new due diligence obligations apply to the companies,  **their subsidiaries, and the supply chain.**  Companies are liable for the actions of their suppliers.

**The orignal CSDDD impacted companies with 500 employees and a turnover of €150 million. The final CSDDD, after long and difficult negotiations that nearly resulted in the failure of the directive, impacts companies with 1000 employees and a turnover of €450 million.**

  

**Next step**

The Directive will enter into force 20 days after its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. Member States will have two years to transpose the Directive into national law and communicate the relevant texts to the Commission. One year later, the rules will start to apply to companies, with a gradual phase-in between 3 and 5 years after entry into force.

A set of guidelines to be issued by the Commission will help companies to conduct due diligence.

  

**Which companies are affected?**

1. Large EU limited liability companies and partnerships with at least 1000 employees and at least EUR 450 million turnover (net) worldwide. These are about 6,000 companies.

2. Large non–EU companies that have EUR 450 million turnover (net) in the EU. These are about 900 companies.

  

**Businesses will have to bear costs:**

1. The costs of establishing and operating the due diligence process.

2. Transition costs, including expenditure and investments to adapt a company’s own operations and value chains to comply with the due diligence obligation, if needed.

  

**How will the new rules be enforced?**

The rules on corporate sustainability due diligence will be enforced through:

1. **Administrative supervision:** Member States will designate an authority to supervise and enforce the rules, including through injunctive orders and effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties (in particular fines). At European level, the Commission will set up a European Network of Supervisory Authorities that will bring together representatives of the national bodies to ensure a coordinated approach.

2. **Civil liability:** Member States will ensure that victims get compensation for damages resulting from an intentional or negligent failure to carry out due diligence.

---

**24 April 2024 - The European Parliament approved the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)**

The European Parliament approved with 374 votes (against 235 and 19 abstentions) the CSDDD, agreed on with the Council, requiring firms and their upstream and downstream partners, including supply, production and distribution to prevent, end or mitigate their adverse impact on human rights and the environment. Such impact will include slavery, child labour, labour exploitation, biodiversity loss, pollution or destruction of natural heritage.

The rules will apply to EU companies and parent companies with over 1000 employees and a worldwide turnover higher than 450 million euro. **It will also apply to companies with franchising or licensing agreements** in the EU ensuring a common corporate identity with worldwide turnover higher than 80 million euro if at least 22.5 million euro was generated by royalties.

**Non-EU companies,** parent companies and companies with franchising or licensing agreements in the EU reaching the same turnover thresholds in the EU will also be covered. These firms will have to integrate due diligence into their policies, make related investments, seek contractual assurances from their partners, improve their business plan or provide support to small and medium-sized business partners to ensure they comply with new obligations. Companies will **also have to adopt a transition plan to make their business model compatible with the Paris Agreement global warming limit of 1.5°C.**

**Fines and compensation of victims** - Member states will be required to provide companies with detailed online information on their due diligence obligations via practical portals containing the Commission’s guidance. They will also create or designate a supervisory authority to investigate and impose penalties on non-complying firms.

These will include  **“naming and shaming” and fines of up to 5% of companies’ net worldwide turnover.**  The Commission will establish the European Network of Supervisory Authorities to support cooperation and enable exchange of best practices. Companies will be liable for damages caused by breaching their due diligence obligations and will have to fully compensate their victims.

**Next steps**

The directive now also needs to be formally endorsed by the Council, signed and published in the EU Official Journal. It will enter into force twenty days later. Member states will have two years to transpose the new rules into their national laws.

The new rules (except for the communication obligations) will apply gradually to EU companies (and non-EU companies reaching the same turnover thresholds in the EU):

From 2027 to companies with over 5000 employees and worldwide turnover higher than 1500 million euro;

From 2028 to firms with over 3000 employees and a 900 million euro worldwide turnover;

From 2029 to all the remaining companies within the scope of the directive (including those over 1000 employees and worldwide turnover higher than 450 million euro).

---

**14 December 2023 - We have a deal between the Council and the Parliament.**

The Council and the European Parliament reached a provisional deal on the corporate sustainability due diligence directive (CSDDD), which aims to enhance the protection of the environment and human rights in the EU and globally.

The due diligence directive will set obligations for large companies regarding actual and potential adverse impacts on human rights and the environment, with respect to their own operations, those of their subsidiaries, and those carried out by their business partners.

**The compromise strengthens the provisions** related to the obligation of means for large companies to adopt and put into effect, through best efforts, a transition plan for climate change mitigation.

args.summary:
The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD/CS3D), enacted as Directive (EU) 2024/1760, requires large companies to conduct human rights and environmental due diligence across their operations, subsidiaries, and chains of activities, following the six-step OECD Due Diligence Guidance framework (integrating due diligence into policies; identifying/assessing adverse impacts; preventing/ceasing/minimizing impacts; assessing effectiveness; communicating; providing remediation).

**Legislative History & Timeline:**
- **April 2024:** European Parliament approved CSDDD (374 votes for, 235 against). Original scope covered companies with 1,000+ employees and €450M+ worldwide turnover (EU companies) and non-EU companies with €450M+ EU turnover, plus franchising/licensing entities. Fines up to 5% of net worldwide turnover and civil liability provisions were included.
- **May 2024:** Council gave final approval. Thresholds adjusted from the earlier 500-employee/€150M proposal to 1,000 employees/€450M due to difficult negotiations.
- **July 5, 2024:** Published in Official Journal. Original phased implementation: companies with 5,000+ employees/€1.5B turnover from July 2027; 3,000+ employees/€900M from July 2028; remaining companies from July 2029.

**Key 2025-2026 Amendments (Omnibus Simplification Package):**
- **April 2025 (Directive (EU) 2025/794):** Postponed implementation timelines by one year—transposition extended to July 26, 2027; first-wave application (3,000+ employees/€900M) moved to July 26, 2028; remaining companies to July 26, 2029. Non-EU companies with €900M+ EU turnover also applied from 2028.
- **December 9, 2025:** Council and Parliament struck provisional agreement further simplifying CSRD and CSDDD, raising thresholds to 5,000 employees and €1.5B net turnover.
- **February 24, 2026 (Directive (EU) 2026/470, "Omnibus I"):** Formally adopted. Key changes include: scope narrowed to companies with 5,000+ employees and €1.5B+ turnover; companies may focus due diligence on areas where adverse impacts are most likely and prioritize direct business partners; obligation to adopt climate transition plans (Article 22) removed; EU harmonized civil liability regime removed; penalties capped at 3% of net worldwide turnover (down from 5%); transposition deadline postponed to July 26, 2028; companies must comply by July 2029.

**2026 Political Context:**
- May–June 2026 debates shifted from compliance to competitiveness, with the Council presenting Omnibus as a simplification measure while sustainability specialists criticized the dilution of due diligence obligations.
- The CSDDD was not repealed but significantly recalibrated—reducing the number of companies in scope and limiting trickle-down effects on SMEs.
- The Trump administration did not directly cause the delay (no legal causation exists in EU legislative records), but indirectly influenced the political climate by reinforcing anti-ESG narratives and competitive concerns, strengthening the case of EU factions opposing sustainability legislation.
- Unresolved legal questions include: whether Omnibus is temporary recalibration or structural retreat from ESG regulation; interpretation of "appropriate measures" and "best efforts" standards; and civil liability evolution through national tort law, consumer protection, directors' duties, and strategic litigation risks.

**Due Diligence Obligations (Core Duties):** Companies must integrate due diligence into corporate policies and risk management, identify and prioritize adverse impacts, prevent/mitigate/minimize negative impacts, provide remedies, suspend/terminate business relationships as a last resort for severe impacts, engage with stakeholders, establish complaints procedures, and communicate publicly per CSRD/ESRS. The CSDDD also historically required a climate transition plan aligned with the 1.5°C Paris Agreement target and EU climate neutrality objectives.

<webpage_content>
White Paper

# What is the CSRD? Requirements, Scope, and Timeline Explained

The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) is a European Union regulation that requires large companies to disclose standardized, externally audited sustainability information alongside their financial reports. This guide covers what companies are in scope under the updated Omnibus thresholds, what must be reported under the ESRS, how disclosures must be structured, and the current filing timeline.

![image of corporate buildings from a top-down view](/sites/workiva/files/styles/rectangle_720x500/public/csrd-hero-image-en.png.webp)

## What is the CSRD?

The CSRD entered into force on January 5, 2023 and represents the most comprehensive sustainability disclosure mandate the EU has enacted to date. Unlike voluntary frameworks, the CSRD legally requires companies in scope to integrate sustainability disclosures into their annual or management reports, have those disclosures independently verified, and apply digital tagging to make data machine-readable. The directive is implemented through the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), developed by EFRAG, which specify what companies must report and how.

Companies in scope must bring finance, sustainability, audit, and risk teams together in new ways. Financial and sustainability disclosures are no longer separate deliverables. The CSRD requires them to be integrated, cross-referenced, and jointly assured. For many organizations, this means rethinking how data flows between departments, not just what gets reported.

![image of a globe with an image of water](/sites/workiva/files/styles/16_9_1700x956/public/images/resources/intro-csrd-tl-img-new-requirements-en_4.png.webp)

### CSRD requirements

CSRD reporting requirements cover five core obligations for companies in scope:

* **Integration**: Sustainability disclosures must appear within the annual or management report, not as a separate standalone document.
* **ESRS alignment**: Disclosures must follow the ESRS, which cover environmental, social, and governance topics. The simplified ESRS (2026) apply from financial year 2027.
* **Double materiality assessment**: Companies must assess both how sustainability issues affect the company financially and how the company affects the environment and society. This determines which ESRS topics are relevant to disclose.
* **External assurance**: All sustainability disclosures must be independently verified before publication. This is a new requirement with no equivalent in the previous Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD).
* **Digital tagging**: Reported data must be digitally tagged using iXBRLTM tagging to enable machine-readable access to the information.

![image of people walking around from an above view](/sites/workiva/files/styles/16_9_1700x956/public/images/value-props/intro-csrd-tl-img-scope-of-csrd-en.png.webp)

### CSRD scope

The Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470, in force from 18 March 2026, significantly revised CSRD scope. The new thresholds apply from financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027. Under the updated rules:

* **EU companies** must report if they exceed **both** 1,000 employees on average **and** €450 million in net annual turnover (at entity or consolidated level). The previous two-out-of-three criteria test has been replaced by this dual threshold.
* **Non-EU parent companies** must report if they generate net turnover exceeding €450 million in the EU for each of the last two consecutive financial years and have an EU subsidiary or branch that generates more than €200 million in net turnover.

These thresholds narrow the original CSRD scope. The regulation is estimated to cover approximately 90% fewer companies than originally projected, concentrating mandatory reporting on the largest enterprises. Companies that were already reporting under the original NFRD (Wave 1) continue to report under applicable requirements for financial years 2025 and 2026. Member states may grant exemptions to Wave 1 companies that fall below the new Omnibus thresholds for those financial years.

![image of government building with hand drawn icon](/sites/workiva/files/styles/16_9_1700x956/public/images/value-props/intro-csrd-tl-img-CSRD-MANDATED-BY-en.png.webp)

### CSRD timeline

The CSRD was first proposed in 2021 and entered into force on January 5, 2023. The Omnibus I Directive, in force from 18 March 2026, restructured the timeline. The current confirmed schedule is:

* **Wave 1—FY2024 and FY2025 (reporting in 2025 and 2026)**: Companies already within the original NFRD scope continue to report. Wave 1 companies that fall below the new Omnibus thresholds may be exempt for FY2025 and FY2026 if their member state grants an exemption.
* **Wave 2—FY2027 (reporting in 2028)**: EU companies exceeding both 1,000 employees and €450 million net annual turnover that were not already reporting under the NFRD. These companies will apply the simplified ESRS (2026), which the European Commission adopted on 3 July 2026.
* **Wave 3—FY2028 (reporting in 2029)**: Non-EU parent companies meeting the revised Article 40a thresholds (€450 million EU net turnover; qualifying subsidiary or branch exceeding €200 million).

The simplified ESRS (2026), finalized by the European Commission on July 3, 2026, reduce mandatory reporting data points by more than 60% compared to the original ESRS adopted in 2023. They apply to financial years beginning on or after January 1, 2027. Early voluntary adoption for FY2026 is permitted.

## CSRD fundamentals

Following the Omnibus I revisions, the CSRD applies to a significantly smaller population of companies than originally intended. From financial year 2027, mandatory reporting covers large EU companies exceeding both 1,000 employees and €450 million in net annual turnover, and non-EU parent companies with more than €450 million in EU net turnover paired with a qualifying subsidiary or branch exceeding €200 million. Companies within the original NFRD scope (Wave 1) continue to report during the transition period. See the Scope section above for the complete threshold breakdown.

The [European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS)](/blog/csrd-what-are-european-sustainability-reporting-standards-esrs "CSRD: What are the final European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS)? ") are the technical standards that specify what companies must disclose under the CSRD and how those disclosures should be structured. They are developed by EFRAG and adopted by the European Commission as delegated acts. The original ESRS—adopted in July 2023—covered 12 standards:

* **General**: ESRS 1 (General requirements), ESRS 2 (General disclosures)
* **Environmental**: E1 – Climate Change, E2 – Pollution, E3 – Water and Marine Resources, E4 – Biodiversity and Ecosystems, E5 – Resource Use and Circular Economy
* **Social**: S1 – Own Workforce, S2 – Workers in the value chain, S3 – Affected communities, S4 – Consumers and end users
* **Governance**: G1 – Business Conduct

On July 3, 2026, the European Commission adopted the simplified ESRS (2026), a revised set of standards that reduce mandatory data points by more than 60% and apply from financial year 2027. The simplified ESRS maintain the 12-topic structure but provide additional materiality flexibility and clarify how companies identify which disclosures are relevant to their operations. Early voluntary adoption for FY2026 is permitted. ESRS 1 sets out the principles that underpin all [sustainability reporting](/resources/what-is-sustainability-reporting "What is Sustainability Reporting? A Complete Guide") under the framework. ESRS 2 specifies the general disclosures every in-scope company must provide regardless of its materiality assessment. For all other standards, companies must conduct a double materiality assessment to determine which topics and metrics are relevant to disclose.

The CSRD establishes a shared framework for non-financial reporting and integration of financial and sustainability disclosures. Policymakers, investors, clients, and consumers increasingly recognize that sustainability, finance, and risk information are inherently linked. Standardized, audited reports give stakeholders a consistent basis for evaluating a company's [ESG metrics](/resources/what-is-esg-environmental-social-governance "What is ESG?") alongside its financial performance and risk resilience.

The EU has long held that investors and consumers are entitled to understand the ESG impact of businesses in a clear, easily comparable way. The NFRD provided an early step in this direction, but it lacked the scope, standardization, and assurance requirements to make disclosures reliably comparable. Investors found that many [ESG reports](/resources/esg-reporting-101-what-you-need-know "ESG Reporting 101: What It Is, Why It Matters, and How to Get Started") omitted important information, used differing metrics, and had different areas of focus—making it difficult to trust the data or benchmark companies against one another.

That inconsistency created friction for sustainable investment, one of the EU's stated policy priorities. The CSRD addresses this by mandating a single framework with audited outputs, making ESG disclosures as comparable and verifiable as financial statements.

Under the CSRD, companies must disclose material information across five topic areas: the environment, their treatment of staff and approach to social matters, human rights, anti-bribery and anti-corruption, and board diversity. More broadly, the CSRD aims to present sustainability information in a way that connects directly to business activities and financial performance. Disclosures must cover:

* The environment
* Treatment of staff and approach to social matters
* Human rights
* Anti-bribery and anti-corruption
* Board diversity

Which specific disclosures are required within each topic depends on a company’s double materiality assessment. Not every company will report on every ESRS topic. The framework is designed to focus reporting on the issues that are most material to each organization’s specific context and value chain.

The CSRD replaces the NFRD, which governed non-financial reporting in the EU before 2023. The shift from NFRD to CSRD is significant across four dimensions:

1. **Scope**: The NFRD covered approximately 11,700 large public-interest entities with more than 500 employees. The CSRD, even after the Omnibus revisions, applies to a larger population of companies, including large private companies and non-EU parent companies that previously had no NFRD obligations.
2. **Standardization**: The NFRD did not prescribe a specific reporting standard. Companies could choose from GRI, TCFD, or other voluntary frameworks. The CSRD mandates the ESRS, creating a single comparable standard across all companies in scope.
3. **Assurance**: The NFRD had no mandatory external audit requirement. Under the CSRD, all sustainability disclosures must be independently assured, the same verification requirement that applies to financial statements.
4. **Integration**: The NFRD allowed sustainability information to be published separately. The CSRD requires it to sit within the annual or management report, integrated with and cross-referenced to financial information.

Companies that reported under the NFRD should not assume their existing processes are sufficient for CSRD compliance. The ESRS require significantly more granular data, a formal double materiality assessment, and a level of auditability that most NFRD-era sustainability programs were not built to support.

![Inner courtyard of the European Parliament building](/sites/workiva/files/styles/rectangle_1440x810/public/images/resources/intro-csrd-tl-img-exec-summary-en.png.webp)

## Research Report: CSRD Year One in Review

Primary research into 50 ESRS-aligned reports: Topical disclosures, sustainability impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) and external assurance.

[Read Ebook](/resources/research-report-csrd-year-one-review)

## CSRD reporting requirements

When must companies comply with the CSRD?

### When must companies comply with the CSRD?

Compliance timelines depend on which reporting wave a company falls into under the post-Omnibus structure.

The CSRD entered into force in January 2023. The compliance rollout was restructured following the adoption of the Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470 in March 2026:

* **Wave 1 (FY2024 onward)**: Companies already within the NFRD scope continue reporting. Wave 1 companies that fall below the new Omnibus thresholds may receive a member state exemption for FY2025 and FY2026.
* **Wave 2 (FY2027, reporting in 2028)**: Large EU companies with more than 1,000 employees and more than €450 million in net annual turnover that were not previously reporting under the NFRD.
* **Wave 3 (FY2028, reporting in 2029)**: Non-EU parent companies generating more than €450 million in EU net turnover with a qualifying subsidiary or branch exceeding €200 million.

Each EU member state transposes the CSRD into national law and may choose to enforce it with country-specific additions. Some countries have historically gold-plated sustainability reporting requirements—widening scope or adding obligations beyond the minimum directive. Companies operating across multiple EU jurisdictions should verify applicable national requirements.

What do CSRD reporting requirements entail?

### What do the reporting requirements entail?

CSRD reporting requirements go beyond a simple ESG narrative. Companies must produce retrospective and forward-looking disclosures that are integrated with their financial statements, independently assured, and digitally tagged.

Key features of the requirements include:

* **Looking both back and ahead**: Companies must provide both retrospective and forward-looking analyses, including quantitative information (measured impact to date) and qualitative information (targets, strategy, and risk assessment).
* **Double materiality**: Companies must assess and disclose both how they impact social and environmental issues, and how those issues impact the company. EFRAG has provided detailed guidance on how to [conduct a double materiality assessment](/resources/interactive-sustainability-guide-double-materiality-assessment "Interactive Sustainability Guide: Double Materiality Assessment").
* **Scope 3 emissions disclosure**: Most notably, the CSRD requires disclosure of scope 3 emissions where these are material (subject to the company’s double materiality assessment). Scope 3 covers indirect emissions across the entire value chain, from upstream suppliers to the use of sold products.
* **External assurance**: All sustainability reporting information must pass through an independent audit process before publication. This is new. The NFRD had no equivalent requirement.

[Double materiality](/blog/what-double-materiality-heres-what-you-need-know "What is Double Materiality? Here's What You Need to Know") remains a core element of the CSRD under the Omnibus amendments. The simplified ESRS (2026) clarify and streamline the assessment process, but the fundamental obligation to assess both financial materiality and impact materiality remains.

How must CSRD reports be presented?

### How must CSRD reports be presented?

CSRD reports must be included within the company’s annual or management report. Sustainability and financial information cannot be published separately.

This requirement ensures that financial and ESG disclosures are published at the same time and considered as a whole. ESRS 2 specifies that companies must explain the relationships between sustainability, financial, and risk information through narrative disclosures and by linking relevant sections. Financial and sustainability data must be truly integrated and not simply placed side by side in the same document.

Reports must also use digital iXBRLTM tagging, enabling regulators and investors to access sustainability data in a machine-readable format consistent with financial reporting standards.

How does the CSRD fit in with other legislations?

### How does the CSRD fit in with other legislations?

The CSRD sits within a broader package of EU sustainability regulation and is designed to work alongside—not duplicate—the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) and the EU Taxonomy.

The CSRD, SFDR, and EU Taxonomy work together to support sustainable investment across the EU:

* **CSRD**: Governs how companies report sustainability information—the scope, standards, and assurance requirements.
* **SFDR**: Sets ESG disclosure obligations for financial market participants—how asset managers and banks report on the sustainability of their products.
* **EU Taxonomy**: Provides a classification system defining which economic activities qualify as environmentally sustainable. Companies reporting under the CSRD must also include [EU Taxonomy](/resources/introduction-eu-taxonomy "An Introduction to the EU Taxonomy") alignment data where applicable.

The simplification effort that produced the Omnibus I Directive also included targeted changes to the EU Taxonomy reporting requirements, with the aim of reducing duplication between the three frameworks.

EFRAG has also strengthened alignment between the CSRD’s ESRS and the ISSB’s IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards, with the simplified ESRS (2026) including financial materiality requirements and signposting provisions designed to support companies reporting under both frameworks.

What are the challenges of CSRD disclosure?

### What are the challenges of CSRD disclosure?

The most significant challenges are data scale, cross-team coordination, and audit readiness—areas where companies reporting under the NFRD often start with a meaningful gap.

Because the CSRD requirements are far more detailed than those of the NFRD, companies must gather large volumes of ESG data that need to be accurate, traceable, and independently verifiable. Scope 3 emissions extend beyond a company’s direct operations to cover the full value chain, including upstream and downstream transportation, distribution, and the use of sold products and are particularly complex to track and attribute.

Finance and sustainability teams will need greater visibility into each other’s data. In many organizations, numbers that were previously managed separately must now be incorporated into integrated disclosures, categorized consistently, and cross-referenced between sections of the annual report. This changes how those teams collaborate day to day.

The external assurance requirement adds another layer of rigor: all information in the report must be traceable from source through to final disclosure. As data passes between systems and teams, companies need controls in place to maintain accuracy at every step.

Companies that reported under the NFRD face a significant step up. Organizations with no prior sustainability reporting history face an even steeper challenge: building data infrastructure, cross-functional workflows, audit-ready controls from scratch and often on a compressed timeline.

The CSRD is transposed into national law by each EU member state, and enforcement approaches vary. Some jurisdictions have introduced serious penalties for non-compliance, including significant fines, though the specific enforcement framework depends on national legislation. Companies with operations in multiple EU countries should verify the requirements and penalties applicable in each jurisdiction.

## How Workiva supports CSRD compliance

CSRD compliance is a data and process challenge that spans finance, sustainability, audit, and risk teams. The Workiva platform is built to connect those teams in a single, audit-ready workspace where financial and sustainability data flows from source to disclosure without re-entry.

### Connected workflows

According to Workiva's CSRD Year One in Review research, sustainability statements now account for an average of one-third of the annual report, making integrated, audit-ready workflows a core part of CSRD compliance.

### Built for ESRS

The Workiva platform provides built-in support for ESRS reporting requirements, XBRL® and iXBRL tagging, double materiality assessment workflows, and multi-framework data collection across GRI, TCFD, SASB, and CDP.

### Audit-ready by design

The platform maintains an audit trail so sustainability disclosures can withstand the same level of scrutiny as financial statements. Over 6,500 organizations worldwide use Workiva, including 85% of the Fortune 1000® by revenue.

[Explore CSRD reporting](/solutions/csrd-reporting)

## Getting ready for the CSRD

### Cross-functional alignment

The CSRD has direct implications for sustainability, finance, risk, and audit teams. Meeting its requirements takes full C-level and board engagement, a clear vision, defined goals, and genuine cross-functional collaboration across teams that have often worked in separate tracks.

### Start preparing now

The CSRD is advancing a shift toward verifiable, integrated disclosure, where financial and sustainability data are governed and disclosed as a unified whole. Even if your organization's mandatory filing date is years away, the data infrastructure decisions made now will determine whether you can comply with confidence or scramble to catch up.

### Stay current on regulation

The regulatory landscape is still evolving. The simplified ESRS (2026) have been finalized, but transposition into national law continues through March 2027. As requirements are clarified at the member state level, it is important to assess the processes and tools that underpin your organization's daily operations: Is your data accessible, traceable, and connected across the relevant teams? Are your systems built to adapt as standards evolve? Having these foundations in place will prepare you for current and future CSRD requirements and for the broader shift toward audit-ready sustainability reporting.
