SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Debevoise & Plimpton legal briefing provides an overview of the European Commission's Simplification Omnibus Package, published on 26 February 2025, which proposes significant changes to the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), and the EU Taxonomy Regulation. The package aims to reduce administrative burdens by at least 25% for EU companies and at least 35% for SMEs.

**Key Changes to CSRD:**
- Scoping threshold raised from 250 to more than 1,000 employees (plus existing €50M turnover or €25M balance sheet thresholds), taking approximately 35,000 of 45,000 companies (about 80%) out of scope.
- Non-EU parent undertaking threshold raised from €150M to €450M aggregate EU turnover, and branch threshold raised from €40M to €50M.
- Listed SMEs (fewer than 1,000 employees) will be out of scope.
- Voluntary reporting standards will be introduced based on the existing VSME standards.
- ESRS reporting standards to be revised via Delegated Act within six months, reducing mandatory datapoints, prioritizing quantitative metrics over narrative, prioritizing interoperability with ISSB standards.
- No sector-specific reporting standards will be created.
- Double materiality principle remains unchanged.
- Value chain information requests capped at information contained in voluntary standards for companies with up to 1,000 employees.
- Assurance guidelines to be issued by 2026; plans to transition from limited to reasonable assurance removed.
- A separate proposal postpones CSRD application by two years for companies due to first report for 2025 or 2026 financial years.
- Member States that haven't transposed CSRD (Luxembourg, Germany, Netherlands) may pause implementation.

**Key Changes to CSDDD:**
- First-wave application postponed from 2027 to July 2028; Member State transposition deadline delayed by one year to July 2028.
- Due diligence obligations reduced to direct business partners only (not entire chain of activities), with qualification for "plausible information" of adverse impacts at indirect partner level.
- Information requests to business partners with fewer than 500 employees limited to information in voluntary CSRD reporting standards.
- Termination of business relationships replaced with suspension as last resort.
- Stakeholder engagement list narrowed (removing consumers and national human rights/environmental/civil society institutions), and only required for certain due diligence parts.
- Monitoring re-assessment changed from annually to every five years (with caveat for reasonable grounds).
- Pan-EU civil liability regime removed; recourse based on existing Member State law; no pan-EU principle for organisations to bring actions on behalf of victims.
- Requirement for financial penalties commensurate to net worldwide turnover deleted; 5% cap requirement deleted.
- Financial sector downstream due diligence exemption made permanent (review clause removed).
- Transition plan obligation changed to "adopt" but not "put into effect," aligning wording with CSRD.

**Key Changes to Taxonomy:**
- Companies with net turnover exceeding €450M must report under Taxonomy; others may "opt in" if they wish to claim alignment.
- Non-financial undertakings under €450M turnover must disclose turnover and CapEx alignment, may choose to report OpEx.
- Partial Taxonomy alignment claims permitted (e.g., without DNSH criteria).
- Proposed amendments to Delegated Acts allow omission of reporting on activities representing less than 10% of turnover, CapEx or OpEx; simplified reporting templates; simplified technical screening criteria on chemicals.
- Asset managers may omit reporting where less than 10% of assets by value report under Taxonomy, and are not required to report on investee companies with fewer than 1,000 employees.

The proposals will go through the EU legislative process (European Parliament and Council). The postponement proposal is expected to be adopted quickly in 2025 with transposition by year end.
</summary>

- New dual thresholds for CSRD scope: companies must have BOTH more than 1,000 employees AND more than €450 million net turnover (previously 250+ employees and €50M+ turnover)

- Double materiality assessment now allows top-down or bottom-up approaches; limited assurance remains the standard, with full reasonable assurance postponed

- Wave 1 (NFRD companies, 500+ employees, public interest): already reporting (FY2024 reports published 2025). Those now below new thresholds get transition exemption for FY2025–2026 (Member State option). Wave 1 companies may omit ESRS E4, S2, S3, S4 for FY2025–2026.

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] CEAOB guidelines on limited assurance on sustainability reporting ---
URL: https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/8ac2df18-2ae1-4bc7-9d87-a4a740e48f5e_en?filename=240930-ceaob-guidelines-limited-assurance-sustainability-reporting_en.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document contains the CEAOB (Committee of European Auditing Oversight Bodies) guidelines on limited assurance on sustainability reporting, adopted on 30 September 2024. These non-binding guidelines were developed in response to the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD, EU 2022/2464), which entered into force on 5 January 2023. The CSRD requires large companies to prepare sustainability statements under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) starting from financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2024, and mandates limited assurance engagements by statutory auditors or other assurance services providers ("practitioners"). Since the European Commission is not required to adopt formal assurance standards until 1 October 2026 at the latest, the guidelines fill the interim gap period and aim to avoid fragmentation and promote consistency across EU Member States.

The guidelines are organized into several key sections covering general principles and approach, disclosures under Article 8 of the Taxonomy Regulation, digitalisation, the limited assurance report, and other overarching provisions.

Key principles covered include: (1) the objective of obtaining limited assurance that sustainability information is free from material misstatements, recognizing that less work is required than for reasonable assurance; (2) treatment of material misstatements, which differ from the "double materiality" concept used by entities in preparing reports; (3) procedures for risk identification and assessment, including inquiries, analytical procedures, and physical observations; (4) special attention to the entity's process for determining material matters under the double materiality principle; (5) forward-looking information and estimates, where practitioners should remain critical but are not required to provide guarantees; and (6) communication requirements between practitioners and statutory auditors regarding connectivity between financial and sustainability statements.

Specific provisions address Article 8 Taxonomy Regulation disclosures (covering assessment of eligible/aligned economic activities, KPI reconciliation, and consistency with other ESRS information), the limited assurance report format and content (including the negative form of expression for conclusions, qualified/adverse conclusions for material misstatements, and disclaimer of conclusion for scope limitations), representation letters, use of experts, documentation requirements, subsequent events, and specific provisions for comparative information (first year), value chain information, group/consolidated information, and information incorporated by reference. The guidelines also address joint engagements performed by multiple practitioners, including requirements for balanced distribution of work, cross-review procedures, and joint conclusions.

The guidelines explicitly state they are non-binding and do not override or replace national pronouncements. The appendices include a glossary of terms, references to relevant EU law (Accounting Directive 2013/34/EU, Audit Directive 2006/43/EC, Audit Regulation 537/2014, Taxonomy Regulation 2020/852, Transparency Directive 2004/109/EC, and Delegated Regulation 2023/2772 on ESRS), and detailed provisions for joint engagements by multiple practitioners.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In a limited assurance engagement, practitioners perform less extensive procedures than in a reasonable assurance engagement: the amount of work is expected to be less than for a reasonable assurance engagement that would be performed in the same circumstances."

--- SOURCE 2: FAQs: fundamentals to assurance on sustainability reporting - Accountancy Europe ---
URL: https://accountancyeurope.eu/publications/faqs-fundamentals-to-assurance-on-sustainability-reporting

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Accountancy Europe (published 6 January 2025) is a comprehensive FAQ document explaining the fundamentals of assurance on sustainability reporting, structured in two parts: key concepts of assurance and the EU regulatory framework.

**Context:** The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) obliges companies to disclose sustainability information in their management report according to the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) in digital machine-readable format. The CSRD introduces an EU-wide assurance requirement for limited assurance over sustainability reporting as from 2025 (covering 2024 ESRS reporting).

**Key Concepts:**
- **What is assurance:** An assurance engagement is a mandatory or voluntary check of sustainability information disclosed by a company. It enhances credibility of reported information but does not validate a company's performance as 'sustainable'.
- **How assurance is performed:** Follows a risk-based approach with three stages (planning, execution, reporting), requiring year-long cooperation among a multi-disciplinary team. Procedures include inquiry, testing internal controls, analysing transactions, and third-party confirmations.
- **Types of assurance:** Limited vs. reasonable assurance engagements. Limited assurance involves fewer procedures and less evidence; reasonable assurance (typical of financial statement audits) is the highest level but not absolute.
- **Risk-based approach:** Resources are focused on areas with higher risk of material misstatements relating to impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs).
- **Materiality:** The double materiality concept is embedded in CSRD and ESRS. The practitioner's materiality determination is based on professional judgment and considers users' needs.
- **Output:** A publicly available assurance report expressing the practitioner's conclusion, plus a separate non-public report communicating significant matters (e.g., internal control deficiencies) to management.
- **Assurance report elements:** Practitioner's conclusion, scope, applicable reporting framework, responsibilities, inherent limitations, professional standards used, and summary of work performed.
- **Types of conclusions:** Unmodified (clean/positive/unqualified), and modified conclusions including disclaimer, adverse, and qualified.
- **Management responsibilities:** Preparing sustainability information per reporting standards, designing internal controls, and providing practitioner access to all relevant information and staff.

**EU Regulatory Framework:**

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## CSRD Assurance and Audit Requirements: What Companies Need to Know in 2026

This article (by João Aguiam) explains the mandatory assurance requirements under the EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), which for the first time in EU history requires sustainability reports to be independently verified, much like financial statements.

### Why Assurance is Required
The CSRD mandates third-party assurance to build credibility, reduce greenwashing, standardise quality across the 12 ESRS standards, and align sustainability data with the rigour of financial reporting.

### Assurance Levels
- **Limited Assurance (2024–2028):** Auditors review the sustainability report for material misstatements using analytical procedures, inquiries with management, and reviews of internal controls. This is a "nothing came to our attention" conclusion rather than a full deep-dive.
- **Reasonable Assurance (expected 2028+):** Equivalent to financial audit standards, involving substantive testing, data verification, transaction sampling, and rigorous controls testing. The European Commission will adopt limited assurance standards first (expected via ISSA 5000 from IAASB) and develop reasonable assurance standards by October 2028.

### Who Needs Assurance (Phased Timeline)
| Wave | Companies | First Report |
|---|---|---|
| Wave 1 | Large public-interest entities (500+ employees, already under NFRD) | 2025 (FY 2024) |
| Wave 2 | Other large companies (250+ employees, €50M+ revenue, €25M+ assets — 2 of 3 criteria) | 2026 (FY 2025) |
| Wave 3 | Listed SMEs (opt-out until 2028) | 2027 (FY 2026) |
| Wave 4 | Non-EU companies with €150M+ EU revenue | 2029 (FY 2028) |

All waves require limited assurance.

### Who Can Perform Assurance
- **Statutory Auditors:** The default option — the firm auditing financial statements can also handle sustainability assurance if they have ESG expertise.
- **Independent Assurance Service Providers (IASPs):** Some EU member states allow non-statutory auditors to perform this role (e.g., France historically allowed OEC). Depending on national transposition.

Key selection considerations: ESG expertise (financial auditors may not understand Scope 3 or biodiversity metrics), industry knowledge, independence rules (a firm providing CSRD consulting cannot typically also audit), and cost. Assurance and advisory must be kept separate.

### What Auditors Check
1. **Governance and process** — clear structure, defined roles and responsibilities for data collection/sign-off
2. **Double materiality assessment** — proper conduct, stakeholder engagement, documented rationale for material and omitted topics
3. **Data quality and controls** — data sources, internal controls, traceability to source systems, reasonable documented estimates
4. **Disclosure completeness** — all mandatory ESRS disclosures, cross-cutting standards (ESRS 1 and ESRS 2), consistency with materiality assessment
5. **Consistency with financial statements** — alignment with management report, no contradictions

### Preparation Roadmap
- Start at least 6 months early; engage the assurance provider for a pre-assurance readiness assessment
- Build an audit trail — every data point needs a clear source, documented methodology, and evidence of review/approval
- Invest in internal controls (segregation of duties, reconciliations, version control, escalation paths)
- Conduct a dry run (pre-assurance engagement or internal audit)
- Document everything — materiality methodology, stakeholder engagement, data collection procedures, assumptions (especially Scope 3), board approvals

### Common Pitfalls
Treating assurance as a formality, poor data granularity, inconsistent reporting boundaries (must align with financial consolidation scope), ignoring value chain data (upstream and downstream), and last-minute provider selection.

### Consequences of Failure
Qualified, adverse, or disclaimer opinions can lead to regulatory scrutiny, reputational damage, investor concerns, and potential legal liability for directors.

### Cost Estimates
- Mid-sized companies: €20,000–€60,000 for limited assurance
- Large corporates: €50,000–€150,000+
- Complex multinationals: €150,000–€500,000+ (expected to rise with reasonable assurance transition)

### Next Steps
Confirm your CSRD timeline/wave, engage an assurance provider 6–12 months before deadline, assess data traceability, run a gap analysis against ESRS requirements, and consider expert consulting help.

- **April 2025 (Directive (EU) 2025/794):** Postponed implementation timelines by one year—transposition extended to July 26, 2027; first-wave application (3,000+ employees/€900M) moved to July 26, 2028; remaining companies to July 26, 2029. - May–June 2026 debates shifted from compliance to competitiveness, with the Council presenting Omnibus as a simplification measure while sustainability specialists criticized the dilution of due diligence obligations.
- The CSDDD was not repealed but significantly recalibrated—reducing the number of companies in scope and limiting trickle-down effects on SMEs.
- The Trump administration did not directly cause the delay (no legal causation exists in EU legislative records), but indirectly influenced the political climate by reinforcing anti-ESG narratives and competitive concerns, strengthening the case of EU factions opposing sustainability legislation.

The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) is an EU regulation that entered into force on January 5, 2023, requiring large companies to disclose standardized, externally audited sustainability information integrated with their financial reports. It was significantly revised by the Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470, in force from 18 March 2026, which narrowed scope to approximately 90% fewer companies than originally projected.

**CSRD Scope (updated thresholds):** EU companies must report if they exceed BOTH 1,000 employees on average AND €450 million in net annual turnover (replacing the previous two-out-of-three criteria test). Non-EU parent companies must report if they generate over €450 million in EU net turnover for two consecutive years and have an EU subsidiary or branch exceeding €200 million in net turnover. New thresholds apply from financial years beginning on or after January 1, 2027.

**Five Core CSRD Requirements:** (1) Integration — disclosures must appear within the annual or management report; (2) ESRS alignment — disclosures must follow the European Sustainability Reporting Standards; (3) Double materiality assessment — companies must assess both financial and impact materiality; (4) External assurance — all disclosures must be independently verified (new under CSRD, no NFRD equivalent); (5) Digital tagging — data must be tagged using iXBRL for machine-readable access.

**CSRD Timeline (post-Omnibus):**
- Wave 1 (FY2024–FY2025, reporting 2025–2026): Companies already in NFRD scope continue reporting; member states may grant exemptions for those below new thresholds.
- Wave 2 (FY2027, reporting 2028): Large EU companies exceeding both thresholds not previously under NFRD. Apply simplified ESRS (2026).
- Wave 3 (FY2028, reporting 2029): Non-EU parent companies meeting revised Article 40a thresholds.

**ESRS Standards:** The original ESRS adopted July 2023 covered 12 standards (ESRS 1 general requirements, ESRS 2 general disclosures, E1–E5 environmental, S1–S4 social, G1 governance). The simplified ESRS (2026), adopted by the European Commission on July 3, 2026, reduce mandatory data points by over 60% and apply from FY2027, with early voluntary adoption for FY2026 permitted. They maintain the 12-topic structure but offer additional materiality flexibility.

**CSRD vs. NFRD differences:** Broadened scope (including large private and non-EU companies), mandatory ESRS standardization (vs. voluntary frameworks like GRI/TCFD under NFRD), mandatory external assurance, and required integration of sustainability disclosures into annual reports. The NFRD covered approximately 11,700 large public-interest entities with 500+ employees.

**Relationship to other legislation:** CSRD works alongside SFDR (asset manager/product ESG disclosures) and the EU Taxonomy (classification of sustainable economic activities), with targeted changes to reduce duplication. **Key reporting features:** Companies must provide both retrospective and forward-looking disclosures, including Scope 3 emissions where material, quantitative and qualitative information, and digitally tagged reports integrated with financial statements. The double materiality assessment remains core even under Omnibus amendments.

**Challenges:** Data scale (especially Scope 3 emissions across the full value chain), cross-team coordination between finance and sustainability teams, and audit readiness. Companies must ensure data is traceable from source to final disclosure. National enforcement varies by member state, with some jurisdictions imposing significant fines.

- Since 18 March 2026, CSRD reporting is mandatory only for companies with more than 1,000 employees AND more than €450m net turnover (both criteria cumulatively).
- The "Stop-the-Clock" proposal pushes back reporting deadlines for Wave 2 and Wave 3 companies by two years. Companies that already had to report for 2024 (Wave 1) are unaffected.

**Revised ESRS Changes (draft published 6 May 2026):**
- Mandatory data points reduced by over 60%; total data points cut by over 70%
- Reporting costs per company expected to fall by over 30%
- Sector-specific standards removed
- Audit remains "Limited Assurance" (the planned switch to "Reasonable Assurance" was dropped)
- Value chain cap limits reporting obligations for suppliers to a new voluntary standard (VS), developed from the VSME standard, preventing large companies from passing obligations to smaller value-chain partners

**Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) remains mandatory** and is the strategic core of CSRD compliance.

**EU Taxonomy Omnibus Changes:**
- Full taxonomy reporting only for companies with >1,000 employees and >€450m turnover
- Materiality threshold allowing omission of reporting on activities under 10% of revenue/CapEx/OpEx
- Simplified voluntary reporting for companies with >1,000 employees but under €450m turnover (at least €50m)
- DNSH criteria to be revised, starting with pollution criteria
- OpEx disclosure only required if at least 25% of turnover comes from taxonomy-eligible activities

**CSDDD Omnibus Changes:**
- Implementation postponed one year (first mandatory application in 2028, two waves instead of three)
- Due diligence obligations limited to direct business partners (Tier 1)
- EU-wide civil liability abolished (national regulations apply instead)
- Fines no longer linked to turnover (5% cap removed)
- No obligation to terminate business relationships
- Annual reviews abolished (reviews every 5 years)

**Timeline of Key Dates:**
- November 2024: Omnibus package announced by Commission President von der Leyen
- February 2025: First "Simplification Omnibus" package officially presented
- 18 March 2026: New thresholds entered into force
- 6 May 2026: Revised ESRS draft published (consultation until 3 June 2026)
- 19 March 2027: Deadline for member states to transpose CSRD into national law
- July 2028: First mandatory application of CSDDD

**Germany-Specific Context:**
- Germany has not yet transposed the CSRD into national law (public hearing took place 10 April 2026); the NFRD remains in force for now. Entry into force expected during 2026, with no obligation to apply the new ESRS for reporting year 2025 unless retroactive.

**Companies' Recommended "No Regret Moves":**
1. Clarify responsibilities for sustainability
2. Conduct or complete a Double Materiality Assessment (core of CSRD and a strategic tool)
3. Define a sustainability strategy with goals, measures, and KPIs
4. Create a voluntary sustainability report using the VSME/VS standard
5. Put sustainability goals into practice with transparent milestones and monitoring

While the Omnibus brings relief (less bureaucracy, more time, lower audit costs, less value-chain burden), challenges include unclear German national implementation, continued stakeholder expectations for ESG data, potential lack of comparability of voluntary reports, and criticism that extended deadlines may delay transformation.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Sarah Hill-Smith (Commonwealth Climate Law) explains what company directors need to know about CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) reporting following the Omnibus I package, approved by the European Parliament on 16 December 2025 and expected to come into force in early 2026.

**Key changes to CSRD scope under Omnibus I:**
- Approximately 42,000 of the ~50,000 companies originally in CSRD scope (90%) fall out of scope.
- From FY 2027 (reporting in 2028), CSRD will only apply to: large EU-listed companies; EU companies with over 1,000 employees AND net annual turnover over €450m; and non-EU companies generating over €450m turnover in the EU with an EU subsidiary/branch generating over €200m turnover (raised from previous €150m).
- Listed SMEs and financial holding undertakings will be exempt.
- A Review Clause allows thresholds to be revisited in the future.
- The original CSRD scope would have covered all EU-listed companies (besides micro-entities), large EU companies meeting two of three thresholds (250 employees, €50m turnover, €25m balance sheet), and non-EU companies with €150m+ EU turnover.

**Timeline implications by "wave":**
- First Wave (~11,000 EU listed companies, banks, insurers with 500+ employees): already reporting since FY 2024. Quick Fix Delegated Act (July 2025) extends reliefs from FY 2024/25 to FY 2026 — all First Wave companies may omit "anticipated financial effects"; those under 750 employees may omit Scope 3 GHG emissions, ESRS E4 (biodiversity), and S1-S4 (social); those over 750 employees may omit E4, S2-S4, and specified S1 datapoints. Omnibus I enables Member States to exempt de-scoped First Wave companies from reporting in FY 2025 and 2026.
- Second Wave (large companies not already reporting): delayed two years by Stop-the-Clock Directive (April 2025) to FY 2027 (reports due 2028), though many now fall out of scope.
- Third Wave (listed SMEs): delayed to FY 2028 (reports due 2029), though nearly all now de-scoped.
- Fourth Wave (non-EU companies): must report on FY 2028 in 2029 under new higher thresholds.

**Standards and content changes:**
- Current ESRS (amended by Quick Fix) remains the legally applicable framework until revised standards are adopted.
- EFRAG published draft simplified ESRS on 3 December 2025: standards halved in length, mandatory datapoints reduced ~61%, all voluntary disclosures deleted, simpler top-down double materiality assessments, more proportionality/reliefs for undue cost or effort, less value chain data pressure, more principles-based narrative reporting, and alignment with ISSB where possible. Commission expected to adopt via delegated act by summer 2026, with application from FY 2027.
- Sector-specific ESRS abandoned by Omnibus I (despite "huge" market demand, e.g., for oil & gas and mining). Commission may issue sector guidance instead.
- Value chain reliefs from FY 2027: companies under 1,000 employees can refuse sustainability information requests beyond future VSME (voluntary SME standards); in-scope companies get a "comply or explain" option for first three years of value chain reporting.
- Additional reliefs: conditional information exemptions (trade secrets, seriously prejudicial commercial position, classified information) and M&A relief for acquired/merged/divested companies.

**Next steps:** Omnibus I will be published in the Official Journal and comes into force 20 days later. EU Member States get ~12 months to transpose. Nine states (Germany, Spain, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Cyprus, Czech Republic) had not fully transposed CSRD as of 30 September 2025.

**Upsides:** Regulatory certainty in 2026; shift from box-ticking to strategic disclosures; integrated reporting; potential cost savings estimated by EFRAG at €4.7b for First and Second Wave companies between FY 2027-2032 (44% reduction, though critiqued as optimistic); and space for voluntary action by the ~42,000 de-scoped companies, motivated by internal preparedness, value creation, physical risk management, market expectations, and the easy entry point in revised ESRS.

**Board takeaways:** Scope assessment becomes a group perimeter exercise; boards should require scope mapping of EU group entities, listed subsidiaries, third-country parents, and planned structural changes; build flexible systems that can adapt if thresholds shift again; test materiality judgements against sector peers; and ask management targeted questions on scope, readiness/controls/assurance, materiality, value chain strategy, risk management, and change management.
</summary>

URL: https://www.nixonpeabody.com/insights/alerts/2026/03/02/california-climate-disclosure-laws-update

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This client alert from Nixon Peabody LLP (March 2, 2026) provides a status update on California's landmark climate disclosure statutes — SB 253 (Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act) and SB 261 (Climate-Related Financial Risk Act) — following the California Air Resources Board's (CARB) unanimous approval of implementing regulations on February 26, 2026.

**Key Facts:**
- SB 253 requires entities "doing business" in California with at least $1 billion in annual revenue to disclose Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by August 10, 2026, and Scope 3 emissions by 2027 or later.
- SB 261 requires entities with at least $500 million in annual revenue to publish a climate-related financial risk report every two years. The first reports were due January 1, 2026, but enforcement is paused due to an injunction.
- "Doing business" in California is defined as actively engaging in transactions for financial gain and either being organized/commercially domiciled in California or having California-based sales exceeding approximately $735,019 (inflation-adjusted).

**Litigation Status:**
- On November 18, 2025, the Ninth Circuit granted an injunction pausing SB 261 enforcement due to a challenge by the US Chamber of Commerce and business groups.
- Oral arguments were heard January 9, 2026, focused on whether the laws unconstitutionally compel protected speech. Plaintiffs argued the laws fail commercial speech tests; the state contended disclosures are tied to commercial transactions, though it acknowledged severability analysis for Scope 3 may be appropriate.
- No decision has been issued and no timeline was provided for a ruling.

**Regulatory Status:**
- CARB posted proposed regulations December 23, 2025; adopted the final regulations February 26, 2026.
- CARB rejected an exemption for insurance agencies, maintaining its authority to exempt insurers, governments, and nonprofits, noting CDI's disclosure program is mandatory and captures more companies than SB 253.
- CARB declined to extend the August 10, 2026 deadline, citing its enforcement discretion approach and that good-faith compliance efforts are sufficient.
- The injunction applies only to SB 261, not SB 253.
- A second rulemaking will establish reporting dates beyond 2026 and address reporting content, format, and data assurance.

**Next Steps for Companies:**
1. Continue SB 253 compliance efforts (Scope 1 and 2 by August 10, 2026; plan for Scope 3 in 2027+).
2. Treat SB 261 reporting as voluntary for now but be prepared to publish reports promptly if the injunction is lifted.
3. Monitor the Ninth Circuit closely — a ruling could narrow, invalidate, or uphold all or part of the statutes.
4. Document all compliance efforts to demonstrate good faith for CARB's enforcement discretion.
5. Assess whether the "doing business in California" threshold applies (sales > ~$735,019).
6. Engage with CARB's second rulemaking through public comment.
7. Consider the broader mandatory climate disclosure trend internationally (EU CSRD, ISSB standards) even if California laws are delayed or struck down.

Authors: Danielle O. Griffin (Associate) and Alison B. Torbitt (Partner) from Nixon Peabody's San Francisco office.

This article from Baker Tilly (updated July 2, 2026) provides a comprehensive update on California's two pivotal climate disclosure laws: Senate Bill 253 (SB 253) and Senate Bill 261 (SB 261). The article reflects CARB's latest implementation updates, including the delayed reporting deadline, withdrawal of the proposed regulation, and upcoming clarifying revisions for public comment.

**SB 253 (Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act):** Requires annual public disclosure of Scope 1, 2, and 3 GHG emissions by U.S.-organized entities with revenues exceeding $1 billion conducting business in California, reported in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. First disclosure deadline was extended from August 10, 2026 to November 10, 2026 following CARB's withdrawal of the previously approved regulation for limited clarifying revisions (announced June 24, 2026). The updated rule will undergo a 15-day public comment period before resubmission to the Office of Administrative Law. CARB confirmed at its November workshop that limited assurance will not be required for 2026 submissions. Entities with fiscal years ending January 1-February 1, 2026 report FY 2026 data; all others report FY 2025 data.

**SB 261 (Climate-Related Financial Risk Act):** Requires biennial disclosure of climate-related financial risks under the TCFD framework, applying to U.S.-organized entities with revenues over $500 million doing business in California. Enforcement is temporarily paused following a preliminary injunction by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals. CARB issued an enforcement advisory on December 1, 2025, confirming it will not enforce the January 1, 2026 deadline and will set an alternate reporting date after the appeal resolves. The public docket is open for voluntary submissions.

**Compliance considerations:** Revenue is defined using "gross receipts" per California Revenue and Taxation Code Section 25120(f)(2), assessed at the individual company level, with aggregation for unitary businesses. CARB proposes to exclude property holdings and payroll criteria from the "doing business" definition. Parent companies may file consolidated reports for in-scope subsidiaries. Exemptions include entities with only teleworking employees in California, insurance-regulated entities, government entities, not-for-profits, and charitable organizations. Holding companies and mutual funds typically don't meet revenue thresholds. CARB plans a flat fee structure with first-year fees due September 10, 2026.

**Penalties:** SB 253 non-compliance penalties capped at $500,000 per reporting year; SB 261 penalties capped at $50,000 per year. CARB will exercise enforcement discretion for good-faith first-year submissions. SB 253 reporting timeline shows assurance escalation: limited assurance on Scope 1 & 2 expected in 2027, reasonable assurance by 2030, and limited Scope 3 assurance beginning no earlier than 2030.

**Key compliance actions recommended:** Determine applicability, develop comprehensive GHG inventories (Scope 1, 2, 3), implement controlled reporting processes, and complete climate risk assessments aligned with TCFD or ISSB frameworks — with continued preparation for SB 261 despite the current stay.
</summary>

## CARB Issues Proposed Regulations Implementing SB 253 and SB 261

This blog post from the Energy Legal Blog® (January 6, 2026) discusses California Air Resources Board (CARB) proposed regulations implementing California's corporate climate disclosure laws, SB 253 and SB 261.

### Background on SB 253 and SB 261
- **SB 253**: Requires U.S. companies with annual revenues over $1 billion doing business in California to report greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions annually. First report covering Scope 1 and 2 emissions is due **August 10, 2026**; Scope 3 reporting begins in 2027.
- **SB 261**: Requires U.S. companies doing business in California (excluding insurance companies) with annual revenues exceeding $500 million to disclose climate-related financial risk reports every two years. The original January 1, 2026 deadline is currently **unenforceable due to an injunction**; CARB will set a new deadline after litigation resolves.

### Legal Challenges
- A coalition led by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce challenged the constitutionality of both laws (First Amendment claims).
- U.S. District Court for the Central District of California denied the preliminary injunction motion.
- On **November 18, 2025**, the Ninth Circuit granted an injunction pending appeal for **SB 261 only**, suspending its enforcement, while declining to enjoin SB 253.
- Ninth Circuit oral arguments scheduled for **January 9, 2026**.

### CARB Draft Regulations (Issued December 1, 2025)
CARB's initial rulemaking is narrowly focused on three objectives: (1) establishing fee structure to fund program administration, (2) clarifying entities subject to fees, and (3) setting the first-year reporting deadline for Scope 1 and 2 emissions under SB 253. Other elements (detailed reporting requirements, assurance standards, enforcement provisions) will be addressed in subsequent rulemakings.

**Key Definitions:**

## California SB 253 and SB 261: What Businesses Need to Know

This Persefoni article provides a comprehensive overview of California's two landmark climate disclosure laws—SB 253 (Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act) and SB 261 (Climate-Related Financial Risk Act)—signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom in October 2023. The article covers implementation timelines, key requirements, current regulatory status, and compliance guidance for affected companies.

### Key Requirements

**SB 253** requires U.S.-based public and private companies with more than $1 billion in annual revenue doing business in California to report Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions beginning in 2026, with Scope 3 reporting and assurance anticipated to begin in 2027. Approximately 5,400 organizations are estimated to be affected. The law requires reporting in accordance with GHG Protocol standards, with penalties up to $500,000 per reporting year for non-compliance. A Scope 3 safe harbor exists if disclosures are made in good faith with reasonable basis.

**SB 261** mandates biennial public reporting on climate-related financial risks and mitigation strategies by companies with over $500 million in annual revenue. Penalties are up to $50,000 per year. Reports must be published on company websites and posted to a CARB public docket (open December 1, 2025 through July 1, 2026).

### Implementation Timeline

- **October 2023:** Newsom signs both bills into law; CARB charged with finalizing requirements
- **July 2024:** Proposed two-year delay fails to materialize; implementation date of January 1, 2026 remains
- **September 2024:** SB 219 amendment passed, extending CARB rulemaking to July 2025 and providing flexibility
- **September 2025:** CARB releases preliminary list of affected companies
- **December 2025:** CARB posts proposed initial regulation materials; issues SB 261 enforcement advisory following Ninth Circuit injunction
- **January 2026:** Ninth Circuit hears oral argument in Chamber of Commerce v. Sanchez (constitutional challenge); SB 261 injunction remains in effect as of April 2026
- **February 2026:** CARB Board approves initial regulation (revenue thresholds, fees, August 10, 2026 deadline)
- **June 2026:** CARB withdraws regulation package for clarifying changes; proposes moving first-year Scope 1 & 2 deadline from August 10 to November 10, 2026
- **July 2026:** CARB proposes five Scope 3 categories beginning 2027, limited assurance for Scope 1 & 2, and annual November 10 reporting deadline

### Scope 3 Proposals (2027+)

CARB proposes initially requiring five of fifteen Scope 3 categories: Purchased goods and services (Cat 1), Fuel- and energy-related activities (Cat 3), Waste generated in operations (Cat 5), Business travel (Cat 6), and Employee commuting (Cat 7). The remaining ten categories would be voluntary. Limited assurance proposed under standards including ISSA 5000, ISAE 3000/3410, AICPA AT-C 210/205, AA1000AS v3, and ISO 14064-3, with reasonable assurance required by 2030.

### Exemptions

Tax-exempt nonprofits, government entities and majority-government-owned companies, businesses whose only California activity is wholesale electricity transactions, and businesses with only employee compensation/payroll activity in California. Insurance companies are exempt from SB 253 in 2026 but proposed for inclusion in 2027; they remain exempt from SB 261.

### Compliance Guidance

Recommended preparation steps include: collecting emissions data aligned to GHG Protocol, assessing climate risks using TCFD framework, building cross-functional collaboration, investing in auditable technology, documenting processes and assumptions, evaluating organizational boundary approaches (equity share vs. control), selecting GHG accounting methods, and identifying assurance providers to avoid capacity bottlenecks.

### Why It Matters

California is the first U.S. state to require climate transparency at this level and is becoming the world's fourth-largest economy. The laws reflect a global push for corporate climate disclosure, including the EU's CSRD and pending SEC regulations. Companies already measuring emissions stand to gain competitive advantages and investor confidence.
</summary>

<summary>
## SEC Climate Disclosure Rule: Status, Requirements, and Outlook (May 2026)

**Current Status:** The SEC climate disclosure rule (Release No. 33-11275), adopted March 6, 2024 in a 3-2 vote under Chair Gary Gensler, has never been enforced. The SEC voluntarily stayed the rule on April 4, 2024; withdrew its legal defense on March 27, 2025; and on May 4, 2026 submitted a proposed rule titled "Rescission of Climate-Related Disclosure Rules" (RIN 3235-AN76) for White House regulatory review — the first formal step toward repeal. On May 7, 2026, the SEC confirmed it would not renew its defense and would reconsider through notice-and-comment rulemaking. On May 8, 2026, challengers asked the Eighth Circuit to lift the abeyance and vacate the rule outright (citing the February 2026 Fifth Circuit decision in Airlines for America v. DOT). The case (Iowa v. SEC, No. 24-1522) remains in abeyance as of May 2026.

**Key Rule Requirements (if ever enforced):**
- Six disclosure areas under Regulation S-K Items 1501-1506 plus S-X Article 14: climate risk governance, strategy/business impact, risk management processes, GHG emissions (material Scope 1 and 2 only, no Scope 3), financial statement footnote impacts, and phased assurance.
- Physical risk disclosure (S-K 1502): acute risks (hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, wildfires) and chronic risks (heat, sea-level rise, drought); companies must identify geographic locations of exposed properties; climate change must be "a significant contributing factor" (not sole cause) to trigger disclosure.
- 1% financial threshold (S-X Article 14): expensed losses from severe weather ≥1% of pre-tax income (minimum $100,000); capitalized costs ≥1% of stockholders' equity (minimum $500,000). Carbon offset and REC costs if material to climate targets.
- Phase-in schedule (never took effect): Large Accelerated Filers primary disclosures FY 2025, GHG FY 2026, limited assurance FY 2029, reasonable assurance FY 2033; Accelerated Filers FY 2026/FY 2028/FY 2031; SRCs/EGCs/non-accelerated FY 2027 with full GHG and assurance exemptions.
- Safe harbor (S-K 1507) extended PSLRA protections to transition plans, scenario analysis, internal carbon pricing, and climate targets (including for IPOs/SPACs), but not to Scope 1/2 emissions.
- The final rule was significantly narrower than the 2022 proposal: Scope 3 eliminated entirely, materiality qualifier applied throughout, board climate expertise disclosure removed, line-item financial disclosures replaced with 1% threshold footnotes, and phase-in extended by 2-6 years after 24,000+ comment letters.

**Legal Timeline:** Adopted March 6, 2024 → stayed April 4, 2024 → challenges consolidated in Eighth Circuit mid-2024 → SEC withdrew defense March 27, 2025 (Commissioner Caroline Crenshaw sole dissenter, calling it "an unprecedented abdication of the Commission's regulatory responsibilities") → 18 states plus DC intervened April 2025 → Eighth Circuit ordered continued abeyance September 2025 → rescission proposal submitted May 4, 2026 → motion to vacate filed May 8, 2026 (pending).

**Critical Context:** The SEC's 2010 interpretive guidance (Release No. 33-9106) remains fully in effect and requires public companies to disclose material climate risks under existing Regulation S-K/S-X — covering climate legislation/regulation impacts, international accord effects, indirect regulatory/business consequences, and physical impacts. This obligation predates the 2024 rule by 14 years and applies regardless of the stay.

**Comparison with State Laws:** California SB 253 applies to public AND private companies with >$1B CA revenue (Scope 1 & 2, plus Scope 3 from 2027; first compliance deadline August 2026; in effect). CA SB 261 requires TCFD-aligned risk reports for companies >$500M CA revenue (enforcement paused by injunction). New York passed its own climate legislation in February 2026. California's patchwork may be more complex than the federal rule given broader scope.

**What Companies Should Do Now:** (1) Comply with binding 2010 SEC guidance; (2) Prepare for California SB 253's 2026 deadline; (3) Track converging international frameworks (IFRS S2/ISSB standards in UK, Australia, Singapore); (4) Meet rising investor expectations (CDP, proxy advisors) regardless of regulation. Practical steps: map physical risks across material locations, estimate severe weather losses against the 1% pre-tax income threshold, document risk identification processes, and prepare board-level climate governance documentation.

**Conclusion:** The rule formalized the most detailed federal climate reporting requirements ever proposed but is unlikely to be enforced. However, the disclosure direction it codified is embedded in state laws, international standards, and investor expectations. As of May 2026, the most likely outcomes are formal repeal, court-ordered vacatur, or both.

**Author:** Govind Balachandran, founder of Continuuiti (a climate risk assessment platform).

WHY IT MATTERS: Climate change impacts pose enormous risks to the US financial system, including physical risks (damaged infrastructure, severe weather, wildfires, sea-level rise) and transitional risks (changing investment values due to shifts in energy/climate policy or consumer demand). A growing number of companies are setting net-zero goals and GHG emissions targets, but their reporting is too fragmented and inconsistent to be useful to investors and regulators. The SEC has been taking steps to inform people about how climate risks can affect companies, investors, and financial markets.

KEY TIMELINE EVENTS (reverse chronological):
- June 1, 2026: SEC informed Eighth Circuit it issued proposed rescission of climate risk rule; will submit status report by Aug. 31, 2026 (State of Iowa v. SEC, No. 24-01522)
- May 29, 2026: SEC released proposed rescission of climate-related risk disclosure rules; comments due 60 days after Federal Register publication
- Feb. 26, 2026: California Air Resources Board approved adoption of the California Greenhouse Gas Reporting and Climate Financial Risk Disclosure Initial Regulation implementing SB 253 and SB 261; first reporting deadline Aug. 1, 2026 for GHG scopes 1 and 2
- Nov. 18, 2025: Ninth Circuit granted injunction pending appeal of California's climate risk reporting rule; GHG reporting rule (Aug. 2026 deadline) not paused; oral argument set for Jan. 9, 2026 (Chamber of Commerce v. Sanchez, No. 25-5327)

- Mar. 27, 2025: SEC voted to end its legal defense of the climate-related risk disclosure rule
- March 6, 2024: SEC narrowly voted to release its final climate-related risk disclosure rule requiring public companies to report material climate-related risks and, for some large companies, GHG emissions if material; multiple lawsuits followed
- March 21, 2024: Eighth Circuit selected via lottery to hear consolidated challenges to the SEC rule
- Sept. 14, 2023: California passed SB-253 (requires companies with $1B+ annual revenue doing business in CA to disclose scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions) and SB-261 (requires companies with $500M+ annual revenue to disclose climate-related financial risk)
- May 20, 2021: Biden issued Executive Order 14030 requesting a Climate-Related Financial Risk Strategy
- Prior administration actions include the Federal Reserve's climate scenario exercises, Treasury's Climate-related Financial Risk Advisory Committee (CFRAC), CFTC's Climate Risk Unit, SEC's Climate and ESG Task Force, and various proposed and final rules from 2020-2024

SB-261 (Greenhouse Gases: Climate-Related Financial Risk Act) requires companies with over $500 million annual revenues to disclose climate-related financial risk.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This legal update from Clark Hill PLC, authored by Charles R. Berry on May 19, 2026, reports on the SEC's formal process to rescind its climate-related disclosure rules. On May 4, 2026, the SEC submitted a proposed rulemaking titled "Rescission of Climate-Related Disclosure Rules" to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs for review—the first formal step toward rescission through notice-and-comment rulemaking, over two years after the rules were adopted.

Key timeline of events:
- The Rules were proposed in 2022 and adopted on March 6, 2024 by a 3-2 SEC vote, after receiving over 14,000 comments.
- Within 10 days of adoption, nine court petitions were filed across several federal courts, including a lawsuit by 25 Republican state attorneys general arguing the SEC exceeded its authority, an action by the Sierra Club claiming the rules didn't go far enough, and a stay request led by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

**Key components of the rule:**
- Disclosures required outside financial statements include: material scope 1 and scope 2 GHG emissions (with phased-in assurance for large accelerated and accelerated filers), governance and oversight of material climate-related risks, material impact of climate risks on strategy/business model/outlook, risk management processes, and material climate targets and goals.

**Implementation considerations:** The vast majority of companies will need the transition period to develop reporting capabilities, data requirements, and processes/controls. ## SEC Climate Disclosure Rule - Overview (Last Updated: March 7, 2024)

### What It Is
On March 6, 2024, the US SEC adopted its final ruling on "The Enhancement and Standardization of Climate-Related Disclosures," requiring U.S. listed companies to disclose climate-related information in registration statements and annual reports. The rule was finalized two years after its initial proposal (March 2022) and became effective May 6, 2024.

### Key Disclosure Requirements (12 items)
The final rule requires registrants to disclose:
1. Climate-related risks with material impact on business strategy, results, or financial condition
2. Actual and potential material impacts of climate risks on strategy, business model, and outlook
3. Quantitative/qualitative descriptions of material expenditures from mitigation/adaptation activities
4. Transition plans, scenario analysis, or internal carbon price usage
5. Board oversight and management roles regarding climate risks
6. Processes for identifying, assessing, and managing climate risks
7. Climate-related targets/goals materially affecting the business
8. Scope 1 and/or Scope 2 GHG emissions (for large accelerated filers and accelerated filers, with exemptions for smaller reporting companies and emerging growth companies)
9. Assurance reports (limited assurance initially, reasonable assurance later for LAFs)
10. Costs/losses from severe weather events (subject to 1% and de minimis thresholds)
11. Costs related to carbon offsets and renewable energy credits (RECs)
12. Qualitative description of how estimates/assumptions were impacted by climate risks

### Filing Requirements
- Climate disclosures must be filed in registration statements and Exchange Act annual reports
- Can be placed in a separate section or incorporated by reference (Risk Factors, Description of Business, MD&A)
- Electronic tagging in Inline XBRL required

### Enforcement Scope
- Applies to all publicly-listed SEC reporting companies, including foreign private issuers
- Large accelerated filers (LAFs): market cap above $700 million
- Small companies with >$10 million assets and 500+ equity holders may also be covered under Section 12(g)

### Compliance Timeline
- **March 6, 2024**: Rule adopted on 3-2 vote
- **May 6, 2024**: Rule takes effect (60 days after Federal Register publication)
- **2024**: LAFs should begin assessing/tracking ESG governance and GHG emissions
- **2025**: LAFs begin first disclosures (Reg. S-K and S-X) for fiscal year 2025
- **2026**: LAFs must disclose Scope 1 & 2 emissions; AFs begin all disclosure requirements
- **2027**: SRCs, EGCs, and NAFs fall under requirements

### Assurance Timeline Table
| Filers | Scope 1 & 2 GHG Disclosures | Limited Assurance Required |
|--------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| Large accelerated filer ($700M+ cap) | Fiscal year 2026 | 2029 |
| Accelerated filer & non-accelerated filer | Fiscal year 2027 | 2031 |
| Smaller reporting company | Fiscal year 2028 | Exempted |

### Key Provisions & Accommodations
- Scope 3 GHG emissions are NOT required (excluded from final rule)
- Safe harbor from private liability for climate disclosures (excluding historical facts) on transition plans, scenario analysis, internal carbon prices, and targets
- SRCs and EGCs exempt from GHG emissions disclosure
- Delayed filing allowed for GHG disclosures (Form 10-Q second quarter or Form 20-F amendment)
- GHG disclosures for registration statements: most recent fiscal year at least 225 days prior to effectiveness

### Regulatory Context
- Rule aligns with TCFD (Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures, now under IFRS's ISSB) with four core pillars: Governance, Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics and Targets
- Mirrors California's SB 253 (Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act) and SB 261 (Climate-Related Financial Risk Disclosure Act) from 2023
- The SEC also has additional ESG proposals pending: board diversity disclosure (all NASDAQ-listed companies) and human capital management reporting (hiring practices, workplace culture, employee well-being, DEI)

### Recommended Next Steps for Companies
1. **Leadership structure**: Clarify board's role in ESG oversight; establish ESG working groups
2. **Materiality assessment**: Conduct to determine most relevant sustainability themes, goals, targets, and KPIs
3. **Data systems**: Implement robust sustainability reporting and data management systems for GHG emissions tracking (spreadsheets become insufficient for larger companies); ensure reporting archiving, version control, and governance
4. **Third-party attestation**: LAFs and AFs need assurance reports from credible partners for Scope 1 & 2 emissions
5. **Non-compliance risks**: Potential meaningful fines, reputational harm, and investor risk (penalties not yet fully defined)

- The financial statement disclosure requirement was pared back, removing the need to disclose climate-related event impacts on each line item of financial statements.
- Disclosure applies to both domestic and foreign private issuers in annual reports (Forms 10-K and 20-F) and registration statements. Foreign private issuers using IFRS (rather than US GAAP) may apply IFRS for financial statement metrics. MJDS filers (Form 40-F) are exempt.

Timeline and context:
- Initial disclosures for large accelerated filers are due in 2026, with emissions and financial expenditure disclosures due in 2027. GHG emissions data may be forward incorporated into a company's second quarter 10-Q or filed in a 10-K/A.
- The SEC's initial climate rule proposal was published on March 21, 2022, generating more than 24,000 public comments. Adoption was delayed several times.
- During the delay, other climate disclosure rules emerged, including three California laws (SB 253, SB 261, AB 1305) and the EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), which have broader Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions reporting requirements expected to apply to thousands of US companies.
- The new rules become effective 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.
- Compliance dates are based on fiscal years beginning in a given calendar year (FYBs). All filing dates assume December 31 fiscal year-ends.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Big Problems with SEC Climate Disclosure Mandate - Competitive Enterprise Institute ---
URL: https://cei.org/studies/big-problems-with-sec-climate-disclosure-mandate

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study from the Competitive Enterprise Institute (CEI), authored by Stone Washington, criticizes the SEC's mandatory climate disclosure rule. The 500-page rule, finalized in 2024, would require publicly traded companies to annually disclose climate and energy-use information, including Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (indirect from purchased electricity), and Scope 3 (supplier/customer value-chain) greenhouse gas emissions.

Key arguments against the rule include:

1. **Legal issues**: The rule reportedly exceeds the SEC's statutory authority by redefining the Supreme Court's interpretation of "materiality" from the Northway decision, violates the nondelegation doctrine/major questions doctrine, and lacks congressional authorization. The author notes no court has ever deemed climate-related risk factors as worthy of mandatory disclosure. The DC Circuit's National Association of Manufacturers v. SEC (2016) precedent, striking down conflict-free minerals disclosure, is cited as relevant precedent.

2. **Cost burden**: The SEC's own estimates project compliance costs rising from $3.8 billion to $10.2 billion annually (a $6.4 billion increase). Average firms would pay approximately $864,864 extra per year across roughly 7,400 public companies. The rule would require an estimated 39 million additional work hours. One macroeconomic estimate suggests a $25 billion GDP loss by the late 2020s. The SEC requested $101 million in additional funding for ESG-related staffing, but received less — Enforcement filled only 14 of 125 target positions (11%), Investment Management filled 4 of 13 (31%), and Corporation Finance filled 9 of 65 (14%).

3. **Scope 3 concerns**: The requirement would compel information from unregulated private entities (including farmers, ranchers, facility owners) outside SEC jurisdiction, create conflicting overlaps for suppliers contracting with multiple public companies, and draw legitimacy from the TCFD (a Swiss-created NGO) rather than US disclosure standards. The author argues the EPA already collects mandatory emissions data from companies producing 5,000+ metric tons of CO2 annually, making the SEC rule redundant.

4. **Historical context**: Prior to 2022, the SEC resisted mandatory climate disclosures. The NRDC sued the SEC in the early 1970s and failed. The DC Circuit ruled in the SEC's favor in 1979. The SEC issued only non-binding guidance in 2010 and admitted in 2016 it was powerless to mandate climate disclosures absent congressional directive.

5. **Public and institutional opinion**: Support is mixed — strongest among young Millennial/Gen Z investors and ESG rating/proxy advisory firms (especially Glass Lewis and ISS, which control 94% of the proxy advisory market), while weakest among affected public company employees. Only 21% of companies had internal ESG working groups. Polls show low willingness to pay for climate policy implementation (40% of Americans unwilling to spend even $1 annually on higher energy prices). The author argues proxy advisory firms benefit financially from the rule through their ESG consulting services, creating conflicts of interest.

The author concludes the rule should be reconsidered, arguing the SEC should leave climate policy to the EPA and focus on financially material disclosures. The analysis identifies potential constitutional challenges under the First Amendment, Axon v. FTC (2023), and the compulsion of nonmaterial information.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The SEC's own estimates find that mandatory climate disclosures will increase annual compliance costs from $3.8 billion to $10.2 billion, a $6.4 billion rise."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The Unconsidered Costs of the SEC's Climate Disclosure ... ---
URL: https://www.sec.gov/comments/s7-10-22/s71022-20132304-302836.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an opinion/analysis piece by Dr. Matthew Winden, Chair and Associate Professor of Economics at the University of Wisconsin-Whitewater, arguing that the SEC's proposed Climate Disclosure Rule would impose substantial economy-wide costs that exceed its benefits to investors and would fail an appropriate cost-benefit test.

**Key Arguments:**

1. **The Rule:** The SEC's proposed rule would require public companies to disclose both direct and transition climate change risks, including greenhouse gas emissions in three categories: Scope 1 (direct operations), Scope 2 (purchased electricity), and Scope 3 (indirect sources like suppliers and customers).

2. **Limited Investor Benefits:** The author argues that roughly 20% of public companies already voluntarily disclose ESG metrics, so the rule adds little new information to markets. Since 2010, companies have already been required to report material climate-related risks.

3. **Compliance Costs:** The SEC estimates incremental direct costs of $6.37 billion annually—165% of current SEC compliance costs of $3.85 billion. Using the REMI (Regional Economic Models, Inc.) computable general equilibrium model, the author models impacts including: approximately $25 billion in U.S. GDP foregone annually and 200,000 fewer jobs per year once fully implemented (by 2025). This equals roughly 0.1% of U.S. GDP and jobs. The hardest-hit sectors would be capital-intensive ones like manufacturing, finance, construction, and real estate.

4. **Anti-Competitiveness:** Compliance costs would disadvantage U.S. public companies relative to private and foreign firms, potentially shifting carbon-intensive production overseas with little net global emissions benefit. Without border adjustment taxes or demand changes, emissions would simply be displaced internationally.

5. **Retail Investor Losses:** Higher disclosure costs may incentivize firms to stay private or go private, depriving retail investors of lucrative returns—citing that the top 20 IPOs in the 3 years before June 2021 returned between 569% and 1,477%.

6. **Market Inefficiency:** The rule's prescriptive-sounding guidance could lead to technological "lock-in," directing capital to existing technologies at the expense of nascent alternatives, reducing market efficiency.

7. **Alternative Policy:** The author advocates for comprehensive legislative action, such as a carbon tax with border adjustments, which would apply economy-wide and better incentivize emissions reductions (commercial and industrial sectors only represent 30% of emissions). The author warns the rule may reduce incentives for meaningful congressional climate legislation—creating a "second best" policy response that delays effective action.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The SEC estimates companies will incur incremental direct costs of $6.37 billion for compliance with this new rule, a figure fully 165% of current SEC compliance costs of $3.85 billion – this will more than double current SEC regulatory compliance costs."

URL: https://www.gibsondunn.com/sec-proposes-rescission-of-climate-related-disclosure-rules

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Gibson Dunn client alert (June 3, 2026) reports on the SEC's formal proposal, issued May 29, 2026, to rescind its climate-related disclosure rules (the "Climate Rules") adopted in March 2024 under the Gensler Commission. The Climate Rules established a climate-related disclosure framework for registration statements and annual reports, covering climate-related risks, governance, risk-management processes, and financial statement requirements for severe weather events. The rules generated significant litigation immediately after adoption, and in April 2024 the SEC stayed their effectiveness pending consolidated litigation in the Eighth Circuit. In March 2025, the SEC voted to abandon its defense of the rules, and in May 2026 notified the Eighth Circuit of its decision to propose rescission through notice-and-comment rulemaking.

Key details: The Proposal was published in the Federal Register on June 3, 2026, with comments due by August 3, 2026. The Proposal does not itself terminate the Climate Rules—it initiates an APA notice-and-comment process. The SEC estimates annualized cost savings from rescission of approximately $4.9 billion per year over 10 years across all affected registrants. The Proposal cites concerns raised by commenters and litigants, and notes the court has not made any decision on the merits. Gibson Dunn advises that commenters should submit views addressing practical, legal, and economic implications, particularly quantitative and qualitative data on the effects of the Climate Rules, to build a well-developed administrative record supporting the durability of any final action. The alert was prepared by Gibson Dunn lawyers including Mellissa Campbell Duru, Elizabeth Ising, Thomas J. Kim, Ronald O. Mueller, Lori Zyskowski, and Jack Strachan.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: The SEC's Final Climate Rule: Your Guide To Compliance ---
URL: https://getgoodlab.com/resources/preparing-for-the-secs-upcoming-esg-climate-disclosure-requirements

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Good.Lab provides a comprehensive guide to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) final climate disclosure rule, known as "The Enhancement and Standardization of Climate-Related Disclosures for Investors." The rule was finalized on March 6, 2024, through a 3-2 vote after receiving an unprecedented 24,000 comment letters during its two-year development process. It represents the first federal climate reporting regulation in the U.S.

**Key requirements:**
- Large Accelerated Filers (LAF, public float >$700M, ~2,500 companies) and Accelerated Filers (AF, public float $250-700M, ~900 companies) must report material Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions, with third-party assurance requirements.
- All covered reporters must disclose financially material climate risks aligned with the Taskforce on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) framework, including governance, strategy, risk management, transition plans, scenario analysis, and internal carbon pricing.
- Scope 3 emissions disclosure is not required for any company. Smaller companies (NAF, SRC, EGC) are exempt from emissions reporting.
- Physical climate risks (costs from severe weather, sea level rise) must be reported when exceeding 1% of turnover before tax—the only non-material disclosure requirement.
- Materiality follows the Supreme Court definition: a fact is material if a reasonable investor would view it as significantly altering the "total mix" of information.

**Compliance timeline:**
- 2026: LAFs make first climate risk disclosures (FY25 data)
- 2027: LAFs report Scope 1/2 emissions; AFs make first climate risk disclosures
- 2028: NAFs, SRCs, and EGCs make first climate risk disclosures; AFs begin collecting emissions data
- 2029: AFs report Scope 1/2 emissions
- 2030: LAFs obtain limited assurance on emissions
- 2032: AFs obtain limited assurance on emissions
- 2034: LAFs obtain reasonable assurance on emissions

**Impact on private companies:** Although not directly bound, private companies will be affected through supply chain data requests, increased stakeholder expectations, IPO preparation benefits, competitive advantages, and California's SB 253 and SB 261 rules (which require ~10,000 companies doing business in California to report Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions beginning 2026).

**Compliance costs:** The SEC estimates compliance costs range from under $197,000 to over $739,000 depending on reporting extent, compared to the original proposal's estimated $530,000 average first-year cost.

**Preparation steps:** Understand compliance requirements, conduct a materiality assessment, complete a climate risk assessment, and start collecting emissions data. 

**Penalties:** The SEC does not specify fixed penalties, but has issued millions in fines for greenwashing—the largest being a $19 million fine against Deutsche Bank in 2023. Non-compliance also carries reputational risks, which 55% of companies now consider a top 5 operating risk.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Large Accelerated Filers (LAF) and Accelerated Filers (AF) are expected to report on and obtain assurance for material Scope 1 and 2 emissions. Smaller companies are exempt. All companies are exempt from disclosing Scope 3."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: SEC Climate Disclosure Guidance ---
URL: https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/services/audit-assurance/articles/sec-climate-disclosure-guidance.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Deloitte "Heads Up" publication analyzes the SEC's landmark final rule on climate-related risk disclosures, issued on March 6, 2024. The rule requires registrants to provide comprehensive climate-related disclosures in their annual reports and registration statements, beginning with annual reports for the year ending December 31, 2025, for calendar-year-end large accelerated filers.

**Key components of the rule:**
- Disclosures required outside financial statements include: material scope 1 and scope 2 GHG emissions (with phased-in assurance for large accelerated and accelerated filers), governance and oversight of material climate-related risks, material impact of climate risks on strategy/business model/outlook, risk management processes, and material climate targets and goals.
- Financial statement footnote disclosures include impacts from severe weather events and natural conditions on financial estimates/assumptions, plus roll-forward of carbon offsets and renewable energy credits (RECs) if material to meeting climate targets.

**Key changes from the proposed rule:**
- Established a materiality threshold for scope 1 and scope 2 GHG emissions with delayed filing allowed (by second fiscal quarterly report of the following year).
- Gave flexibility in determining organizational boundary for GHG emissions.
- Eliminated the scope 3 GHG emission disclosure requirement.
- Removed the line-item-by-line-item financial impact evaluation requirement, replacing it with an aggregate threshold exceeding 1% of pretax income or total shareholders' equity.
- Lengthened the adoption timeline: nearly 2 years for most disclosures, 3 years for GHG emission information, and 6 years for limited assurance over GHG emissions.
- Exempted smaller reporting companies (SRCs), emerging growth companies (EGCs), and nonaccelerated filers from GHG emission disclosure and related attestation requirements.

**Materiality and safe harbor:** The rule adopts the US Supreme Court definition of materiality ("a substantial likelihood that a reasonable investor would consider it important..."). A safe harbor protects registrants from liability for transition plans, scenario analysis, internal carbon pricing, and targets/goals disclosures (excluding historical facts).

**Attestation and controls:** Financial statement disclosures are subject to existing audit requirements and ICFR. All non-financial statement disclosures are subject to DCPs. Scope 1 and 2 GHG disclosures require limited assurance (phased in) for large accelerated and accelerated filers, with reasonable assurance later for large accelerated filers.

**Affected companies and timing:** All domestic and foreign registrants except asset-backed issuers must provide disclosures. The rule becomes effective 60 days after Federal Register publication. Domestic registrants may disclose emission information in their second-quarter Form 10-Q. Foreign private issuers may file via Form 20-F amendment due 225 days after fiscal year-end.

**Legal status:** On April 4, 2024, the SEC voluntarily stayed the effective date pending judicial review by the US District Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, though the stay does not reverse or change any requirements and does not affect the SEC's 2010 interpretive release on climate-change disclosures.

**Comparison with other regulations:** The rule leverages GHG Protocol and TCFD frameworks. Unlike the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards and EU CSRD (which broadly address sustainability/ESG), the SEC rule addresses climate disclosures only. Companies subject to EU CSRD will need to provide more extensive disclosures, including assurance over all climate disclosures.

**Implementation considerations:** The vast majority of companies will need the transition period to develop reporting capabilities, data requirements, and processes/controls. Recommended actions include: establishing/refining climate governance, understanding current climate disclosure state, identifying disclosure and control gaps, assessing reporting/data management, preparing for attestation, developing an action plan (integrating with CSRD/California requirements), and executing while adapting to future developments.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
SEC Chair Gary Gensler noted that the final rule will provide "investors with consistent, comparable, decision-useful information, and issuers with clear reporting requirements."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Heads Up — Comprehensive Analysis of the SEC’s Proposed Rule on Climate Disclosure Requirements (March 29, 2022) | DART – Deloitte Accounting Research Tool ---
URL: https://dart.deloitte.com/USDART/home/publications/deloitte/heads-up/2022/sec-analysis-climate-disclosures

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Deloitte Heads Up publication (Volume 29, Issue 4, March 29, 2022) providing a comprehensive analysis of the SEC's proposed rule on climate disclosure requirements, issued by the SEC on March 21, 2022. The proposed rule would enhance and standardize climate-related disclosures for public companies in their registration statements and annual reports (e.g., Form 10-K).

KEY REQUIREMENTS:
• Financial statement disclosures: Registrants would disclose, in a footnote to audited financial statements, financial impacts of climate-related events (severe weather, flooding, drought, wildfires, extreme temperatures, sea level rise) and transition activities (efforts to reduce GHG emissions). This includes financial impact metrics, expenditure metrics, and discussion of impacts on financial estimates and assumptions. A "bright line" 1% threshold of the related line item (for impact metrics) or total expenditures/capitalized costs (for expenditure metrics) triggers separate disclosure of positive and negative impacts.
• GHG emissions: Disclosure required for Scope 1 (direct emissions), Scope 2 (indirect from purchased energy), and Scope 3 (value chain) emissions. Scope 3 disclosures are required only if material or if the registrant has set a reduction target covering such emissions. Disclosures must be disaggregated by each GHG and aggregated using CO2e, plus GHG intensity metrics (tons of CO2e per unit of revenue and per unit produced).
• Governance: Detailed disclosure of board and management oversight of climate-related risks, including identification of responsible board members/committees, any climate expertise, and oversight processes.
• Climate-related risks: Required disclosure of physical risks (acute and chronic) and transition risks (regulatory, technological, market, liability, reputational), including locations (zip codes) of affected properties, and impacts on strategy, business model, and outlook.
• Climate risk management: Disclosure of processes for identifying, assessing, and managing climate-related risks, including transition plans if adopted.
• Climate targets and goals: Disclosure of scope, time horizon, interim targets, measurement methods, annual progress updates, and use of carbon offsets or renewable energy certificates.
• Attestation: Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions subject to limited assurance during phase-in, then reasonable assurance. Attestation providers must be GHG experts and independent.
• Internal controls: Financial statement disclosures subject to ICFR; other disclosures subject to disclosure controls and procedures and management certifications.
• Location: New "Climate-Related Disclosure" section immediately preceding MD&A; disclosures in audited financial statements only (not interim Form 10-Q filings, but material changes must be disclosed quarterly).

PHASE-IN TIMELINE (assuming finalization by December 2022, calendar year-end registrants):
• Large accelerated filers: all disclosures 2023, Scope 3 in 2024, limited assurance 2024, reasonable assurance 2026
• Accelerated filers: all disclosures 2024, Scope 3 in 2025, limited assurance 2025, reasonable assurance 2027
• Nonaccelerated filers: all disclosures 2024, Scope 3 in 2025, no attestation required
• Smaller reporting companies: exempt from Scope 3, all other disclosures in 2025

AFFECTED COMPANIES: All domestic and foreign registrants except asset-backed issuers, including IPOs and private operating companies merging with registrants (including SPACs). Notably, no exemption is provided for emerging growth companies (EGCs). Materiality follows the Supreme Court's definition (substantial likelihood that a reasonable investor would consider it important).

NOTABLE DIFFERENCES FROM EXISTING FRAMEWORKS: The proposed rule's treatment of subsidiaries/affiliates for GHG boundaries differs from the GHG Protocol—registrants would need to align reporting boundaries with consolidated financial statements.

BACKGROUND CONTEXT: The proposal follows a February 2022 release of company-specific DCF comment letters on climate disclosures (averaging ~6 comments per initial letter, ~5 per follow-up) and a September 2021 "Dear Issuer" letter. A Deloitte survey found 57% of executives cite data availability/quality as their greatest ESG disclosure challenge, only 21% have an ESG council, and 82% believe they need additional resources for ESG disclosures. Comments on the proposed rule were due 30 days after Federal Register publication or May 20, 2022, whichever was later.
</summary>

"The proposed rule would require registrants to disclose, in a footnote to the financial statements, the financial statement impacts of (1) climate-related events, including severe weather events and other natural conditions such as flooding, drought, wildfires, extreme temperatures, and sea level rise, and (2) transition activities, including 'efforts to reduce GHG emissions or otherwise mitigate exposure to transition risks.'"
</key_excerpts>
