* California Climate Disclosure Laws – Countdown to Disclosure: What Companies Need To Know About Reporting Deadlines, CARB Guidance and Ongoing Litigation



October 13, 2025

# California Climate Disclosure Laws – Countdown to Disclosure: What Companies Need To Know About Reporting Deadlines, CARB Guidance and Ongoing Litigation

Authors: 

* [Stephanie M. Hurst](/en/people/h/hurst-stephanie-m),
* [Paul C. de Bernier](/en/people/d/de-bernier-paul-c),
* [Dario J. Frommer](/en/people/f/dario-j-frommer),
* [McKaela R. Broitman](/en/people/b/mckaela-r-broitman)

[Generate PDF](https://1npdf11.onenorth.com/pdfrenderer.svc/v1/ABCpdf11/GetRenderedPdfByUrl/california-climate-disclosure-laws--countdown-to-disclosure-what-companies-need-to-know-about-reporting-deadlines-carb-guidance-and-ongoing-litigation.pdf/?url=https://www.mayerbrown.com/en/pdf/insights/publications/2025/10/california-climate-disclosure-laws--countdown-to-disclosure-what-companies-need-to-know-about-reporting-deadlines-carb-guidance-and-ongoing-litigation)

Share

As discussed in our prior Legal Updates,[1](#_edn1) in late 2023, California enacted a landmark set of climate-related disclosure laws—collectively referred to as the “California Climate Accountability Package”[2](#_edn2) —comprising:

* **SB 253** (*Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act*), requiring disclosures of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions; and
* **SB 261** (*Climate-Related Financial Risk Act*), requiring disclosures of climate-related financial risks.

As companies prepare for upcoming disclosure deadlines in 2026, uncertainty remains regarding certain key aspects of these laws.

In this Legal Update, we address recent key developments. These include “additional guidance” from the California Air Resources Board (CARB), ongoing legal challenges and CARB’s preliminary “list of entities” potentially subject to SB 253 and SB 261 (Preliminary CARB List).

#### Recap of SB 253 and SB 261

As a reminder, SB 253 and SB 261,[3](#_edn3) each of which was amended by SB 219,[4](#_edn4) impose climate-related corporate disclosure requirements as follows:

* SB 253 requires US companies—public and private—doing business in California with annual global (not just California) revenues of more than $1 billion to disclose, on an annual basis, (a) Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions, starting in 2026, and (b) Scope 3 GHG emissions, starting in 2027.
* SB 261 requires US companies—public and private—doing business in California with annual global (not just California) revenues of more than $500 million to disclose climate-related financial risks and measures taken to mitigate and adapt to such risks, starting January 1, 2026. Insurance companies are exempted, and this is a biennial requirement.

#### Recent CARB Updates

Given the ambiguity around the nature and scope of certain requirements, CARB has been active in recent months as it has worked to implement and clarify the application of SB 253 and SB 261, including hosting two virtual public “workshops” and issuing various guidance. This Legal Update outlines where things stand after the following CARB activities:

* **Virtual Public Workshops:** CARB hosted two virtual public workshops (CARB Workshops) for SB 253 and SB 261, including to solicit further public feedback. These were held on May 29, 2025 (First Workshop)[5](#_edn5) and August 21 (Second Workshop).[6](#_edn6) During the First Workshop, CARB offered more conceptual and preliminary options, whereas, during the Second Workshop, CARB had incorporated stakeholder feedback received in connection with the First Workshop and offered more refined and concrete proposals for ongoing stakeholder feedback. The public comment period for such proposals concluded on September 11.
* **Responses to Frequently Asked Questions:** On July 9, CARB published an FAQ document titled [*California Corporate Greenhouse Gas Reporting and Climate-Related Financial Risk Disclosure Programs: Frequently Asked Questions Related to Regulatory Development and Initial Reports*](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-07/FAQs Regarding California Climate Disclosure Requirements_ver1.pdf) (the FAQs Guide). The FAQs Guide is designed to assist companies potentially subject to SB 253 and SB 261 navigate the regulatory development process, better understand applicability and identify initial steps toward compliance.
* **SB 261 Compliance Checklist:** On September 2, CARB published a [draft compliance checklist](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-09/Climate Related Financial Risk Report Checklist.pdf) (the SB 261 Checklist) for SB 261. The SB 261 Checklist offers guidance on reporting frameworks, disclosure content and procedural requirements, with the goal of supporting transparent, decision-useful reporting for investors and other stakeholders.
* **Preliminary List of Potentially Covered Entities:** On September 24, CARB published a list of entities potentially subject to SB 253 and/or SB 261. The Preliminary CARB List was drawn from publicly available California Secretary of State data identifying entities “doing business” in California, based on a dataset limited to active filings through March 2022.
* **SB 253 Reporting Templates:** On October 10, CARB published its [Scope 1 and Scope 2 Emissions Draft Reporting Template](https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fww2.arb.ca.gov%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-10%2FSB253_Draft_Scope1_2_GHG_Template.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK) (the SB 253 Template), as well as the related [memo](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/Draft Memo_Scope1%262TemplatePublicRelease.pdf) (the SB 253 Template Memo) providing guidance on how to use the SB 253 Template. CARB has solicited stakeholder feedback with respect to both the SB 253 Template and the SB 253 Template Memo, which feedback may be submitted through a [public docket](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/public-comments/draft-reporting-template-scope-1-and-scope-2-ghg-emissions). The deadline to provide feedback is October 27, 2025.

Key takeaways from CARB’s guidance are set forth below:

#### Initial Reporting Deadlines

The current state of play regarding the initial reporting deadlines is as follows:

* **SB 261**: Companies must publish climate risk reports by **January 1, 2026**, posting links on their websites and in CARB’s new public “docket” (to be open from December 1, 2025 through July 1, 2026).
* **SB 253**: CARB has proposed **June 30, 2026** as the initial deadline for Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions disclosure. The initial deadline for Scope 3 GHG emissions disclosure would begin in 2027, with the exact date to be determined.

##### Defining Which Entities Are Within the Scope of SB 253 and SB 261

* **Defining “Doing Business” in California:** CARB’s early focus has been on how to define which entities fall within the laws’ scope. While the laws require compliance from certain entities “doing business” in California, the term was not expressly defined. Although CARB has considered whether tax nexus rules, corporate databases, or some combination of these and other sources may be relevant to the definition, the precise connection to California under the “doing business” standard has yet to be definitively resolved.

The initial proposal by CARB was to use the definition of “doing business” set forth in the California Revenue and Tax Code (RTC) Section 23101 with some modifications. This definition of “doing business” sets a low threshold that would bring companies with minimal ties to California within scope, with an entity considered to be doing business if it, for example, “engage[s] in any transaction for the purpose of financial gain within California” or exceeds minimal sales, property or payroll thresholds, with the 2024 thresholds being $735,019, $73,502 and $73,502, respectively.[7](#_edn7)

Following public feedback that this RTC definition may be too broad, during the Second Workshop, CARB noted that it was evaluating alternative approaches, including reliance on existing databases to identify covered entities.

While the California Franchise Tax Board’s data was discussed, CARB noted statutory restrictions on its use. In contrast, the California Secretary of State’s business entity database—listing entities with a designated agent for service of process in California—was highlighted as a potential tool.

CARB also referenced its ongoing analysis of California Secretary of State and Dunn & Bradstreet data to validate a preliminary list of potentially covered entities, which CARB released near the end of September (i.e., the Preliminary CARB List). Importantly, however, CARB emphasized that companies are ultimately responsible for compliance regardless of whether they appear on the Preliminary CARB List or as part of CARB’s outreach efforts.

* **Defining Parent-Subsidiary Relationships:** During the First Workshop, CARB had initially proposed adopting a definition of parent-subsidiary relationships that builds off of the Cap-and-Trade[8](#_edn8) program’s concept of “corporate association,” which requires disclosure of certain corporate relationships based on certain “indicia of ownership interest or control.” This proposal considered the following to define parent-subsidiary relationships:
  + The company is considered a subsidiary of another where the parent or holding company owns more than 50% of its voting stock.
  + The subsidiary has a different legal entity name than its parent or holding company.
  + The parent or holding company has a controlling interest in its subsidiary and therefore is able to influence the subsidiary’s operations, management and financial decisions.

CARB invited stakeholder input on whether this operational control threshold is appropriate or if alternative standards or additional factors should be considered.

At the Second Workshop, CARB reaffirmed this approach (i.e., building on the Cap-and-Trade program’s approach) and proposed leveraging commercial ownership databases, cross-referenced with the California Secretary of State and California Franchise Tax Board records to identify applicable parent-subsidiary relationships. CARB also sought stakeholder feedback on the potential for a voluntary self-reporting process that would allow companies to disclose parent-subsidiary relationships and consolidate reporting across commonly controlled entities.

Subject to further refinement from CARB’s forthcoming implementing regulations, the expectation is that parent companies would not automatically be brought into scope of SB 253 and SB 261 merely because one of their subsidiaries is subject to one or both of these laws. In other words, in order to be a covered entity subject to one or both of SB 253 and/or SB 261, such entity must itself meet the relevant revenue thresholds, be a US entity and be considered to be doing business in California. That said, CARB has clarified that reporting under SB 253 and SB 261 may be consolidated at that parent level such that a parent company may report on behalf of its covered subsidiaries.

* **Potential Exemptions:** On its face, SB 261 exempts regulated insurance companies, but SB 253 does not provide exemptions.

However, in response to public feedback, during the Second Workshop, CARB considered whether additional exemptions might be appropriate and proposed that the following would be exempt from both SB 253 and SB 261:

* Nonprofit organizations;
* Companies whose only presence in California consists of teleworking employees; and
* The California Independent System Operator (CAISO) or business entities engaged solely in wholesale electricity transactions occurring in interstate commerce.

CARB clarified that government entities are outside the scope of the laws.

* **Defining “Revenue”:** CARB’s treatment of “revenue” has shifted as it worked through stakeholder feedback. Initially, CARB proposed defining “revenue” by reference to the definition of “gross receipts” under RTC Section 25120(f)(2). CARB invited stakeholder input, including on whether this definition was consistent with prevailing business practices, how it should be applied in the parent-subsidiary context, and whether alternative definitions of “revenue” should be considered for purposes of SB 253 and SB 261.

At the Second Workshop, CARB acknowledged that “gross receipts” may not be a suitable metric. In particular, stakeholders raised concerns regarding data confidentiality limitations, challenges in verification and the overly expansive scope of the definition. CARB, seeking to be aligned with the methodologies used by such sources as Dunn & Bradstreet and Standard & Poor, proposed that “revenue” would be defined as the “total global amount of money or sales a company receives from its business activities, such as selling products or providing services,” without deductions for operating costs or business expenses.

* **Estimated Number of Potentially Covered Entities:**
  + The legislative history for SB 253 and SB 261 suggested the number of potentially covered entities to be quite significant—5,344 for SB 253, and 10,000+ for SB 261.
  + However, during the Second Workshop, CARB suggested that the proposed revisions to key elements defining which entities would be covered by these climate-related disclosure laws would significantly reduce the number of entities potentially within scope—2,596 for SB 253 and 4,160 for SB 261.

* **Preliminary CARB List:** The Preliminary CARB List identifies entities potentially subject to SB 253 and/or SB 261. It was derived from data from the California Secretary of State relating to entities doing business in California. The Preliminary CARB List does not take into account potential exemptions to SB 253 and SB 261 that were discussed during the Second Workshop.

As noted above, in connection with publishing the Preliminary CARB List, CARB reiterated that potentially covered entities are responsible for compliance with SB 253 and SB 261, even if such entities are not included on the Preliminary CARB List. CARB also requested [stakeholder feedback to the Preliminary CARB List](https://survey123.arcgis.com/share/0893ede53c234aac8d5334df0f091f36?portalUrl=https://gis.carb.arb.ca.gov/portal). It would be prudent to submit survey feedback sooner rather than later to potentially inform CARB’s rulemaking process. However, there’s no official cutoff date announced for the survey itself.

##### SB 253: GHG Emissions Disclosure Guidance

* **Independent Verification of Data; Assurance:** Verification by an independent third party is required at a limited-assurance level for Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions disclosure starting in the initial 2026 reporting year, escalating to reasonable assurance in 2030.

During the Second Workshop, CARB suggested that limited assurance would include:

* Sampling plans;
* Reviews of data management systems;
* Limited data checks;
* Limited conformance checks;
* Process documentation;
* Log of any found and corrected errors by the covered entity; and
* Report and statement at the conclusion of the review.

CARB also identified potential standards for such third-party assurance, including (a) the International Standard on Sustainability Assurance (ISSA) 5000, issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB), (b) AccountAbility AA1000 Series of Standards developed by AccountAbility, (c) ISO 14060 family developed by the International Organization for Standardization and (d) the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) standards.

* **Template Disclosures:** As noted above, on October 10, 2025, CARB published the SB 253 Template, as well as the SB 253 Template Memo to guide the use of the SB 253 Template. Covered entities are not required to use the SB 253 Template, with its use being voluntary for the initial reporting cycle in 2026.

The SB 253 Template is organized into several sections, including the following: (a) organization information, (b) third-party verification, (c) inventory boundary, (d) Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions disclosure, (e) methodology, (f) de minimis / minor sources, (g) California MRR (i.e., California Mandatory Reporting Regulation) fields (if applicable) and (h) emissions reductions (if applicable). The SB 253 Template also includes optional fields for future reporting years, such as base year emissions, which are intended to support intraorganizational comparisons and provide greater transparency.

In addition, the SB 253 Template provides several potential pertinent reporting fields that touch on the following:

* *Emissions Intensity Metrics*: Covered entities can provide at least one intensity or efficiency ratio (e.g., emissions per $1 million in revenue). These ratios allow stakeholders to compare performance between companies of varying sizes and across different industries.
* *Industry Classification*: Covered entities can categorize their GHG emissions using the 2-digit North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes, enabling consistent sector-based analysis.
* *Transparency in Methods*: Covered entities can identify the source and year of Global Warming Potential (GWP) values and emissions factors and provide a brief description of the calculation method used.
* *Alignment with the California MRR*: Covered entities can include California MRR facility identification numbers, which ensure alignment of data with CARB’s other regulatory databases.

These templates are currently in draft form, with CARB seeking stakeholder feedback on key areas, including (a) disclosure by source vs. by gas; (b) organizational boundaries; and (c) emissions reduction initiatives.

* **Enforcement Discretion:** CARB will allow companies to use existing data for the first reporting cycle and will exercise enforcement discretion[9](#_edn9) to accommodate companies needing time to implement new data collection processes.

##### SB 261: Climate-Related Financial Risk Disclosure Guidance

* **Framework Options:** The SB 261 Checklist confirms that covered entities may select from several established reporting frameworks to structure their disclosures:
  + Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) Final Report (2017) or any successor framework;
  + International Financial Reporting Standards Sustainability Disclosure Standards (IFRS S2); or
  + Other frameworks developed in accordance with regulated exchanges, national governments or US federal regulations.

Each report must:

* Identify the chosen framework;
* Specify which recommendations have been addressed; and
* Explain any omissions or plans for future inclusion.

This approach enables covered entities to adopt a phased path toward full compliance, while maintaining transparency and accountability in their climate risk reporting.

* **Core Disclosure Requirements:** The SB 261 Checklist outlines minimum disclosure expectation across four key pillars, broadly consistent with TCFD and IFRS S2 principles:
  + *Governance*: Describe the covered entity’s governance framework for managing climate-related financial risk, including board and management oversight.
  + *Strategy*: Identify short-, medium- and long-term climate-related risks and opportunities, and explain how these affect the covered entity’s operations, business strategy and financial planning (where material).
  + *Risk Management*: Explain the process used to identify, assess and manage climate-related risks and how those considerations and processes are integrated into the covered entity’s overall risk management.
  + *Metrics and Targets*: Disclose the metrics and targets used to evaluate and manage material climate-related risks and opportunities, including measures adopted to mitigate and adapt to those risks.

* **Practical SB 261 Disclosure Guidance:** In addition to outlining key disclosure expectations, CARB provided further implementation guidance designed to ease the obligations of covered entities during the first reporting cycle:
  + *Qualitative Scenario Analysis*: CARB encourages the use of climate scenarios to inform strategic disclosures. Scenario analysis may be qualitative or quantitative, reflecting stakeholder feedback that quantitative modeling may be duplicative of SB 253 requirements or unduly burdensome.
  + *Consolidated Reporting*: A subsidiary is not required to file a separate SB 261 report if its parent company reports on its behalf. Consolidated, parent-level reporting is permitted.
  + *GHG Emissions Disclosures*: While some reporting frameworks include Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 GHG emissions metrics, CARB confirmed that GHG emissions disclosures are not required for the initial SB 261 reporting period, acknowledging stakeholder feedback regarding potential overlap with SB 253 reporting requirements and data availability constraints.
  + *Data Source*: For initial reports, covered entities should rely on the most recent and best available data, whether based on calendar year or fiscal year reporting, to ensure consistency and verifiability.

In addition, unlike the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS E1), SB 261 does not expressly require formal transition plans, although it does require a covered entity to identify measures it is taking to reduce and/or adapt to relevant climate-related financial risks. This is functionally similar to a transition plan mandated by such EU regulation, especially for covered entities aligning with the TCFD or IFRS S2 frameworks.

* **Enforcement Discretion:** CARB did not initially address enforcement discretion for SB 261’s initial reporting year in its Enforcement Notice, issued on December 5, 2024 relating to SB 253. However, in the FAQs Guide, CARB emphasized a practical, phased approach to compliance, recognizing the need for lead time and the use of best available information for initial reports. CARB noted that it would consider good faith efforts to comply in enforcement decisions, particularly during the initial implementation period.

##### Flat Fee Structure

* During the Second Workshop, CARB proposed a flat annual fee structure of $3,106 for SB 253 and $1,403 for SB 261, with covered entities over $1 billion in revenue paying both fees.
* Even if parent-level consolidated reports are filed, subsidiaries are still required to pay separate entity fees.

##### Timeline for Draft Regulations

* **SB 253:** Under SB 253, CARB was initially required to provide implementing regulations by January 1, 2025. This deadline was extended under SB 219 to July 1, 2025.

During the First Workshop, and despite the delay in issuing implementing regulations (which CARB suggested would not be issued until the end of 2025), the sponsors of SB 253 and SB 261—Senators Scott Wiener and Henry Stern—confirmed that the initial reporting deadlines would not be delayed.

During the Second Workshop, CARB announced a clearer timeline for issuing the implementing regulations, which would be on an accelerated schedule, with draft regulations targeted for publication on October 14, 2025, followed by a 45-day public comment period and final Board consideration on December 11-12, 2025.

* **SB 261:** Under SB 261, CARB is not expressly required to issue implementation regulations. During the First Workshop, however, CARB requested public feedback as to how it should implement SB 261 (e.g., formal regulation, guidance, etc.). Whether regulations or only guidance will be issued in connection with SB 261 remains to be seen.

#### Federal Litigation Developments

While there have been several challenges, some of which are still ongoing, the bottom line is that both laws remain very much in effect, subject to CARB’s ongoing interpretive activity.

As discussed in our [February 2024 Legal Update](https://www.mayerbrown.com/en/insights/publications/2024/02/lawsuit-challenges-recent-california-climate-disclosure-laws), several business and industry trade organizations, including the US Chamber of Commerce and the California Chamber of Commerce, filed a lawsuit in January 2024 in federal court against CARB (and its representatives) seeking to overturn SB 253 and SB 261.

As a refresher, the plaintiffs in that case contend that SB 253 and SB 261:

* Violate the First Amendment by compelling speech (Count I);
* Are preempted by the US Constitution and federal law, including the Clean Air Act, and violate the Supremacy Clause (Count II); and
* Violate the US Constitution’s limitations on extraterritorial regulation, including the Dormant Commerce Clause (Count III).

Further, as discussed in our [February 2025 Legal Update](https://www.mayerbrown.com/en/insights/publications/2025/02/californias-climate-disclosure-laws-navigating-the-latest-updates), the Court ruled on certain dispositive motions, including:

* Denying the plaintiffs’ motion for summary judgment, which had addressed Count I (the First Amendment claims); and
* Granting the defendants’ motion to dismiss as follows: (a) Counts II and III as to SB 253 were dismissed without prejudice; (b) Count II as to SB 261 was dismissed with prejudice; and (c) Count III as to SB 261 was dismissed without prejudice.

Following the Court’s ruling on the defendants’ motion to dismiss, there have been several developments in the case:

* **Denial of Preliminary Injunction:** On February 25, 2025, the plaintiffs filed a motion for preliminary injunction seeking to enjoin the defendants from implementing, applying, or taking any action to enforce SB 253 and SB 261. In that motion, the plaintiffs argued that SB 253 and SB 261 violate the First Amendment by compelling speech on a controversial topic, are overbroad, and impose immediate and irreparable harm on affected businesses. On August 13, 2025, the Court denied the plaintiffs’ motion for preliminary injunction, finding that the plaintiffs had not shown a likelihood of success on the merits of their facial First Amendment challenges to SB 253 and SB 261.
* **Denial of Injunction Pending Appeal:** On August 20, 2025, the plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal and a motion for injunction pending appeal with the District Court. While the District Court denied this motion for injunction pending appeal on September 11, the appeal of the District Court’s initial denial of the motion for preliminary injunction on August 13, 2025 remains pending in the Ninth Circuit.
* **Pending Ninth Circuit Injunction Pending Appeal:** Following the plaintiffs’ notice of appeal and the District Court’s denial of the plaintiffs’ motion for injunction pending appeal, the plaintiffs filed a motion for injunction pending appeal on September 15, 2025 in the Ninth Circuit and requested relief by November 3, 2025. This motion for injunction pending appeal remains pending.

#### Practical Takeaways to Prepare for Compliance

Despite ongoing uncertainty, early preparation remains critical for potentially covered entities. SB 253 and SB 261 place California at the forefront of global climate reporting, and companies that proactively align with these standards will be best positioned to meet regulatory requirements and manage risk.

To support timely readiness for the looming deadlines, potentially covered entities should consider taking the following steps:

* **Confirm Applicability:**
  + Review the Preliminary CARB List to determine whether the company or its parent or subsidiaries have been identified.
  + Verify annual global revenue and assess whether the company is “doing business” in California under CARB’s proposed definitions.
  + Identify covered entities and subsidiaries under CARB’s proposed ownership threshold or control test and determine whether reporting will be consolidated.

* **Strengthen Governance:**
  + Establish or enhance board and management oversight of climate-related disclosures, with clear allocation of responsibilities.
  + Integrate climate oversight into existing governance and risk management frameworks.

* **Establish Robust Control Systems and Ensure Coordination:**
  + Strengthen internal controls and train teams on data integrity, evidence gathering and assurance readiness.
  + Align legal, finance, sustainability and communications functions to ensure consistent, compliant disclosures.
  + Formalize internal processes for preparation, review and validation of disclosures under SB 253 and/or SB 261.

* **Preparing for SB 253 Reporting (GHG Emissions):**
  + Map and validate data sources for Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 GHG emissions.
  + Align methodologies with the GHG Protocol.
  + Engage assurance providers early to prepare for limited assurance disclosures in 2026 and reasonable assurance by 2030.

* **Preparing for SB 261 Reporting (Climate-Related Financial Risk):**
  + Select a reporting framework (e.g., TCFD or IFRS S2) and identify gaps across the four pillars: (a) governance, (b) strategy, (c) risk management and (d) metrics and targets.
  + Conduct or update a climate risk assessment, considering both transition and physical risks.
  + Integrate scenario analysis (qualitative or quantitative) into strategic planning and financial modeling.
  + Develop a disclosure and communications plan for investors and other stakeholders.

Our team is closely monitoring CARB’s regulatory developments. If you have questions about SB 253, SB 261 or California’s climate disclosure requirements and how they may apply to your company, please contact any of the authors of this Legal Update.

2 A third law was passed together with SB 253 and SB 261—AB 1305 (also known as the *Voluntary Carbon Market Disclosures Act*). AB 1305, which is already in effect, is not discussed in this Legal Update. For additional information on AB 1305, see our prior Legal Update, *[New California Anti-Greenwashing Law Goes Live on January 1, 2024 – What You Need to Know if You Make Certain “Green” Claims](https://www.mayerbrown.com/en/insights/publications/2023/12/new-california-antigreenwashing-law-goes-live-on-january-1-2024--what-you-need-to-know-if-you-make-certain-green-claims)*, dated December 7, 2023.

For additional information regarding SB 219, see our February 2025 Update.

While this bill amends both SB 253 and SB 261, it does not directly affect potentially covered entities. Rather, this bill is a budget-related bill that, among other things, streamlines the CARB rulemaking process by exempting CARB regulations under SB 253 and SB 261 from review under the California Environmental Quality Act.

5 CARB published a [recording of the First Workshop](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PF-obXuy-w4), and the [First Workshop’s related PowerPoint slides](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-05/SB 253 261 Workshop slides 5-29.pdf).

This is a Mayer Brown legal publication (dated October 13, 2025) analyzing California's climate disclosure laws—SB 253 (Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act) and SB 261 (Climate-Related Financial Risk Act)—collectively the "California Climate Accountability Package." The article addresses recent California Air Resources Board (CARB) developments, litigation status, reporting deadlines, and compliance guidance.

**Key Requirements Recap:**
- SB 253: Requires US companies (public and private) doing business in California with annual global revenues over $1 billion to disclose Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions starting 2026, and Scope 3 emissions starting 2027.
- SB 261: Requires US companies doing business in California with annual global revenues over $500 million to disclose climate-related financial risks biennially starting January 1, 2026. Insurance companies are exempt.

**CARB Recent Activities:**
- Two virtual public workshops held (May 29 and August 21, 2025)
- FAQ document published July 9, 2025
- SB 261 draft compliance checklist published September 2, 2025
- Preliminary list of potentially covered entities published September 24, 2025 (based on California Secretary of State data through March 2022)
- SB 253 reporting template and memo published October 10, 2025 (feedback deadline October 27, 2025)

**Reporting Deadlines:**
- SB 261: Climate risk reports due by January 1, 2026, with website links and CARB public docket (open December 1, 2025 through July 1, 2026)
- SB 253: Proposed June 30, 2026 deadline for Scope 1 and 2; Scope 3 beginning 2027

**Key Interpretive Developments:**
- "Doing business" definition still unresolved; CARB initially proposed RTC Section 23101 definition (low threshold: $735,019 sales, $73,502 property/payroll thresholds for 2024) but is considering alternatives
- CARB proposed exemptions for nonprofits, teleworking-only companies, and CAISO/wholesale electricity entities
- "Revenue" definition shifting from "gross receipts" toward total global amount of money/sales without deductions
- Estimated covered entities reduced from legislative estimates (5,344 for SB 253; 10,000+ for SB 261) to CARB's revised estimates (2,596 for SB 253; 4,160 for SB 261)
- Parent companies not automatically in scope merely because subsidiaries are covered; consolidated parent-level reporting permitted
- Proposed flat annual fees: $3,106 for SB 253 and $1,403 for SB 261 (subsidiaries must pay separate fees even with consolidated reporting)

**SB 253 Assurance Requirements:**
- Limited assurance required for Scope 1 and 2 starting 2026, escalating to reasonable assurance by 2030
- Potential standards: ISSA 5000, AccountAbility AA1000, ISO 14060, AICPA standards
- CARB exercising enforcement discretion for first reporting cycle with good faith efforts

**SB 261 Framework Options:**
- TCFD, IFRS S2, or other regulated frameworks permitted
- Four disclosure pillars: Governance, Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics and Targets
- GHG emissions disclosures NOT required for initial SB 261 reporting period
- Qualitative or quantitative scenario analysis encouraged
- No formal transition plans required (unlike EU CSRD/ESRS E1), but functionally similar expectations

**Litigation Status:**
- US Chamber of Commerce and California Chamber of Commerce filed suit in January 2024 challenging the laws (First Amendment compelled speech, federal preemption, Dormant Commerce Clause claims)
- Court denied plaintiffs' preliminary injunction motion on August 13, 2025
- Appeal pending in Ninth Circuit; motion for injunction pending appeal filed September 15, 2025

**Timeline for Regulations:**
- CARB draft regulations targeted for publication October 14, 2025, with 45-day comment period and final Board consideration December 11-12, 2025
- SB 261 does not expressly require implementing regulations

**Practical Takeaways:** Companies should confirm applicability via the Preliminary CARB List, strengthen governance, establish internal controls, prepare GHG data sources aligned with GHG Protocol, engage assurance providers early, select reporting frameworks, and conduct climate risk assessments.

# CARB Delays Rulemaking

Weekly Policy Insight

21 October 2025

## **LAST CALL: Register for the US SIF Fall Policy Webinar**

Join US SIF on **Wednesday, October 22 at 2pm** for our quarterly policy webinar to hear the latest updates from the White House, Congress, the SEC, and beyond.

**Register** [here](https://us02web.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_cd7q8LmHQ7uoE4xcwJa0lA)**.** (Registration is now closed)

---

## **CARB Delays and Additional Comment Opportunities**

California Air Resources Board [released an update](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/our-work/programs/corporate-ghg-reporting/resources) last week on the timeline of their proposed rulemaking regarding fee regulation for California’s corporate climate disclosure rules. The proposed rule will now likely be released in Q1 2026 rather than in October 2025. This will not delay the reporting deadline dates.

**Feedback galore:** CARB explained the delay is due to the large volume of public comments which the agency is receiving. Opportunities to comment have included general feedback following public workshops and specific feedback on CARB’s [climate-related financial risk report checklist](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-09/Climate%20Related%20Financial%20Risk%20Report%20Checklist.pdf) and its [preliminary list of regulated entities](https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fww2.arb.ca.gov%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-09%2FSB%2520253_261_preliminary_list_092425.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK).

**New opportunity:** CARB released a [draft template for scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas reporting](https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fww2.arb.ca.gov%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-10%2FSB253_Draft_Scope1_2_GHG_Template.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK) as voluntary guidance for covered 2026 reporting entities. CARB seeks public comment on the template and its [associated memo guidance,](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/Draft%20Memo_Scope1%262TemplatePublicRelease.pdf) specifically looking for feedback on the template’s structure, substance, and alignment with SB 253’s overarching objectives.

**Weigh in:** Submit public comments [here](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/public-comments/draft-reporting-template-scope-1-and-scope-2-ghg-emissions) by **October 27, 2025.**

---

## **What We’re Watching This Week**

**Week 4 of the government shutdown:** The Senate is set to vote for the 11th time on the Republican bill to fund the government; however, it is expected to fail again. With large swaths of governmental workers receiving reductions-in-force notices over the last couple weeks, federal agency action has remained quite limited.

args.summary:
This is a Weekly Policy Insight from US SIF (published October 21, 2025) covering developments in California climate disclosure regulation and federal government activities.

Key updates:
1. The California Air Resources Board (CARB) announced a delay in its proposed rulemaking for fee regulation under California's corporate climate disclosure rules (SB 253/SB 261). The proposed rule is now expected to be released in Q1 2026 instead of October 2025. This delay will NOT affect reporting deadline dates.
2. The delay is attributed to the large volume of public comments CARB has received, including feedback from public workshops and on CARB's climate-related financial risk report checklist and its preliminary list of regulated entities.
3. CARB released a new draft template for scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas reporting as voluntary guidance for covered 2026 reporting entities. Public comments on the template and associated memo guidance were due by October 27, 2025, with feedback sought on structure, substance, and alignment with SB 253's objectives.
4. The US SIF Fall Policy Webinar was scheduled for October 22, 2025 (registration closed at publication).
5. Regarding the federal government shutdown: it was in Week 4, with the Senate preparing for its 11th vote on a Republican funding bill expected to fail again. Widespread reductions-in-force notices had limited federal agency action.

This webpage covers the California Air Resources Board (CARB) Virtual Public Workshop held on August 21, 2025, regarding the implementation of California's corporate climate disclosure legislation package: SB 253, SB 261, and SB 219 (collectively referred to as "the 200s"). The workshop was CARB's second public workshop on this regulatory package.

Key topics covered:

1. **Background and Context**: SB 253 applies to US-based companies doing business in California with annual revenues over $1 billion, requiring disclosure of Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions. First reporting year for Scope 1 and 2 is 2026 (for 2025 emissions); Scope 3 reporting begins in 2027 (for 2026 emissions). Third-party assurance starts with limited assurance in 2026, moving to reasonable assurance by 2030. SB 261 applies to US companies with revenues over $500 million, requiring biennial climate-related financial risk disclosures posted publicly on company websites beginning January 1, 2026. SB 219 is a companion bill modifying SB 253 and 261.

2. **Definitions and Scope**: Staff are considering definitions for "revenue" (either using California tax code gross receipts definition or a draft alternative) and "doing business in California" (considering presence on the California Secretary of State database). Proposed exemptions include nonprofit organizations, companies with only teleworking employees in California, government entities, the California Independent System Operator (CAISO), and wholesale electricity transactions in interstate commerce. Staff estimate approximately 4,200 entities subject to SB 261 and about 2,600 subject to SB 253.

3. **Fee Structure**: Staff propose a flat fee per covered entity, calculated as total annual program cost divided by number of covered entities. There is a one-time $20.7 million charge to repay temporary funding from the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund. Recurring annual costs are approximately $13.9 million. Estimated fees: ~$3,316 per entity under SB 253 and ~$1,443 per entity under SB 261. Timeline: 3-week public comment period closes September 11, 2025; notice of proposed rulemaking on October 14, 2025; board hearing mid-December 2025.

4. **SB 261 Guidance**: Draft guidance covers the four TCFD/IFRS principles—governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets. CARB will accept good faith efforts and best available data for the first reporting cycle. CARB will post a public docket in December 2025 for companies to post links to their reports, open until July 1, 2026.

5. **SB 253 Reporting**: Staff propose a June 30, 2026 deadline for Scope 1 and 2 reporting. Draft reporting templates will be posted by end of September 2025.

6. **Assurance Criteria**: Staff are considering standards including ISSA 5000, AA 1000, ISO 14060 family, and AICPA for assurance providers. CARB will leverage its existing verification framework principles including independence, objectivity, and conflict of interest requirements.

7. **Public Comments**: Multiple stakeholders provided input. Key themes included questions about investment fund exemptions, fiscal year versus calendar year reporting, fee payment structures for parent-subsidiary relationships, and verification concerns regarding Scope 3 emission reporting methods under the GHG Protocol.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Stibbe law firm provides an EU ESG regulatory wrap-up covering legislative developments finalized in late 2025 and expected initiatives in 2026.

**Key 2025 Developments:**
- **Omnibus I** (amending CSRD and CSDDD) reached near-final status in December 2025, pending Council adoption. It reduces the scope of both directives, postpones application dates, and changes substantive requirements. Large public interest entities still in scope must report on 2025 and 2026 financial years.
- **EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR)** amendments were approved just before the original 30 December 2025 application date, postponing application by one year to 30 December 2026, introducing a simplified regime for downstream operators/traders, and requiring a mandatory simplification review by the Commission by April 2026.
- The **Environmental Omnibus** was published, proposing simplification of European environmental regulations to accelerate the energy transition.

On 26 February 2026, the EU published Directive (EU) 2026/470 (the "Omnibus I Directive"), which entered into force on 19 March 2026. This law substantially revises two flagship EU Green Deal instruments: the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CS3D), as part of the European Commission's simplification agenda to reduce regulatory burdens, especially on SMEs, while preserving core sustainability ambitions.

Public-interest companies not meeting the new thresholds will not report for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2027. The European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) will be revised via delegated act within 6 months to prioritize quantitative data, remove less-important data points, distinguish mandatory vs. voluntary elements, and improve international interoperability. The Commission can no longer adopt binding sector-specific standards, instead providing non-binding guidance. Companies may omit certain information (commercial harm, trade secrets, classified info) with disclosure of exemption use. Limited assurance standards deadline deferred to 1 July 2027; reasonable assurance obligation removed. A "value-chain cap" allows companies with 1,000 employees or fewer ("protected undertakings") to refuse information requests beyond voluntary standards (to be defined by the Commission by 19 July 2026). Key changes to the CS3D: The directive now applies only to EU companies with more than €1.5 billion net worldwide turnover and 5,000 employees on average, plus companies with EU franchise/licensing agreements earning royalties exceeding €75 million and €275 million worldwide net turnover. Due diligence obligations are restructured into a two-stage process (scoping exercise based on reasonably available information, then targeted in-depth assessment). The climate transition plan reporting requirement is repealed. The harmonized civil liability regime is removed (liability determined by national law). Pecuniary penalties now capped at 3% of net worldwide turnover (previously based on turnover without harmonized cap). Full harmonization is extended to broader core provisions (identification duty, prioritization of impacts, addressing impacts, complaints mechanisms, monitoring, reporting) to prevent Member State "gold-plating." Information requests to business partners with fewer than 5,000 employees are limited to information that cannot reasonably be obtained otherwise. Transposition deadline: 26 July 2028; application postponed to 26 July 2029.

These changes reflect a global shift toward maintaining competitiveness, particularly against the United States, where federal sustainability requirements are being rolled back even as some states like California move forward with climate reporting. <summary>
The European Commission introduced the Omnibus Simplification Package in response to concerns over complexity in sustainability regulation, proposing amendments to streamline corporate sustainability reporting while maintaining the EU's environmental goals. A first draft was released on February 26, 2025, and the content remains under negotiation.

The package targets four key regulations: the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the EU Taxonomy Regulation, the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The Commission's explicit goal is to reduce reporting burdens by 25% for large companies and 35% for SMEs.

Key proposed amendments include:
- **EU Taxonomy**: Voluntary reporting for companies with turnover below €450 million, partial alignment reporting, simplified templates, and exemption for companies under 1,000 employees or €450 million turnover.
- **CSRD**: Raising the reporting threshold from 250 to 1,000 employees (exempting ~85% of currently covered businesses), revising ESRS standards, and delaying reporting start dates to January 1, 2028 for waves 2 and 3. On April 3, 2025, the EU Commission voted to postpone CSRD compliance by two years for all companies except the first wave. First wave companies report FY2024 in 2025; second wave (250+ employees) reports in 2028 (FY2027); third wave (listed SMEs) reports in 2029 (FY2028).
- **CSDDD**: One-year delay in transposition (to July 26, 2027) and first application (July 26, 2028), removal of transition plan requirement for climate change mitigation, simplified stakeholder definition, narrowed due diligence scope to tier 1 suppliers, and removal of the EU-wide civil liability regime.
- **CBAM**: New de minimis threshold exempting importers handling fewer than 50 tonnes annually, first-year flexibility allowing certificate purchases from February 2027 instead of end of 2026, and revision of the '80% rule' to a '50% rule' for certificate holdings.

The legislative process is lengthy, involving first reading, negotiations, second reading, conciliation, and third reading across EU institutions. The Council requires a qualified majority (55% of member states representing 65% of the EU population). Germany and France support delays, but broader support is needed.

Major concerns include wasted investments in sustainability reporting—raised by companies like Nestlé, Unilever, Mars, and Primark—though the Commission states the package will not alter the substance of existing laws. The Commission plans to revise ESRS through a delegated act and launch the "Improving Sustainability Reporting for Businesses" project.

Businesses are advised to: continue investing in sustainability for long-term value, maintain current reporting practices to avoid legal penalties (fines, restrictions on EU funding), monitor legislative developments closely, and invest in transparency and stakeholder communication as ESG factors remain key for investors and consumers.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Dcycle (a sustainability data platform company) explains the updated CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) reporting timeline following the Omnibus I package, which entered into force on 18 March 2026 via Directive (EU) 2026/470. This is the most significant change to EU sustainability reporting since the CSRD was adopted in 2022.

KEY CHANGES UNDER OMNIBUS I:
- New dual thresholds for CSRD scope: companies must have BOTH more than 1,000 employees AND more than €450 million net turnover (previously 250+ employees and €50M+ turnover)
- Approximately 90% of companies previously in scope are now excluded; the number dropped from an estimated 50,000 to roughly 5,000 companies
- ESRS (European Sustainability Reporting Standards) are being simplified, with a Delegated Act expected by Q3/Q4 2026; mandatory datapoints reduced by approximately 61% (from ~1,073 to ~320)
- Double materiality assessment now allows top-down or bottom-up approaches; limited assurance remains the standard, with full reasonable assurance postponed

UPDATED WAVE CALENDAR:
- Wave 1 (NFRD companies, 500+ employees, public interest): already reporting (FY2024 reports published 2025). Those now below new thresholds get transition exemption for FY2025–2026 (Member State option). Wave 1 companies may omit ESRS E4, S2, S3, S4 for FY2025–2026.
- Wave 2 (large companies, 1,000+ employees AND €450M+ turnover): postponed from FY2025 to FY2027 (report in 2028); simplified ESRS applies; voluntary early adoption possible for FY2026.
- Wave 3 (listed SMEs, small/non-complex credit institutions, captive insurance): postponed from FY2026 to FY2028 (report in 2029); VSME-based standards.
- Wave 4 (third-country companies with €150M+ EU turnover): unchanged at FY2028 (report in 2029); non-EU ESRS Delegated Act not expected before October 2027.

CSDDD CHANGES: Threshold raised to 5,000+ employees AND €1,500M+ turnover; transposition by 26 July 2028; application from 26 July 2029. Most mid-market companies are now out of scope.

SPAIN'S SITUATION: Spain has not transposed CSRD into national law (LEIS bill stuck in Parliament since November 2024); Spain faces infringement proceedings along with Austria, Czech Republic, Germany, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, and Portugal. However, Royal Decree 214/2025 makes organisational carbon footprint calculation mandatory for companies under Ley 11/2018 (250+ employees, €20M assets or €40M turnover), with first publication due 2026 using FY2025 data, including a mandatory five-year GHG reduction plan. Omnibus I requires Member State transposition by 19 March 2027. CSDDD transposition deadline for Spain is July 2026.

GUIDANCE FOR COMPANIES NOW OUT OF SCOPE: The article advises that ~90% of companies removed from CSRD scope should not stop collecting ESG data. Investors/banks still require ESG data for lending and EU Taxonomy alignment; supply chain partners under CSRD/CSDDD will continue requesting Scope 3 data; VSME (Voluntary Standard for SMEs) is emerging as the de facto reporting baseline; voluntary reporting under simplified ESRS may be available from FY2026. The article recommends shifting data infrastructure toward VSME compliance, voluntary disclosure, and supply-chain readiness rather than dismantling it. For logistics companies, a sector-specific article is referenced.
</summary>

KEY CHANGES UNDER THE OMNIBUS PROPOSAL:
- Scope narrowing: CSRD will primarily apply to large companies with more than 1,000 employees and either €50 million in turnover or €25 million in balance sheet total (tightened from the current three-of-two criteria of €50M turnover, €25M balance sheet, or 250 employees).

TRANSITION TIMELINES:
- Large companies: Full CSRD compliance by 2027
- Listed SMEs: Transition period until 2028

PREPARATION STEPS for companies: Review reporting obligations under the new thresholds, focus supply chain due diligence on direct suppliers, prepare for voluntary EU Taxonomy reporting, monitor regulatory changes (proposal still under discussion), and invest in ESG data management systems.

NON-EU COMPANIES: Those generating more than €450 million in turnover in the EU must comply with CSRD and align with ESRS.

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] CEAOB guidelines on limited assurance on sustainability reporting ---
URL: https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/8ac2df18-2ae1-4bc7-9d87-a4a740e48f5e_en?filename=240930-ceaob-guidelines-limited-assurance-sustainability-reporting_en.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document contains the CEAOB (Committee of European Auditing Oversight Bodies) guidelines on limited assurance on sustainability reporting, adopted on 30 September 2024. These non-binding guidelines were developed in response to the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD, EU 2022/2464), which entered into force on 5 January 2023. The CSRD requires large companies to prepare sustainability statements under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) starting from financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2024, and mandates limited assurance engagements by statutory auditors or other assurance services providers ("practitioners"). Since the European Commission is not required to adopt formal assurance standards until 1 October 2026 at the latest, the guidelines fill the interim gap period and aim to avoid fragmentation and promote consistency across EU Member States.

The guidelines are organized into several key sections covering general principles and approach, disclosures under Article 8 of the Taxonomy Regulation, digitalisation, the limited assurance report, and other overarching provisions.

Key principles covered include: (1) the objective of obtaining limited assurance that sustainability information is free from material misstatements, recognizing that less work is required than for reasonable assurance; (2) treatment of material misstatements, which differ from the "double materiality" concept used by entities in preparing reports; (3) procedures for risk identification and assessment, including inquiries, analytical procedures, and physical observations; (4) special attention to the entity's process for determining material matters under the double materiality principle; (5) forward-looking information and estimates, where practitioners should remain critical but are not required to provide guarantees; and (6) communication requirements between practitioners and statutory auditors regarding connectivity between financial and sustainability statements.

Specific provisions address Article 8 Taxonomy Regulation disclosures (covering assessment of eligible/aligned economic activities, KPI reconciliation, and consistency with other ESRS information), the limited assurance report format and content (including the negative form of expression for conclusions, qualified/adverse conclusions for material misstatements, and disclaimer of conclusion for scope limitations), representation letters, use of experts, documentation requirements, subsequent events, and specific provisions for comparative information (first year), value chain information, group/consolidated information, and information incorporated by reference. The guidelines also address joint engagements performed by multiple practitioners, including requirements for balanced distribution of work, cross-review procedures, and joint conclusions.

The guidelines explicitly state they are non-binding and do not override or replace national pronouncements. The appendices include a glossary of terms, references to relevant EU law (Accounting Directive 2013/34/EU, Audit Directive 2006/43/EC, Audit Regulation 537/2014, Taxonomy Regulation 2020/852, Transparency Directive 2004/109/EC, and Delegated Regulation 2023/2772 on ESRS), and detailed provisions for joint engagements by multiple practitioners.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In a limited assurance engagement, practitioners perform less extensive procedures than in a reasonable assurance engagement: the amount of work is expected to be less than for a reasonable assurance engagement that would be performed in the same circumstances."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: FAQs: fundamentals to assurance on sustainability reporting - Accountancy Europe ---
URL: https://accountancyeurope.eu/publications/faqs-fundamentals-to-assurance-on-sustainability-reporting

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Accountancy Europe (published 6 January 2025) is a comprehensive FAQ document explaining the fundamentals of assurance on sustainability reporting, structured in two parts: key concepts of assurance and the EU regulatory framework.

**Context:** The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) obliges companies to disclose sustainability information in their management report according to the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) in digital machine-readable format. The CSRD introduces an EU-wide assurance requirement for limited assurance over sustainability reporting as from 2025 (covering 2024 ESRS reporting).

**Key Concepts:**
- **What is assurance:** An assurance engagement is a mandatory or voluntary check of sustainability information disclosed by a company. It enhances credibility of reported information but does not validate a company's performance as 'sustainable'.
- **How assurance is performed:** Follows a risk-based approach with three stages (planning, execution, reporting), requiring year-long cooperation among a multi-disciplinary team. Procedures include inquiry, testing internal controls, analysing transactions, and third-party confirmations.
- **Types of assurance:** Limited vs. reasonable assurance engagements. Limited assurance involves fewer procedures and less evidence; reasonable assurance (typical of financial statement audits) is the highest level but not absolute.
- **Risk-based approach:** Resources are focused on areas with higher risk of material misstatements relating to impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs).
- **Materiality:** The double materiality concept is embedded in CSRD and ESRS. The practitioner's materiality determination is based on professional judgment and considers users' needs.
- **Output:** A publicly available assurance report expressing the practitioner's conclusion, plus a separate non-public report communicating significant matters (e.g., internal control deficiencies) to management.
- **Assurance report elements:** Practitioner's conclusion, scope, applicable reporting framework, responsibilities, inherent limitations, professional standards used, and summary of work performed.
- **Types of conclusions:** Unmodified (clean/positive/unqualified), and modified conclusions including disclaimer, adverse, and qualified.
- **Management responsibilities:** Preparing sustainability information per reporting standards, designing internal controls, and providing practitioner access to all relevant information and staff.

**EU Regulatory Framework:**
- **CSRD key changes:** Enlarged company scope, mandatory ESRS, machine-readable reporting (tagging), and mandatory limited assurance. A possible move to reasonable assurance in 2028 is foreseen, subject to EC assessment.
- **Who provides assurance:** CSRD mandates statutory auditors to express opinions on sustainability reporting; Member States may allow another statutory auditor or an Independent Assurance Service Provider (IASP). Shareholders with >5% voting rights or capital can request an accredited third party report.
- **Scope of assurance:** Opinion on compliance with CSRD (including ESRS compliance, identification process, and mark-up compliance) and compliance with EU Taxonomy Regulation Article 8.
- **Standards used:** The EC must adopt an EU limited assurance standard by 1 October 2026, based on the International Standard on Sustainability Assurance (ISSA) 5000, with CEAOB technical advice expected by May 2025. Member States may apply national standards in the interim. CEAOB has adopted non-binding guidelines for the transition period. The EC shall adopt reasonable assurance standards by 1 October 2028 if deemed feasible.
- **Educational qualifications:** Statutory auditors must obtain knowledge in sustainability reporting standards, sustainability analysis, due diligence processes, and assurance standards, plus pass an exam and complete at least eight months of practical training. Transitional arrangements exist for those who qualified before 1 January 2024 or intend to complete accreditation by 1 January 2026.
- **Supervision:** Member States must have independent audit oversight bodies (AOBs) cooperating within CEAOB, plus investigations and sanctions regimes extended to sustainability reporting assurance. Equivalent requirements apply where IASPs are authorised.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"An assurance engagement is a (mandatory or voluntary) check of sustainability information disclosed by a company. Independent external assurance enhances information's credibility and supports investors and other users in making decisions related to sustainability matters."
</key_excerpts>

This webpage from Coolset (updated March 18, 2026) provides a comprehensive guide to ISSA 5000 (International Standard on Sustainability Assurance 5000) and its relationship to CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) compliance.

**What is ISSA 5000:** It is the new international standard on sustainability assurance developed by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB). It provides a framework for auditors to verify sustainability information across all topics and industries. It was officially approved on September 20, 2024, formally published on November 12, 2024, and is effective December 2026. It is a principles-based standard that works with any reporting framework and supports both limited and reasonable assurance engagements.

**Key Context - EU Omnibus I:** The EU Omnibus I simplification package adopted in February 2025 narrowed CSRD scope to companies with 1,000+ employees (and either more than EUR 50M turnover or more than EUR 25M balance sheet), reducing in-scope companies by approximately 80%. The transition to reasonable assurance has been permanently removed under Omnibus I, with reassessment unlikely before 2030 at the earliest. A "stop-the-clock" directive postpones reporting obligations for wave 2 and wave 3 companies by two years.

**Key ISSA 5000 Requirements for CSRD Compliance:**
- **Objectives:** Provide limited or reasonable assurance that sustainability reports are free from material misstatements.
- **Engagement acceptance:** Auditors evaluate scope of work, reporting boundaries, and level of assurance.
- **Planning:** Auditors assess internal systems and controls, using risk assessment procedures including fraud-related ones.
- **Materiality:** Follows a double materiality approach (financial materiality and impact materiality), aligned with CSRD requirements.
- **Obtaining evidence:** Evidence levels depend on limited vs. reasonable assurance; reasonable assurance requires deeper data examination, especially for forward-looking or qualitative information.
- **Documentation:** Companies must maintain detailed records on how ESG data is collected, calculated, and reported.
- **Reporting:** Auditors issue reports outlining assurance level and procedures used.

**Main Benefits of ISSA 5000:** (1) Enhanced credibility through a globally recognized standard, (2) better transparency and protection against greenwashing accusations, (3) streamlined auditing processes with a universal framework, and (4) faster CSRD compliance.

**Cost Context:** EFRAG estimates limited assurance audit costs at 0.013% to 0.026% of revenue (EUR 13,000 to EUR 26,000 per year for every EUR 10M in revenue). Fines for CSRD non-compliance can reach EUR 10 million.

**EUDR Update (December 2025):** The page also includes a disclaimer noting proposed EUDR changes backed by the European Parliament and Council in November 2025, including a 12-month enforcement delay (30 December 2026 for large/medium operators, 30 June 2027 for small/micro), simplified due diligence for small producers, and narrowed scope for downstream actors. These changes are not yet legally binding.

**Coolset Platform Promotion:** The article promotes Coolset's CSRD compliance platform, which offers double materiality assessment tools, auditor collaboration features, evidence management, and audit-ready reports in .XBRL format.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: CSRD Assurance and Audit Requirements: What Companies Need to Know in 2026 | CSRD Experts Blog ---
URL: https://csrd-experts.com/blog/csrd-assurance-audit-requirements

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## CSRD Assurance and Audit Requirements: What Companies Need to Know in 2026

This article (by João Aguiam) explains the mandatory assurance requirements under the EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), which for the first time in EU history requires sustainability reports to be independently verified, much like financial statements.

### Why Assurance is Required
The CSRD mandates third-party assurance to build credibility, reduce greenwashing, standardise quality across the 12 ESRS standards, and align sustainability data with the rigour of financial reporting.

### Assurance Levels
- **Limited Assurance (2024–2028):** Auditors review the sustainability report for material misstatements using analytical procedures, inquiries with management, and reviews of internal controls. This is a "nothing came to our attention" conclusion rather than a full deep-dive.
- **Reasonable Assurance (expected 2028+):** Equivalent to financial audit standards, involving substantive testing, data verification, transaction sampling, and rigorous controls testing. The European Commission will adopt limited assurance standards first (expected via ISSA 5000 from IAASB) and develop reasonable assurance standards by October 2028.

### Who Needs Assurance (Phased Timeline)
| Wave | Companies | First Report |
|---|---|---|
| Wave 1 | Large public-interest entities (500+ employees, already under NFRD) | 2025 (FY 2024) |
| Wave 2 | Other large companies (250+ employees, €50M+ revenue, €25M+ assets — 2 of 3 criteria) | 2026 (FY 2025) |
| Wave 3 | Listed SMEs (opt-out until 2028) | 2027 (FY 2026) |
| Wave 4 | Non-EU companies with €150M+ EU revenue | 2029 (FY 2028) |

All waves require limited assurance.

### Who Can Perform Assurance
- **Statutory Auditors:** The default option — the firm auditing financial statements can also handle sustainability assurance if they have ESG expertise.
- **Independent Assurance Service Providers (IASPs):** Some EU member states allow non-statutory auditors to perform this role (e.g., France historically allowed OEC). Depending on national transposition.

Key selection considerations: ESG expertise (financial auditors may not understand Scope 3 or biodiversity metrics), industry knowledge, independence rules (a firm providing CSRD consulting cannot typically also audit), and cost. Assurance and advisory must be kept separate.

### What Auditors Check
1. **Governance and process** — clear structure, defined roles and responsibilities for data collection/sign-off
2. **Double materiality assessment** — proper conduct, stakeholder engagement, documented rationale for material and omitted topics
3. **Data quality and controls** — data sources, internal controls, traceability to source systems, reasonable documented estimates
4. **Disclosure completeness** — all mandatory ESRS disclosures, cross-cutting standards (ESRS 1 and ESRS 2), consistency with materiality assessment
5. **Consistency with financial statements** — alignment with management report, no contradictions

### Preparation Roadmap
- Start at least 6 months early; engage the assurance provider for a pre-assurance readiness assessment
- Build an audit trail — every data point needs a clear source, documented methodology, and evidence of review/approval
- Invest in internal controls (segregation of duties, reconciliations, version control, escalation paths)
- Conduct a dry run (pre-assurance engagement or internal audit)
- Document everything — materiality methodology, stakeholder engagement, data collection procedures, assumptions (especially Scope 3), board approvals

### Common Pitfalls
Treating assurance as a formality, poor data granularity, inconsistent reporting boundaries (must align with financial consolidation scope), ignoring value chain data (upstream and downstream), and last-minute provider selection.

### Consequences of Failure
Qualified, adverse, or disclaimer opinions can lead to regulatory scrutiny, reputational damage, investor concerns, and potential legal liability for directors.

### Cost Estimates
- Mid-sized companies: €20,000–€60,000 for limited assurance
- Large corporates: €50,000–€150,000+
- Complex multinationals: €150,000–€500,000+ (expected to rise with reasonable assurance transition)

### Next Steps
Confirm your CSRD timeline/wave, engage an assurance provider 6–12 months before deadline, assess data traceability, run a gap analysis against ESRS requirements, and consider expert consulting help.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"For the first time in EU history, sustainability reports must be independently verified, just like financial statements."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) is an EU regulation that entered into force on January 5, 2023, requiring large companies to disclose standardized, externally audited sustainability information integrated with their financial reports. It was significantly revised by the Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470, in force from 18 March 2026, which narrowed scope to approximately 90% fewer companies than originally projected.

**CSRD Scope (updated thresholds):** EU companies must report if they exceed BOTH 1,000 employees on average AND €450 million in net annual turnover (replacing the previous two-out-of-three criteria test). Non-EU parent companies must report if they generate over €450 million in EU net turnover for two consecutive years and have an EU subsidiary or branch exceeding €200 million in net turnover. New thresholds apply from financial years beginning on or after January 1, 2027.

**Five Core CSRD Requirements:** (1) Integration — disclosures must appear within the annual or management report; (2) ESRS alignment — disclosures must follow the European Sustainability Reporting Standards; (3) Double materiality assessment — companies must assess both financial and impact materiality; (4) External assurance — all disclosures must be independently verified (new under CSRD, no NFRD equivalent); (5) Digital tagging — data must be tagged using iXBRL for machine-readable access.

**CSRD Timeline (post-Omnibus):**
- Wave 1 (FY2024–FY2025, reporting 2025–2026): Companies already in NFRD scope continue reporting; member states may grant exemptions for those below new thresholds.
- Wave 2 (FY2027, reporting 2028): Large EU companies exceeding both thresholds not previously under NFRD. Apply simplified ESRS (2026).
- Wave 3 (FY2028, reporting 2029): Non-EU parent companies meeting revised Article 40a thresholds.

**ESRS Standards:** The original ESRS adopted July 2023 covered 12 standards (ESRS 1 general requirements, ESRS 2 general disclosures, E1–E5 environmental, S1–S4 social, G1 governance). The simplified ESRS (2026), adopted by the European Commission on July 3, 2026, reduce mandatory data points by over 60% and apply from FY2027, with early voluntary adoption for FY2026 permitted. They maintain the 12-topic structure but offer additional materiality flexibility.

**CSRD vs. NFRD differences:** Broadened scope (including large private and non-EU companies), mandatory ESRS standardization (vs. voluntary frameworks like GRI/TCFD under NFRD), mandatory external assurance, and required integration of sustainability disclosures into annual reports. The NFRD covered approximately 11,700 large public-interest entities with 500+ employees.

**Relationship to other legislation:** CSRD works alongside SFDR (asset manager/product ESG disclosures) and the EU Taxonomy (classification of sustainable economic activities), with targeted changes to reduce duplication. EFRAG has strengthened alignment between ESRS and ISSB's IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards.

**Key reporting features:** Companies must provide both retrospective and forward-looking disclosures, including Scope 3 emissions where material, quantitative and qualitative information, and digitally tagged reports integrated with financial statements. The double materiality assessment remains core even under Omnibus amendments.

**Challenges:** Data scale (especially Scope 3 emissions across the full value chain), cross-team coordination between finance and sustainability teams, and audit readiness. Companies must ensure data is traceable from source to final disclosure. National enforcement varies by member state, with some jurisdictions imposing significant fines.

The article concludes with Workiva's platform positioning for CSRD compliance, noting that sustainability statements now account for an average of one-third of annual reports (per Workiva's CSRD Year One in Review research), and recommends organizations begin preparing data infrastructure early since transposition into national law continues through March 2027.
</summary>

**Timeline implications by "wave":**
- First Wave (~11,000 EU listed companies, banks, insurers with 500+ employees): already reporting since FY 2024. Quick Fix Delegated Act (July 2025) extends reliefs from FY 2024/25 to FY 2026 — all First Wave companies may omit "anticipated financial effects"; those under 750 employees may omit Scope 3 GHG emissions, ESRS E4 (biodiversity), and S1-S4 (social); those over 750 employees may omit E4, S2-S4, and specified S1 datapoints. Omnibus I enables Member States to exempt de-scoped First Wave companies from reporting in FY 2025 and 2026.
- Second Wave (large companies not already reporting): delayed two years by Stop-the-Clock Directive (April 2025) to FY 2027 (reports due 2028), though many now fall out of scope.
- Third Wave (listed SMEs): delayed to FY 2028 (reports due 2029), though nearly all now de-scoped.
- Fourth Wave (non-EU companies): must report on FY 2028 in 2029 under new higher thresholds.

**Standards and content changes:**
- Current ESRS (amended by Quick Fix) remains the legally applicable framework until revised standards are adopted.
- EFRAG published draft simplified ESRS on 3 December 2025: standards halved in length, mandatory datapoints reduced ~61%, all voluntary disclosures deleted, simpler top-down double materiality assessments, more proportionality/reliefs for undue cost or effort, less value chain data pressure, more principles-based narrative reporting, and alignment with ISSB where possible. Commission expected to adopt via delegated act by summer 2026, with application from FY 2027.
- Sector-specific ESRS abandoned by Omnibus I (despite "huge" market demand, e.g., for oil & gas and mining). Commission may issue sector guidance instead.
- Value chain reliefs from FY 2027: companies under 1,000 employees can refuse sustainability information requests beyond future VSME (voluntary SME standards); in-scope companies get a "comply or explain" option for first three years of value chain reporting.
- Additional reliefs: conditional information exemptions (trade secrets, seriously prejudicial commercial position, classified information) and M&A relief for acquired/merged/divested companies.

**Next steps:** Omnibus I will be published in the Official Journal and comes into force 20 days later. EU Member States get ~12 months to transpose. Nine states (Germany, Spain, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Cyprus, Czech Republic) had not fully transposed CSRD as of 30 September 2025.

**Upsides:** Regulatory certainty in 2026; shift from box-ticking to strategic disclosures; integrated reporting; potential cost savings estimated by EFRAG at €4.7b for First and Second Wave companies between FY 2027-2032 (44% reduction, though critiqued as optimistic); and space for voluntary action by the ~42,000 de-scoped companies, motivated by internal preparedness, value creation, physical risk management, market expectations, and the easy entry point in revised ESRS.

**Board takeaways:** Scope assessment becomes a group perimeter exercise; boards should require scope mapping of EU group entities, listed subsidiaries, third-country parents, and planned structural changes; build flexible systems that can adapt if thresholds shift again; test materiality judgements against sector peers; and ask management targeted questions on scope, readiness/controls/assurance, materiality, value chain strategy, risk management, and change management.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Omnibus I will come into force at EU-level twenty days after publication in the Official Journal, which is expected in early 2026."
</key_excerpts>
