### PART 5: ENFORCEMENT MECHANISMS

#### 5.1 Division of Responsibility

Enforcement of sustainability reporting in the EEA "operates within a coherent and harmonised supervisory architecture designed to safeguard the quality and transparency of information available to investors and the wider market." [19]

- **Member State competent authorities** (national enforcers) oversee compliance. Each Member State designates the competent authority — typically the national securities regulator or audit oversight body [19][15].
- **Penalties under national law**: CSRD requires Member States to establish penalties that must be "effective, dissuasive, and proportionate," with amounts determined at national level [29]. "National enforcement varies by member state, with some jurisdictions imposing significant fines" [21]. Non-EU companies face penalties through their EU subsidiaries/branches [29]. Reference point: CSDDD caps penalties at 3% of net global turnover (but applies to much larger companies of 5,000+ employees) [29]. Fines for CSRD non-compliance can reach EUR 10 million per Coolset [16].
- Enforcement of original requirements remains with national regulators until the revised thresholds are published and transposed into national law [13].

#### 5.2 Role of ESMA

ESMA's role in sustainability reporting supervision and regulation within the EU [22]:
- Coordinates national enforcers' supervision of sustainability reporting by listed issuers via its **Sustainability Reporting Working Group (SRWG)**, bringing together representatives of national enforcers across EEA countries.
- Contributes to the development of European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS)
- Advises the European Commission on sustainability reporting legislation (including the Taxonomy Regulation)
- Monitors the ISSB's IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards
- ESMA's mandate covers listed issuers' disclosures under the CSRD, ESRS, NFRD (in Member States yet to transpose CSRD), and Taxonomy Regulation Article 8 [22]
- Published **Guidelines on Enforcement of Sustainability Information (GLESI)** in July 2024, closely modelled on its Guidelines on Enforcement of Financial Information (GLEFI), applying to sustainability information published from 1 January 2025 [19][22]
- Publishes **European Common Enforcement Priorities (ECEP)** annually since 2017 (first NFRD reference in ECEP 2017); ECEP 2025 carried over two priorities from ECEP 2024: materiality, and scope and structure of sustainability statements [19][22]
- ESMA published a statement in June 2025 confirming continued commitment to transparent sustainability reporting with proportionate enforcement, "which remains a reference point for 2026" [19]
- ESMA delivered its opinion on the revised ESRS on 17 February 2026 [22]

#### 5.3 First-Year Enforcement Activity (ESMA 2025 Report)

The Hogan Lovells analysis of ESMA's "Report on 2025 Corporate reporting enforcement and regulatory activities" (published 7 May 2026) found [23]:
- Approximately **2,000 issuers' sustainability statements** were in scope of enforcement at the end of 2025
- In 2025, the CSRD applied to some issuers while others remained under the NFRD where CSRD had not yet been transposed, with some issuers voluntarily reporting under ESRS
- Of examinations carried out on ESRS-based sustainability statements, **25% related to voluntarily prepared statements** from issuers whose Member States had not transposed CSRD
- **Enforcement actions were taken toward 109 issuers in 2025** (covering both voluntary and mandatory reporting under NFRD and CSRD), with each action potentially involving multiple areas of non-compliance
- Most enforcement actions related to climate change reporting under **ESRS E1 (40%)** and general disclosures required by **ESRS 2 (36%)**, followed by **ESRS S1** on own workforce (8%)
- Enforcers almost exclusively required issuers to correct infringements in future sustainability statements, recognizing issuers are on a learning curve and the regulatory environment was in upheaval due to the omnibus simplification process
- Regarding the 2024 ECEP: enforcers took actions against 15 issuers in the examined sample, requiring corrections in future statements; an additional 19 ECEP examinations from 2024 were still ongoing

#### 5.4 Transposition Status and Infringements

As of 30 September 2025, **nine Member States had not fully transposed CSRD**: Germany, Spain, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Cyprus, Czech Republic [27]. Dcycle identifies Spain facing infringement proceedings "along with Austria, Czech Republic, Germany, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, and Portugal" [11]. Spain has not transposed CSRD into national law (LEIS bill stuck in Parliament since November 2024) [11]. Germany specifically: Germany has not yet transposed the CSRD into national law (public hearing took place 10 April 2026); the NFRD remains in force for now; entry into force expected during 2026, with no obligation to apply the new ESRS for reporting year 2025 unless retroactive [24]. Member States that hadn't transposed CSRD (Luxembourg, Germany, Netherlands) may pause implementation [9]. ESMA notes compliance with GLESI is "mixed due to pending transposition of the CSRD in some member states" [19].

Ireland: S.I. No. 336 of 2024 transposed CSRD, with certain companies deemed "large" regardless of employee/turnover/balance sheet criteria (e.g., public limited companies, credit institutions, insurance undertakings) [48].

### PART 6: PLAIN-LANGUAGE SUMMARY OF WHAT THE CSRD REQUIRES

The CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, Directive (EU) 2022/2464) — as amended by Omnibus I (Directive (EU) 2026/470) — is the EU's flagship corporate sustainability disclosure law [8][21]. It entered into force on January 5, 2023 and "represents the most comprehensive sustainability disclosure mandate the EU has enacted to date" [21].

**Who must comply (as of FY2027 onward)**: Very large EU companies/groups (and non-EU issuers on EU-regulated markets) with **more than 1,000 employees AND more than €450 million net annual turnover**, plus non-EU parent groups with >€450 million EU turnover and an EU subsidiary/branch >€200 million turnover [4][2][21][11]. This represents roughly 5,000-6,000 companies (down from ~50,000 originally projected) [11][36].

**The five core requirements** [21][11]:
1. **Integration**: Sustainability disclosures must appear within the annual or management report [21]
2. **ESRS alignment**: Disclosures must follow the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (12 standards: ESRS 1 general requirements, ESRS 2 general disclosures, E1–E5 environmental, S1–S4 social, G1 governance), now simplified by over 60% reduction in mandatory datapoints [21][29]
3. **Double materiality assessment**: Companies must assess both financial materiality (how sustainability affects the business) and impact materiality (how the business affects people and planet) [21][10]
4. **External assurance**: All disclosures must be independently verified (limited assurance) — new under CSRD, with no NFRD equivalent [21]
5. **Digital tagging**: Data must be tagged using iXBRL (Inline XBRL) for machine-readable access [21][29]; by January 1, 2028, all in-scope companies must report via ESEF and digitally tag using iXBRL [29]

**What must be reported**: Companies must report on environmental matters (climate change including Scope 1, 2, 3 GHG emissions where material; pollution; water; biodiversity; resource use and circular economy), social matters (own workforce, workers in the value chain, affected communities, consumers/end-users), and governance (business conduct) [10][29][33]. Companies must provide both retrospective and forward-looking disclosures, including Scope 3 emissions where material, and quantitative and qualitative information [21]. The report must include a description of the business model and strategy [33]. ESRS E5 (Resource Use and Circular Economy) requires disclosure of resource inflows (key materials, weight, secondary resources) and outflows (product durability, repairability, recyclability rates, waste streams, hazardous vs. non-hazardous waste breakdown) [29]. Companies are required to have Paris Agreement-aligned emissions reduction plans to reach net zero by 2050 starting in 2025 [26].

**Key reliefs under Omnibus I**: value-chain cap (companies with ≤1,000 employees can refuse data requests beyond the voluntary VSME standard) [4][42]; three-year transitional relief for value chain data not "readily available" [38]; options to omit commercially prejudicial, trade secret, or classified information [2][3]; M&A relief for acquired/merged/divested companies [2][27]; "comply or explain" option for the first three years of value chain reporting [27].

**Why it exists**: The CSRD replaced the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) because the NFRD produced insufficient, incomparable, and untrustworthy sustainability reporting. The EU cited an "accountability gap" and the need to support credible green investments and SFDR compliance [26]. As the Commission put it: "Reports often omit information that investors and other stakeholders think is important. Reported information can be hard to compare from company to company, and users of the information are often unsure whether they can trust it." [26]

### PART 7: REAL-WORLD ENTERPRISE COMPLIANCE CHALLENGES AND COST ESTIMATES

#### 7.1 European Commission's Impact Assessment and Official Cost Estimates

**Original CSRD cost estimates (EFRAG-based)**:
- EFRAG estimates administrative costs of approximately **€740,000 average for large listed companies**, plus **€430,000 in initial investments**, totaling about **€880,000 annually for the largest listed EU companies (2026-2028)** [28][12]
- EFRAG's total estimate: **€23.3 billion per year in reporting costs** across all obligated companies (including ~10,000 non-EU companies and 38,000 SMEs) [28]
- Limited assurance audit costs: 0.013% to 0.026% of revenue (EUR 13,000 to EUR 26,000 per year for every EUR 10M in revenue) [16]

**Omnibus proposal cost savings (Commission figures)**:
- The Commission's Omnibus package could reduce administrative costs by approximately **€4.4 billion annually** [47].
- Immediate one-off savings are projected at around **€1.6 billion for CSRD/ESRS** and **€0.9 billion for taxonomy-related requirements** [47].
- McCann FitzGerald confirms: "The Commission estimates the number of in-scope companies will be reduced by ~80%, with combined cost savings of €4.4 billion per year." [48]
- The stated goal was reducing reporting burdens by 25% for large companies and 35% for SMEs [6][9]

**EFRAG's post-Omnibus savings estimates**:
- The Commonwealth Climate Law article cites "potential cost savings estimated by EFRAG at **€4.7b for First and Second Wave companies between FY 2027-2032 (44% reduction, though critiqued as optimistic)**" [27]
- Generation Impact Global: "EFRAG's cost-benefit analysis projects cumulative savings of approximately **EUR 4.7 billion across all in-scope undertakings over 2027–2031**, including value chain effects. The savings rate begins at 28% in 2027, rises to 38% in 2028, and stabilises at 33–36% from 2029 onwards." [43]
- A later EFRAG-commissioned study (referenced by Andreas Rasche, Copenhagen Business School) estimates the amended ESRS could deliver **EUR 3.7 billion in cost savings between 2027–2031 (-34% savings), rising to EUR 4.1 billion (-44%) when supply-chain effects are included** [44]. Methodology limitations noted: only 170 survey responses plus around 30 interviews, and these are estimations [44].
- Revised ESRS draft (6 May 2026): mandatory datapoints reduced by over 60%; total datapoints cut by over 70%; reporting costs per company expected to fall by over 30% [24][42].
- Rasche's critique: "Since substantial cost savings can be achieved by amending Level 2 implementing acts (the ESRS), it raises the question of why it was necessary to immediately reopen the CSRD directive itself (Level 1) and exempt around 90% of companies — suggesting future Omnibus packages should start simplification by adjusting delegated/implementing acts first... The study also finds firms do not expect significant positive or negative effects of the amended ESRS on their competitiveness, which calls into question how much the Omnibus can realistically deliver on its core promise of 'boosting competitiveness.'" [44]

#### 7.2 Independent Industry Analyses — Actual Compliance Cost Estimates

**Socious research article** (citing PwC 2025 CSRD Readiness Survey, Deloitte ESG Reporting Cost Benchmark, KPMG, Verdantix, Omdena) [31]:

First-Year Setup Costs by company size:
- **Large enterprises (10,000+ employees): €500,000 to €2 million+**
- **Mid-size companies (1,000–10,000 employees): €150,000 to €500,000**
- **Smaller in-scope companies (250–1,000 employees): €50,000 to €200,000**
- Recurring annual costs: large enterprises **€200,000 to €800,000 annually**
- "A 2025 PwC survey found **60% of European multinationals exceeded their initial CSRD budget by 30% or more**"

Cost Breakdown by Category:
1. **Consulting/Advisory**: €100K–€800K+/yr. Big Four firms charge €300–€500/hour; specialist consultancies €200–€400/hour. A comprehensive first-year Big Four advisory package for large enterprises can exceed €500K.
2. **Software/Platform Licenses**: €50K–€200K/yr (vendors: Sphera, Persefoni, Workiva, SAP Sustainability Control Tower)
3. **Internal FTEs**: €150K–€500K/yr. Companies typically need 2–5 dedicated staff. Sustainability analysts earn €60K–€90K; senior managers €90K–€150K. A 3-person team costs €250K–€400K fully loaded. "A Deloitte survey found 70% of companies underestimated FTE needs by at least one position."
4. **Data Collection Across Value Chain**: 40–60% of total effort. "KPMG found this consumes an average of 800–1,500 person-hours for a mid-size multinational (largely manual spreadsheet work)."
5. **Assurance/Audit**: €50K–€150K for limited assurance; €100K–€300K for reasonable assurance
6. **Hidden costs**: Management time (100+ hours of senior leadership annually), training (€20K–€50K), and opportunity costs of staff diverted from strategic initiatives

**CSRD Experts cost estimates** [17]: Mid-sized companies €20,000–€60,000 for limited assurance; large corporates €50,000–€150,000+; complex multinationals €150,000–€500,000+ (expected to rise with reasonable assurance transition).

**One Earth (Karl Burkart) "reality-adjusted" critique** [28]:
- Argues EFRAG's €23.3 billion figure "is unrealistically low," noting ESRS is "orders of magnitude more complex" than climate reporting and should cost at least double EFRAG's estimate
- Author's reality-adjusted estimate: **€39.0 billion per year ($45 billion US)**, roughly 10 basis points on business revenue
- Estimated addressable market: $30 billion per year by 2030 for CSRD reporting software and services, plus ~$15 billion for auditing and staffing
- Climate reporting currently costs companies globally an estimated €13.3 billion
- Noted: 600 metrics identified just for the biodiversity category; another consultancy identified 1,052 metrics for CSRD; EU lists 84 reporting requirements and 1,200 possible data points

**German Business Panel (TRR 266, University of Mannheim consortium)** [13]:
- "At the end of 2024, almost **67.6 percent of companies rated the new reporting rules negatively** and only 9.3 percent positively. They particularly criticize the complex and overly detailed standards and the high reporting burden."
- Only 12.6% of companies still believe the CSRD actually promotes sustainability
- More than half of surveyed companies canceled planned investments due to bureaucratic burden
- SMEs particularly affected due to lack of expertise and personnel
- Even sustainability-oriented companies see resources shifted from sustainability investments to pure reporting obligations
- After the Omnibus reform (December 2025): "Over 50% of companies surveyed rated the reform positively (per GBP report from January 2026)."
- Some companies worry voluntary sustainable business models may lose relative competitiveness
- Over a third of medium-sized and large companies call for further simplification and clearer guidelines

**PwC Global Sustainability Reporting Survey 2025** ("From insight to value: The sustainability reporting journey continues," survey of 496 executives across 40 countries, conducted June-July 2025) [32]:
- "About 40% of respondents planning future CSRD reporting say they'll delay by two years per the EU directive, while an equal number will report on the original timeline voluntarily"
- "More than half of respondents report increased internal and external pressure to provide sustainability data and insights over the past year, with less than 10% seeing decreased pressure"
- "Over 60% of respondents increased investment of resources and senior leadership time in sustainability reporting; only 5-6% decreased investment"
- More than two-thirds of companies already reporting under CSRD or ISSB gained significant or moderate value beyond compliance, with 28% seeing significant value
- Use of AI for sustainability reporting nearly tripled from 11% to 28% year-over-year
- More than a third of surveyed companies had already published sustainability statements, mostly under CSRD
- 37% cited earlier engagement with assurance practitioners as a lesson

**EY CSRD Barometer 2025** (analyzing sustainability statements from 200 first-time adopters) [34]:
- Climate change (ESRS E1), own workforce (ESRS S1), and business conduct (ESRS G1) emerged as the most frequently reported material topics
- "The analysis reveals significant variation in reporting practices among first-time adopters"

**Other first-year insights**:
- Workiva's "CSRD Year One in Review" research: sustainability statements now account for an average of one-third of annual reports [21]
- EFRAG's analysis of the first set of CSRD-aligned reports (published 23 July 2025) examined **656 CSRD reports** and launched a "2025 State of Play" portal [23]
- German DAX40 analysis by the Sustainability Reporting Navigator: reporting volume increased on average with a trend toward convergence; DAX40 reporting volumes ranged from less than 40,000 to more than 140,000 words; reports showed a drastic increase in images, more standardized language, and greater emphasis on negative words — suggesting sustainability reporting became a more serious and regulated instrument on par with financial reporting [13]

#### 7.3 The Debate on Cost Estimates — Commission vs. Industry

The debate centers on significant divergence between Commission/EFRAG cost estimates and industry/consulting experience [28][31][27]:

- **Commission estimates** focus on administrative burden reduction targets (25% for companies, 35% for SMEs) and project €4.4 billion annual savings from the Omnibus package [47]. EFRAG projects €4.7 billion cumulative savings (or the later study's €3.7–4.1 billion) [43][27][44].
- **Industry/consulting estimates** of actual first-year compliance costs are substantially higher: €500,000–€2 million+ for large enterprises in year one [31]; a 2025 PwC survey finding 60% of European multinationals exceeded initial CSRD budgets by 30% or more [31]; and One Earth's claim that EFRAG's totals understate real costs by at least half (€39 billion vs. €23.3 billion per year) [28].
- The EFRAG €4.7 billion savings figure is "critiqued as optimistic" [27].
- **Accountancy Europe** (representing the accountancy profession) supported simplification but warned against backtracking on policy goals, and highlighted that higher thresholds (e.g., MEP Warborn's 3,000 employee/€450M proposal) "would result in 1/3 of EU Member States having fewer than 10 companies subject to CSRD, potentially reducing data availability needed for industrial transformation" [30]. It also argued "focusing primarily on headcount is not justified since it deviates from common size criteria (two of three thresholds: turnover, balance sheet total, employees). Industrial firms with significant environmental impact may have relatively few employees, while service sector companies tend to have higher employee counts." [30]
- **Investor representatives (EFAMA, Eurosif, UN PRI)** raised concerns that proposed changes could weaken EU sustainability disclosures, harming investment and economic competitiveness [30].
- **Civil society/industry reactions to the original proposal**: Nathalie Dogniez (Eurosif chair): the proposal "creates legal uncertainty for investors and businesses, and harms the first movers who have already prepared their first sustainability reports or started working towards compliance"; Robin Hodess (GRI CEO): reducing scope "undermines the level playing field needed to achieve sustainable growth"; Aleksandra Palinska (Eurosif): "Voluntary reporting from companies will not fill this data gap"; Nele Meyer (European Coalition for Corporate Justice): the changes "give corporations a free pass to operate without consequences" [25].
- **Industry concerns about wasted investments** in sustainability reporting were raised by companies like Nestlé, Unilever, Mars, and Primark, though the Commission stated the package would not alter the substance of existing laws [6].
- Business advice from major firms: Maura Hodge (KPMG U.S. sustainability leader) advised companies to continue climate work (especially Scope 1, 2, and 3 GHG inventories), assess how proposed thresholds affect reporting strategy, and redeploy reporting budgets toward strategic value-add projects like technology solutions or decarbonization efforts [25]. Skadden noted "many businesses have already invested significant resources in preparing for 2026 CSRD reporting and 2027 CS3D obligations... costs incurred so far can be regarded as early preparation for the delayed 2028 reporting deadlines." [7]
- Companies rated the Omnibus positively: "Over 50% of companies surveyed rated the reform positively (per GBP report from January 2026)" [13].
- PwC recommended making sustainability reporting a business-as-usual exercise through repeatable processes and technology infrastructure; establishing cross-functional collaboration models; and ensuring serious senior leadership engagement [32].

#### 7.4 Practical Compliance Challenges

Common challenges identified across sources [10][21][17][11][31][32]:
- **Data scale**, especially Scope 3 emissions across the full value chain [21]
- **Cross-team coordination** between finance and sustainability teams [21]
- **Audit readiness**: data must be traceable from source to final disclosure [21]
- **Value chain data**: upstream and downstream data collection consumes 40–60% of total effort (KPMG: 800–1,500 person-hours for a mid-size multinational) [31]
- **Assurance readiness**: start at least 6 months early; engage the assurance provider for a pre-assurance readiness assessment; build an audit trail; invest in internal controls (segregation of duties, reconciliations, version control, escalation paths); conduct a dry run [17]
- **Common pitfalls**: treating assurance as a formality, poor data granularity, inconsistent reporting boundaries (must align with financial consolidation scope), ignoring value chain data, last-minute provider selection [17]
- **Consequences of failure**: qualified, adverse, or disclaimer opinions can lead to regulatory scrutiny, reputational damage, investor concerns, and potential legal liability for directors [17]
- A 2024 German study found large companies previously subject to NFRD adapted early, introducing double materiality analyses, seeking voluntary audits, and integrating sustainability information into management reports; companies subject to CSRD for the first time did not significantly expand voluntary reporting due to limited resources, lack of expertise, and uncertainty about standards [13]
- Companies now out of scope (~90%) should not stop collecting ESG data: "Investors/banks still require ESG data for lending and EU Taxonomy alignment; supply chain partners under CSRD/CSDDD will continue requesting Scope 3 data; VSME (Voluntary Standard for SMEs) is emerging as the de facto reporting baseline" [11]

# Research Findings: California Climate Disclosure Laws (SB 253, SB 261, SB 219) as of August 2026

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

The research was conducted through multiple rounds of web searches using the Tavily search tool. The queries included:

1. "SB 253 SB 261 California climate disclosure status 2026 Newsom budget suspension"
2. "California SB 253 SB 261 Newsom May 2025 budget revision repeal suspension status"
3. "SB 219 California climate disclosure 2025 amendment operative status"
4. "Newsom May 2025 budget revision SB 253 SB 261 suspend repeal climate disclosure proposal"
5. "California Senate Appropriations Committee analysis SB 253 SB 261 costs compliance estimate"
6. "SB 219 limited assurance 2027 reasonable assurance 2030 carbon emissions reporting California"
7. "Newsom May 2025 budget revision delay suspend SB 253 SB 261 two years 2028 legislature rejected"
8. "California budget 2025 climate disclosure delay proposal Newsom CARB funding denied legislature"
9. "Senate Appropriations Committee SB 253 SB 261 fiscal impact $1 million CARB 2023"
10. "Newsom May 2025 budget revision climate disclosure laws suspend repeal SB 253 SB 261 deficit 2025"
11. "California climate disclosure May 2025 budget proposal Newsom delay rejected 2025 legislature outcome"
12. "Senate Appropriations Committee analysis SB 253 fiscal 2023 CARB $1 million implementation cost estimates"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. CURRENT LEGAL AND REGULATORY STATUS AS OF MID-2026

#### 1.1 Do the Laws Remain in Effect? — YES, NO REPEAL OR LEGISLATIVE SUSPENSION HAS BEEN ENACTED

**Critical finding on the Newsom administration's attempts to delay/suspend the laws:** Multiple searches were conducted to verify the existence of a May 2025 budget revision proposal by Governor Newsom to suspend or repeal SB 253 and SB 261. The research surfaced the following related developments, but **no evidence was found that any legislative suspension, delay, repeal, or amended implementation was enacted pursuant to any May 2025 budget proposal.** The laws remain operative as of August 2026:

- **July 2024 two-year delay proposal (predecessor to the May 2025 episode):** The Newsom administration released proposed budget trailer bill language (via the Department of Finance) in July 2024 to delay implementation of both laws by two years — SB 253 Scope 1/2 reporting pushed from 2026 to 2028 and Scope 3 from 2027 to 2029, with CARB rulemaking extended to January 1, 2027; and SB 261 first reports pushed from January 1, 2026 to January 1, 2028. A Newsom spokesperson said the proposal "addresses concerns" about cost, timeline, and the "entirely new and significant workload for the state and the entities covered." [Source: TheCorporateCounsel.net; Cooley PubCo] This proposal was **not enacted** — legislative sponsors publicly rejected it. SB 253 author Senator Scott Wiener told Politico the Department of Finance proposal "does not represent an agreement with the Legislature" and that "The Legislature has *not* agreed to the Administration's proposed delay to SB 253's implementation. The Administration's proposal significantly delays the implementation of a landmark climate action law that already has a 6 year phase-in." [Cooley PubCo] Instead, the legislature enacted **SB 219** (signed September 27, 2024), which retained the 2026 start for Scope 1/2 reporting. [Ramboll; Skadden]

- **Enactment and original signing concerns:** SB 253 (Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act, Wiener) and SB 261 (Climate-Related Financial Risk Act, Stern) were signed by Governor Newsom on **October 7, 2023** (SB 253 is Chapter 382, Statutes of 2023). At signing, Newsom called SB 253's implementation deadlines "likely infeasible" and said the reporting protocol "could result in inconsistent reporting across businesses subject to the measure"; he said SB 261's deadlines gave CARB insufficient time. [Cooley PubCo; E&E News]

- **January 2024 funding omission and May 2024 restoration:** Newsom's initial January 2024-25 budget proposal omitted funding to implement SB 253 and SB 261 — an omission critics said reflected his concerns. E&E News reported implementation would cost roughly **$16 million in the first year** against the state's $291.5 billion total budget; CARB needed **$9 million in fiscal year 2024-25 and $2 million the following year** for the emissions law, and **$13.7 million over the next two fiscal years** for the climate risk law. [E&E News; Climate Vault (estimating ~$9M needed for rulemaking)] In the **May 2024 budget revision**, Newsom said both climate bills were "funded" and that the budget included "no material cuts to the climate agenda." [ESG Dive — Newsom funded article]

- **What the sources confirm as of August 2026:** The most authoritative 2026-dated sources unanimously confirm the laws remain in effect and are being implemented:
  - Nixon Peabody (March 2, 2026): "CARB approved SB 253 and SB 261 regulations, solidifying emissions and climate risk reporting despite an ongoing injunction affecting SB 261 compliance." [Nixon Peabody]
  - Mayer Brown (August 2026): "SB 253 is in effect and companies should continue preparing for the November 10, 2026 deadline; SB 261 obligations are paused but could resume quickly if the injunction is lifted." [Mayer Brown Aug 2026]
  - KPMG: "The Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act, as amended by SB-219, mandates the disclosure of GHG emissions... The effective date for reporting is 2026 for scopes 1 and 2 and 2027 for scope 3." [KPMG]
  - ESG Dive: Despite the federal government's reversal on climate policy, "California continues to enforce its climate risk and emissions disclosure requirements for large companies doing business in the state. Over 3,100 companies are subject to the laws, according to a preliminary list published by CARB." [ESG Dive tracker]

**Note on the May 2025 budget revision:** The California Budget & Policy Center's "First Look" analysis of the Governor's May 14, 2025 May Revision to the 2025-26 budget (which proposed nearly $12 billion in budget actions to close an estimated $7.5 billion 2025-26 deficit) contains **no mention of any proposal to suspend, repeal, or defund SB 253 or SB 261** — the May 2025 revision addressed Medi-Cal cuts, reserves, and other areas, with no new major revenue/tax proposals. [Cal Budget Center] No source confirmed that any suspension/repeal of SB 253 or SB 261 was proposed in or enacted from the May 2025 budget revision. The operative changes to implementation timetables came instead from CARB rulemaking (reporting deadline moved to November 10, 2026) and from the Ninth Circuit injunction (SB 261 enforcement paused), detailed below.

#### 1.2 CARB Rulemaking Status

- **Proposed regulations:** CARB posted draft proposed rulemaking documents on December 9, 2025, and posted the Notice of Public Hearing to Consider the Proposed California Corporate Greenhouse Gas Reporting and Climate-Related Financial Risk Disclosure Initial Regulation, Staff Report, and Proposed Regulation Text on December 23, 2025 (proposed Cal. Code Regs. tit. 17, §§ 96200–96207 for the fee regulation; §§ 96070–96077 per Mayer Brown). A 45-day public comment period ran December 26, 2025 – February 9, 2026, with a public hearing February 26, 2026. [CARB program page; Bracewell; Mayer Brown Aug 2026]
- **Initial rulemaking scope:** The initial rulemaking was narrowly focused on three objectives: (1) establishing the fee structure to fund program administration, (2) clarifying entities subject to fees, and (3) setting the first-year reporting deadline for Scope 1 and 2 emissions under SB 253. Other elements (detailed reporting requirements, assurance standards, enforcement provisions) were deferred to subsequent rulemakings. [Bracewell]
- **Adoption:** CARB **unanimously approved** the initial implementing regulations on **February 26, 2026**, establishing definitions, fee methodology, and setting **August 10, 2026** as the SB 253 initial reporting deadline. CARB declined to change the August 10 deadline at that time despite public comments requesting delay. The package was submitted to the California Office of Administrative Law (OAL) on May 20, 2026 (Step 5 of the APA rulemaking process). [Nixon Peabody; KPMG; Mayer Brown Aug 2026; PwC]
- **Withdrawal and three-month deferral:** On **June 24, 2026**, CARB withdrew the Initial Regulation package from OAL to make limited clarifying changes, deferring the first SB 253 Scope 1 and Scope 2 reporting deadline from **August 10, 2026 to November 10, 2026**. CARB announced it would propose limited changes, published for a 15-day public comment period before resubmission to OAL. [Sidley; Baker Tilly; Mayer Brown Aug 2026]
- **Modified regulations:** On **July 27, 2026**, CARB released the Modified Regulations, (a) confirming the November 10, 2026 first-year deadline, (b) clarifying applicability and allowing parent consolidated reports, (c) codifying first-year enforcement relief (allowing entities to submit Scope 1 and 2 data possessed/collected on or before December 5, 2024, or a letterhead statement if they lacked such data), and (d) codifying Scope 3 reporting relief. The 15-day public comment period ran through **August 11, 2026**, after which the final package goes to OAL for review. The November 10, 2026 deadline "remains contingent on the comment period outcome and OAL approval." [PwC; KPMG; Mayer Brown Aug 2026]
- **Fee notices under modified regulations:** CARB will issue fee-determination notices by **December 10, 2026**, with payment due within 60 days (earlier drafts had September 10, 2026 with 60 days to pay). Fee payments may be consolidated at the parent-company level for qualifying subsidiaries. [Mayer Brown Aug 2026; Bracewell]
- **2027-and-beyond rulemaking:** The modified regulation covers only 2026. A separate CARB rulemaking will establish reporting dates beyond 2026 and address reporting content, format, and data assurance. At a **July 21, 2026 workshop**, CARB previewed the 2027 framework: mandatory Scope 3 reporting beginning 2027 limited to 5 of 15 GHG Protocol categories; annual November 10 reporting deadline; fiscal-year-based reporting reference date (ensuring at least six months between fiscal year-end and reporting deadline); insurance companies brought into scope for 2027; and alignment with GHG Protocol with interoperability with IFRS S2 and EU CSRD. A March 2026 workshop initiated pre-rulemaking for SB 253 2027 reporting, outlining options for organizational boundaries (equity share, operational control, financial control), calculation methodologies, and three potential Scope 3 phase-in options. [KPMG; Mayer Brown Aug 2026; Persefoni]
- **Scope 3 phase-in (5 of 15 categories):** Proposed mandatory Scope 3 categories for 2027: Category 1 (Purchased Goods and Services), Category 3 (Fuel- and Energy-Related Activities), Category 5 (Waste Generated in Operations), Category 6 (Business Travel), and Category 7 (Employee Commuting). The remaining 10 categories would be voluntary with no committed timeline. [Persefoni; Mayer Brown Aug 2026]
- **CARB listening sessions (Aug–Sept 2026):** Six virtual sector-specific listening sessions: Manufacturing/Industrial/Fuel & Life Sciences (Aug 12, 2026), Agriculture/Food/Beverage & Forestry (Aug 19, 2026), Energy/Utilities/Transportation/Logistics & Waste Management (Aug 26, 2026), Retail/Consumer Goods/Technology & Commercial Services (Sept 2, 2026), Banking/Finance & Insurance (Sept 9, 2026); the first (data users) was held August 5, 2026. [Mayer Brown Aug 2026]
- **Other regulatory milestones:** November 18, 2025 — third CARB workshop on fee program, "doing business in California" definitions, the August 10, 2026 deadline, and foreign-parent consolidated reporting. September–October 2025 — CARB released a preliminary list of in-scope companies (September 24, 2025, based on California Secretary of State data through March 2022) and a draft SB 253 reporting template (October 10, 2025). July 9, 2025 — CARB released FAQs. May 29, 2025 — first CARB workshop, which emphasized reporting dates cannot be changed (set in law) and confirmed first-year "good faith efforts" enforcement relief. CARB also issued an Enforcement Notice in December 2024 stating no penalties would be issued in 2026 for incomplete reports where good faith effort is shown. CARB has twice delayed draft regulations (July 2025 and October 14, 2025 deferral to Q1 2026 due to the large volume of public comments). [KPMG; Nelson Mullins; Vinson & Elkins; US SIF; CARB YouTube June 2025 workshop; Dechert] CARB released updated FAQs and an updated SB 261 Checklist on November 17, 2025, and CARB expects to provide additional submission materials by September 1, 2026. [Nixon Peabody Dec 2025; PwC]

#### 1.3 Litigation Status

- **Chamber of Commerce litigation:** A coalition led by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the California Chamber of Commerce, and the American Farm Bureau Federation filed suit in **January 2024** in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California (*Chamber of Commerce of the United States of America v. California Air Resources Board*; on appeal *US Chamber of Commerce, et al. v. Randolph*, No. 25-5327 (9th Cir.)), challenging both laws as unconstitutional compelled speech under the First Amendment, plus Supremacy Clause (federal preemption) and Dormant Commerce Clause/extraterritoriality claims. [Nelson Mullins; Cooley; Bracewell]
- **District court:** The district court dismissed most claims (preemption, Dormant Commerce Clause) but allowed free-speech claims to proceed; on **August 13, 2025**, the court denied the plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction to block the laws. [Kim & Chang; Dechert; ESG Dive tracker]
- **Ninth Circuit — SB 261 injunction:** On **November 18, 2025**, the Ninth Circuit granted an injunction pending appeal **halting enforcement of SB 261 only**, while declining to enjoin SB 253. The Chamber's motion for an injunction pending appeal was denied September 11, 2025, before the November 18 ruling. **Oral arguments were heard January 9, 2026**, focused on whether the laws unconstitutionally compel protected speech; plaintiffs argued the laws fail commercial speech tests, while the state contended disclosures are tied to commercial transactions, though it acknowledged severability analysis for Scope 3 may be appropriate. **No decision has been issued and no timeline was provided for a ruling** as of the March 2026 and August 2026 sources. [Nixon Peabody; Bracewell; Baker Tilly; Mayer Brown Aug 2026; PwC]
- **CARB's response to the injunction:** CARB issued an Enforcement Advisory on **December 1, 2025**, confirming it would not enforce SB 261's January 1, 2026 deadline while the injunction is in effect, and opened a voluntary public reporting docket (open December 1, 2025 through July 1, 2026) for companies to post links to SB 261 reports. CARB will set an alternate reporting date after the appeal resolves. [Nixon Peabody Dec 2025; Nelson Mullins; Baker Tilly]
- **ExxonMobil litigation:** ExxonMobil sued California on **October 24, 2025** (*Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Sanchez*) in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, alleging First Amendment free speech violations and adding an NSMIA preemption claim not raised in the Chamber litigation; its preliminary injunction request was withdrawn after the Ninth Circuit ruling, and the case is on hold pending the Ninth Circuit's resolution. [ESG Dive tracker; Nelson Mullins; Mayer Brown Aug 2026]
- **The injunction applies only to SB 261, not SB 253.** Companies must continue SB 253 compliance efforts. [Nixon Peabody; PwC; Duane Morris]

#### 1.4 Number of Covered Entities

- CARB's preliminary list (September 2025): **over 3,100 companies** potentially subject to the laws (the agency noted the list may be incomplete and that covered entities are responsible for compliance even if not listed). [ESG Dive tracker; ESG Dive rulemaking delay article]
- CARB revised staff estimates (August 2025 workshop): approximately **2,596 entities** subject to SB 253 and **4,160 entities** subject to SB 261 — down from legislative estimates of ~5,344 and 10,000+ respectively. [Mayer Brown Oct 2025; CARB YouTube Aug 2025 workshop]
- Legislative-era estimates: SB 253 estimated to affect ~5,300–5,400 companies; SB 261 over 10,000 companies. [Cooley; Persefoni; Climate Vault; E&E News; Good.Lab (~10,000 affected)]

### 2. REPORTING TIMELINES (OPERATIVE AS OF MID-2026)

#### 2.1 SB 253 (Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reporting)

- **Applicability:** U.S.-organized entities (corporations, partnerships, LLCs — including US subsidiaries of non-US parents) "doing business in California" with **total annual revenues exceeding $1 billion** must annually disclose Scope 1, 2, and 3 GHG emissions per the GHG Protocol. Applies to public and private companies. [SB 253 text via CalMatters; PwC; KPMG; Skadden]
- **Original statutory timeline (as enacted 2023, as amended by SB 219):** Scope 1 and 2 reporting begins **2026** (for fiscal year 2025 data) and Scope 3 reporting begins **2027** (for FY2026 data). SB 219 "retains the original reporting timeline, with Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions reporting starting in 2026 (for reporting year 2025) with limited assurance, and Scope 3 reporting required starting in 2027," while giving CARB flexibility to set the timing of Scope 3 disclosures (removing the prior 180-day-after-Scope-1/2 deadline). [Ramboll; Skadden; KPMG]
- **CARB's operative first-year deadline:** CARB first set the Scope 1 and 2 report deadline at **August 10, 2026** (adopted Feb 26, 2026), then **deferred it three months to November 10, 2026** (via the June 24, 2026 withdrawal and July 27, 2026 Modified Regulations). The November 10, 2026 deadline is contingent on the 15-day comment period outcome and OAL approval. [Sidley; Baker Tilly; Mayer Brown Aug 2026; PwC; Greenplaces; Watershed]
- **Reporting year data:** Entities with fiscal years ending January 1–February 1, 2026 report FY 2026 data; all others report FY 2025 data. CARB clarified that entities not collecting data by its December 5, 2024 Enforcement Notice may submit a letterhead statement instead of a report for the first year, and CARB's draft reporting template is voluntary/not mandatory for 2026. [Baker Tilly; Nelson Mullins; PwC]
- **Scope 3:** First Scope 3 reports begin **2027**; CARB proposes phasing in 5 of 15 GHG Protocol categories initially (see Section 1.2). [KPMG; Mayer Brown Aug 2026; Persefoni]
- **The user's premise that SB 219 pushed Scope 3 to 2028:** The research sources consistently state SB 219 retained Scope 3 reporting beginning in 2027 (not 2028), with CARB given flexibility on exact timing. No source supports a 2028 Scope 3 start as the operative deadline. Operative status as of mid-2026: Scope 3 reporting beginning 2027, with the specific categories and deadline to be set via the 2027-and-beyond rulemaking. [Ramboll; Skadden; KPMG; PwC; Bakertilly]

#### 2.2 SB 261 (Climate-Related Financial Risk Reporting)

- **Applicability:** U.S. entities (public and private, excluding insurance companies) "doing business in California" with **annual revenues over $500 million** must publish a climate-related financial risk report **every two years**, aligned with the TCFD (2017) framework or equivalent frameworks (IFRS S2, other government/exchange-required frameworks including EU CSRD). [PwC; Skadden; Nelson Mullins]
- **Original statutory deadline:** First reports due **January 1, 2026** (covering FY2023/2024 or FY2024/2025 data per CARB FAQs), published on company websites, with links filed to CARB's public docket by July 1, 2026 (docket opened December 1, 2025). [Kim & Chang; Nelson Mullins; Mayer Brown Oct 2025]
- **Operative status as of mid-2026:** **Enforcement is paused** due to the Ninth Circuit's November 18, 2025 injunction; CARB will not enforce the January 1, 2026 deadline and will set an alternate reporting date after the appeal resolves. CARB opened a voluntary public reporting docket. A Ninth Circuit ruling "could narrow, invalidate, or uphold all or part of the statutes." [Nixon Peabody; Baker Tilly; PwC; Nelson Mullins]
- **SB 261 report content:** Climate-related financial risks (physical and transition) and adaptation/mitigation measures across the four TCFD pillars (Governance, Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics and Targets). CARB's November 2025 checklist differs from TCFD in not specifically requiring GHG emissions disclosure and asking for "various scenarios" rather than Paris Agreement-aligned scenario analysis. ESRS-compliant reporting may satisfy SB 261. Scenario analysis NOT required in Year 1; GHG emissions reporting NOT required in Year 1. [PwC; All4Inc; CEMAsys]

### 3. DATA VERIFICATION AND ASSURANCE STANDARDS

#### 3.1 SB 253 Assurance Requirements

- **First-year (2026) relief:** CARB confirmed at its November 2025 workshop and in the July 2026 Modified Regulations that **limited assurance will NOT be required for 2026 submissions** — first-year reports may be submitted with or without assurance. [Baker Tilly; PwC; Watershed; Nixon Peabody Dec 2025]
- **Limited assurance:** Required for **Scope 1 and Scope 2 beginning 2027**, escalating to **reasonable assurance by 2030**. [Baker Tilly; Watershed; Mayer Brown Aug 2026]
- **Reasonable assurance:** Required by **2030** for Scope 1 and 2. [Baker Tilly; PwC; Mayer Brown Aug 2026]
- **Scope 3 assurance:** Limited assurance for Scope 3 beginning **no earlier than 2030** (the statute sets limited Scope 3 assurance in 2030; CARB has authority to establish requirements earlier). [Bakertilly; UL Solutions; Skadden; Ramboll]
- **The user's premise on SB 219 assurance timing:** The user stated SB 219 pushed limited assurance from 2026 to 2027 reporting. The sources confirm: SB 219 retained limited assurance on Scopes 1 & 2 beginning 2026 in the statutory text [Ramboll; Skadden], but CARB's operative implementing regulations **waive the assurance requirement for the 2026 reporting year**, making limited assurance first required for **2027 reporting** — consistent with the user's understanding of the operative result. Reasonable assurance remains 2030. [Bakertilly; Watershed; Mayer Brown Aug 2026; PwC]
- **Who conducts assurance:** Independent third-party assurance providers verified/accredited to recognized standards. Standards under consideration/adopted by CARB include: **ISAE 3000 (Revised), ISAE 3410, ISSA 5000, ISO 14064-3:2019, AICPA attestation standards (AT-C 210/205), and AA1000AS v3.** [Mayer Brown Aug 2026; Persefoni; All4Inc] CARB will leverage its existing verification framework principles including independence, objectivity, and conflict-of-interest requirements. [CARB YouTube Aug 2025 workshop] UL Solutions notes it offers third-party GHG verification aligned with ISO 14064-3 supporting compliance with CSRD, California laws, and voluntary frameworks. [UL Solutions]
- **Safe harbor:** A safe harbor exists for Scope 3 disclosures through 2030 if made in good faith with a reasonable basis. [PwC; Skadden; Watershed; Climate Vault]

#### 3.2 SB 261 Assurance Requirements

- **SB 261 has NO independent third-party assurance or verification requirement.** Multiple sources confirm SB 261 imposes no verification requirement (e.g., Kim & Chang: "No verification requirement" for CRFRA). The reports must be published and posted to CARB's docket; entities may complete reports "to the best of their ability" with explanations of missing disclosures. [Kim & Chang; Skadden; PwC]

### 4. MATERIALITY THRESHOLDS

- **The California laws use revenue-based applicability thresholds, not a materiality concept per se.** SB 253 applies to entities with total annual revenues exceeding **$1 billion**; SB 261 applies to entities with revenues exceeding **$500 million** — in both cases regardless of the materiality of climate risks to the business. [PwC; KPMG; Skadden]
- **Revenue definition:** "Total annual revenue" means "gross receipts" under **California Revenue and Taxation Code Section 25120(f)(2)**, which is broader than financial statement revenue (includes interest, dividends, proceeds of property sales). Total global revenue counts, not just California-generated revenue. An entity must use the lesser of the prior two fiscal years of revenue. Revenue is assessed at the individual company level, with aggregation for unitary businesses. [PwC; Baker Tilly; Nelson Mullins; Kim & Chang; Bracewell]
- **"Doing business in California" definition:** Actively engaging in transactions for financial gain and either (a) being organized/commercially domiciled in California, or (b) having California sales exceeding an inflation-adjusted threshold — **$735,019 for 2024** and **$757,070 for 2025** — or 25% of total sales. Sales include those through agents/independent contractors; wholesale electricity transactions are excluded. CARB proposes to exclude property holdings and payroll criteria from the "doing business" definition. [Nixon Peabody; PwC; Bracewell; Nelson Mullins citing R&TC §23101(b)(1)-(2)]
- **Distinction from other regimes:** The sources note the EU's CSRD applies a double materiality concept (financial and impact materiality), and the SEC's climate rules applied a financial materiality concept, whereas California's framework is purely threshold-based. [PwC; Persefoni; Duane Morris (noting the SEC proposal to rescind its rules, while state laws continue); the Skadden and PwC sources frame California as covering both public and private companies beyond the SEC's scope]
- **Exemptions:** Tax-exempt nonprofits; government entities and entities majority-owned by government; entities whose only California activity is teleworking employees; entities whose only California activity is wholesale electricity transactions (CAISO-related); University of California (SB 253 only); insurance companies (SB 261 fully exempt; CARB extended the insurance exemption to SB 253 for 2026, but insurance companies must begin reporting in 2027 because CDI reporting does not satisfy SB 253); subsidiaries included in a qualifying parent's consolidated report (50%+ ownership threshold per Cap-and-Trade/Cap-and-Invest definition of parent-subsidiary). Holding companies and mutual funds typically don't meet revenue thresholds. [PwC; Baker Tilly; Nelson Mullins; Mayer Brown Aug 2026]

### 5. ENFORCEMENT MECHANISMS

- **CARB's role:** CARB administers both programs — developing and adopting regulations, collecting annual fees, operating reporting/docket systems, and exercising enforcement discretion. CARB is one of six boards, departments, and offices under the California Environmental Protection Agency. [CARB program page; KPMG] CARB "will endeavor to design these programs to be the least burdensome for implementation and compliance." [CARB program page] CARB is authorized (but no longer required, per SB 219) to contract with third-party emissions reporting organizations. [Ramboll; Skadden]
- **California Attorney General:** SB 253 requires CARB to consult with the Attorney General (along with government stakeholders, investors, consumer and environmental justice stakeholders, and reporting entities with demonstrated leadership in GHG accounting) in developing regulations. [SB 253 text via CalMatters] The AG is involved in enforcement of the penalties.
- **Penalties — SB 253:** Administrative penalties up to **$500,000 per reporting year** for non-filing or late filing. [PwC; Skadden; Baker Tilly; Watershed; Greenplaces; Persefoni]
  - **Note on the user's premise:** The user's query referenced penalties "up to $1 million per reporting year for SB 253." The research sources consistently state SB 253 penalties are capped at **$500,000 per reporting year** (some sources describe per-year caps; no source cited a $1 million cap). SB 261 penalties are capped at **$50,000 per year** (the user's premise referenced $500,000 for SB 261, which is not supported by the sources; note Ab 1305, a separate voluntary carbon market law, has penalties up to $2,500 per violation up to $500,000 total). [Skadden on AB 1305; PwC; Baker Tilly]
- **Penalties — SB 261:** Up to **$50,000 per entity per year** for inadequate or missing reports. [PwC; Skadden; Baker Tilly; Watershed]
- **Enforcement discretion:** CARB will exercise enforcement discretion in the first year — no penalties in 2026 for entities demonstrating good-faith compliance efforts. First-year SB 253 relief allows submission of data possessed/collected on or before December 5, 2024, or a letter explaining no such data existed. [PwC; All4Inc; Nixon Peabody; Dechert]
- **Fee enforcement:** Daily penalties for nonpayment of fees (each day counts as a separate violation); CARB may seek injunctions against violators. Entities must keep records proving compliance with thresholds for **five years**. [Bracewell]
- **No inflation adjustments identified:** The sources do not identify any inflation-adjustment mechanism for the statutory penalty amounts; the inflation adjustment applies to the "doing business in California" sales threshold ($735,019 for 2024; $757,070 for 2025). [PwC; Bracewell]
- **CARB fees (annual, flat-rate structure):** Fee formula = total program administration funds (personnel, legal, contracting, contingency, loan repayment) ÷ number of covered entities, with annual inflation adjustments. Estimates: **~$3,106–$3,316 per entity under SB 253** and **~$1,403–$1,443 per entity under SB 261** (figures vary across the Aug 2025 proposed fee schedule and other descriptions). Watershed cites a range of **$2,000–$7,000 per entity**. Entities with $500M–$1B revenue pay only the SB 261 fee; entities over $1B pay both fees (fees are cumulative). Fees are paid annually even though SB 261 reporting is biennial. [All4Inc; CARB YouTube Aug 2025 workshop; Mayer Brown Oct 2025; Nelson Mullins; Watershed]

### 6. PLAIN-LANGUAGE SUMMARY OF WHAT EACH LAW REQUIRES

**SB 253 — Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act (CCDAA; Health & Safety Code § 38532):** If you are a US company (public or private, including US subsidiaries of foreign parents) doing business in California with over $1 billion in total annual global revenue ("gross receipts"), you must annually disclose your greenhouse gas emissions to CARB, calculated in accordance with the GHG Protocol: Scope 1 (direct emissions from operations), Scope 2 (indirect emissions from purchased energy), and Scope 3 (indirect value-chain emissions). First Scope 1 & 2 reports were due August 10, 2026, now deferred to November 10, 2026 (covering FY2025 data for most companies), with Scope 3 reporting starting 2027 (initially limited to 5 of 15 value-chain categories). Independent third-party assurance will be required — limited assurance beginning 2027, reasonable assurance by 2030. Non-compliance penalties up to $500,000 per reporting year; Scope 3 misstatements are protected by a good-faith safe harbor through 2030. [PwC; KPMG; CARB program page; Baker Tilly; Watershed]

**SB 261 — Climate-Related Financial Risk Act (CRFRA; Health & Safety Code § 38533):** If you are a US company doing business in California with over $500 million in total annual revenue (and you are not an insurance company), you must publish a biennial climate-related financial risk report describing physical and transition climate risks and your mitigation/adaptation measures, drafted consistently with the TCFD framework or equivalent (IFRS S2, EU CSRD) across governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics & targets. Reports must be posted on your website and linked in CARB's public docket. First reports were statutorily due January 1, 2026, but enforcement is currently paused by a Ninth Circuit injunction while the constitutional challenge proceeds; CARB will set a new deadline after the appeal resolves and has opened a voluntary docket. No third-party assurance is required. Penalties up to $50,000 per year. [PwC; Skadden; Kim & Chang; Baker Tilly]

**SB 219 (2023/2024 amendment):** Signed September 27, 2024. Amends SB 253 and SB 261 to: allow consolidated reporting at the parent-company level (subsidiaries no longer need separate reports if a qualifying parent files); extend CARB's implementation-guidance deadline (from January 1, 2025 to July 1, 2025); give CARB flexibility on Scope 3 timing (removing the statutory 180-day-after-Scope-1/2 requirement); make CARB's contracting with a third-party emissions reporting organization optional rather than mandatory; and separate annual fee due dates from disclosure filing dates (eliminating advance fee payment obligations). SB 219 retained the 2026 Scope 1/2 / 2027 Scope 3 reporting start dates, meaning no delay in first reporting. [Ramboll; Skadden; Kim & Chang; Clark Nuber; Good.Lab]

### 7. REAL-WORLD COMPLIANCE CHALLENGES AND COST ESTIMATES

#### 7.1 State Fiscal Analyses and CARB Cost Data (from research sources)

- **Implementation cost to the state:** E&E News reported implementation would cost roughly **$16 million in the first year** against the state's $291.5 billion total budget; CARB needed **$9 million in fiscal year 2024-25 and $2 million the following year** for the emissions law, and **$13.7 million over two fiscal years** for the climate risk law. [E&E News]
- **CARB fee-program cost base:** At the August 21, 2025 CARB workshop, staff proposed a flat fee per covered entity calculated as total annual program cost ÷ number of covered entities, including a **one-time $20.7 million charge to repay temporary funding from the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund (GGRF)** and **recurring annual costs of approximately $13.9 million**. Resulting estimated fees: **~$3,316 per entity under SB 253** and **~$1,443 per entity under SB 261** (Mayer Brown's October 2025 analysis cites $3,106 and $1,403, respectively). [CARB YouTube Aug 2025 workshop; All4Inc; Mayer Brown Oct 2025]
- **Funding context (LAO):** The California Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) report on the 2024-25 budget (February 14, 2024) noted the Governor's budget used over three-quarters of the estimated $2.3 billion in discretionary GGRF available in 2024-25 to backfill General Fund reductions, and that the Governor proposed $4.1 billion in General Fund solutions (including $1.1 billion from delaying spending). This report did not specifically address SB 253/SB 261 funding but provides the budget-constraint context. [LAO]
- **The user's request for Senate Appropriations Committee analyses:** No Senate Appropriations Committee analysis of SB 253 or SB 261 was directly surfaced in the research; however, the E&E News cost figures above, the CalMatters bill-history page documenting the legislative hearing process, and the CARB fee-program cost data serve as the fiscal-basis documentation. [E&E News; CalMatters; CARB YouTube Aug 2025 workshop]

#### 7.2 Independent Industry Analyses — Corporate Compliance Cost Estimates

- **Litigation plaintiffs' cost claims:** In the Chamber of Commerce litigation, plaintiffs argued the laws compel speech and impose massive compliance costs — **"Scope 3 reporting alone could exceed $1 million/year per company"** — and create a "patchwork of inconsistent state-by-state regulatory regimes." [Cooley PubCo]
- **Newsom administration concerns:** A Newsom spokesperson said the (2024) delay proposal "addresses concerns about cost, timeline and the entirely new and significant workload for the state and the entities covered by these new requirements." [Cooley PubCo]
- **CARB's environmental-impact/fee framing:** CARB is required to design the programs to be "the least burdensome" and has emphasized minimizing compliance costs. [CARB program page]
- **Fee burden per company:** CARB's flat annual fee schedule ($2,000–$7,000 per entity per Watershed; ~$3,106–$3,316 SB 253 plus ~$1,403–$1,443 SB 261 per the CARB proposals) represents the direct regulatory cost, with subsidiaries paying separate fees even under consolidated parent reporting. [Watershed; Mayer Brown Oct 2025; All4Inc]

#### 7.3 General Cross-Industry Compliance Challenges (from major firms)

- **Uncertainty from litigation and rulemaking delays:** Companies face a "wait-and-see" risk; CARB's delayed rulemaking (from October 2025 to Q1 2026, then the June 2026 withdrawal) meant companies had to prepare "without complete clarity on regulatory requirements," and may need to make judgment calls on the "doing business" definition. [Ramboll; Vinson & Elkins]
- **Data readiness and the December 5, 2024 data cut-off:** First-year enforcement relief allows entities to submit only data possessed before December 5, 2024, or a letter stating no such data existed — companies that began collecting data late face first-year reporting gaps. [PwC; Nelson Mullins; Watershed]
- **Assurance capacity and readiness:** The greatest challenge is Scope 3 verification, which relies on estimates, supplier data, and assumptions of varying quality; companies should conduct internal audits of reporting processes, document methodologies, implement internal controls, engage assurance providers early, and consider pre-assurance reviews/mock audits to avoid assurance-provider capacity bottlenecks. [UL Solutions; Persefoni]
- **Scope 3 supply-chain ripple effect:** Suppliers not directly regulated will likely need to measure and disclose emissions to continue doing business with covered companies. [Climate Vault; Good.Lab]
- **Cross-framework alignment:** Companies are advised that the same emissions inventory and risk assessment can be reused for CDP, SBTi, EcoVadis, GRI, EU CSRD, and ISSB reporting; SB 219 aligns closely with ISSB and the EU CSRD. [Greenplaces; Good.Lab; PwC]
- **Entity-by-entity scope determination:** Parent-subsidiary relationships do not automatically determine applicability — each entity must assess its own obligations (revenue thresholds verified against California Franchise Tax Board filings, using the lesser of the prior two fiscal years); parent companies may file consolidated reports, including for foreign parents reporting for US subsidiaries. [Nelson Mullins; Nixon Peabody Dec 2025; Kim & Chang]
- **Practical recommendations from multiple firms:** (1) Determine applicability entity-by-entity; (2) continue SB 253 Scope 1/2 preparation for the November 10, 2026 deadline; (3) treat SB 261 reporting as voluntary-but-ready, prepared to publish promptly if the injunction lifts; (4) document compliance efforts for CARB enforcement discretion; (5) engage assurance providers early (limited assurance mandatory from 2027); (6) align with GHG Protocol and consider organizational boundary options (equity share, operational control, financial control); (7) monitor the Ninth Circuit, which could narrow, invalidate, or uphold all or part of the statutes. [Nixon Peabody; Mayer Brown; PwC; Watershed; Persefoni; Duane Morris]
- **Regulatory-alignment note:** The SEC proposed on May 29, 2026 (Release No. 33-11421) to rescind its own 2024 climate disclosure rules, but that proposal "would not eliminate the growing network of climate-related disclosure requirements imposed by state governments, foreign jurisdictions and international standard-setting bodies" — including California SB 253 and SB 261. [Duane Morris]

You are a research supervisor. Your job is to conduct research by calling the "ConductResearch" tool. For context, today's date is Mon Aug 24, 2026.

<Task>
Your focus is to call the "ConductResearch" tool to conduct research against the overall research question passed in by the user. 
When you are completely satisfied with the research findings returned from the tool calls, then you should call the "ResearchComplete" tool to indicate that you are done with your research.
</Task>

<Available Tools>
You have access to three main tools:
1. **ConductResearch**: Delegate research tasks to specialized sub-agents
2. **ResearchComplete**: Indicate that research is complete
3. **think_tool**: For reflection and strategic planning during research

**CRITICAL: Use think_tool before calling ConductResearch to plan your approach, and after each ConductResearch to assess progress. Do not call think_tool with any other tools in parallel.**
</Available Tools>

<Instructions>
Think like a research manager with limited time and resources. Follow these steps:

1. **Read the question carefully** - What specific information does the user need?
2. **Decide how to delegate the research** - Carefully consider the question and decide how to delegate the research. Are there multiple independent directions that can be explored simultaneously?
3. **After each call to ConductResearch, pause and assess** - Do I have enough to answer? What's still missing?
</Instructions>

<Hard Limits>
**Task Delegation Budgets** (Prevent excessive delegation):
- **Bias towards single agent** - Use single agent for simplicity unless the user request has clear opportunity for parallelization
- **Stop when you can answer confidently** - Don't keep delegating research for perfection
- **Limit tool calls** - Always stop after 3 tool calls to ConductResearch and think_tool if you cannot find the right sources

**Maximum 3 parallel agents per iteration**
</Hard Limits>

<Show Your Thinking>
Before you call ConductResearch tool call, use think_tool to plan your approach:
- Can the task be broken down into smaller sub-tasks?

After each ConductResearch tool call, use think_tool to analyze the results:
- What key information did I find?
- What's missing?
- Do I have enough to answer the question comprehensively?
- Should I delegate more research or call ResearchComplete?
</Show Your Thinking>

<Scaling Rules>
**Simple fact-finding, lists, and rankings** can use a single sub-agent:
- *Example*: List the top 10 coffee shops in San Francisco → Use 1 sub-agent

**Comparisons presented in the user request** can use a sub-agent for each element of the comparison:
- *Example*: Compare OpenAI vs. Anthropic vs. DeepMind approaches to AI safety → Use 3 sub-agents
- Delegate clear, distinct, non-overlapping subtopics

**Important Reminders:**
- Each ConductResearch call spawns a dedicated research agent for that specific topic
- A separate agent will write the final report - you just need to gather information
- When calling ConductResearch, provide complete standalone instructions - sub-agents can't see other agents' work
- Do NOT use acronyms or abbreviations in your research questions, be very clear and specific
</Scaling Rules>

As a sustainability consultant advising on global ESG reporting strategies, I need a comprehensive comparison of the most recent versions (as of 2026) of three major climate disclosure frameworks: the SEC Climate Disclosure Rule, the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), and California's SB-219 climate disclosure legislation.

My research should cover the following dimensions for each framework:
1. Reporting timelines (including any phased implementation schedules, compliance deadlines, and fiscal year alignment)
2. Data verification standards (including assurance levels, who conducts verification, and any escalation of requirements over time)
3. Materiality thresholds (including how each framework defines materiality—financial materiality vs. double materiality—and any thresholds for applicability/scoping)
4. Enforcement mechanisms (including penalties, regulatory bodies responsible for enforcement, and compliance monitoring approaches)

In addition to the multi-dimensional comparison, my research should provide:
- A short plain-language description of each framework
- A multi-column comparison table covering all dimensions
- Multiple real-world enterprise compliance challenges and cost estimates per framework (drawing from both government reports and reputable industry analyses, such as regulatory impact assessments, consulting firms' cost analyses, and academic or professional accounting bodies' estimates)
- An analysis of strategic implications for multinational enterprises that must navigate overlapping and potentially conflicting ESG reporting requirements across jurisdictions

The analysis should be a general cross-industry overview rather than sector-specific. For cost estimates, I want figures sourced from government documents (e.g., SEC rulemakings, California legislative analyses, EU impact assessments) balanced against independent industry analyses (e.g., from major consulting firms, legal firms, or industry associations). All sources should be reputable and cited.

Context: The query is as of August 2026, so I need the most current versions of these regulations, noting that climate disclosure rules are evolving rapidly—some may be under legal challenge, subject to revision, or in various stages of implementation. The research should acknowledge and account for the current legal and regulatory status of each framework as of mid-2026.

args.research_topic: Research the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Climate Disclosure Rule as it stands as of August 2026, for use in a sustainability consulting analysis. Cover in detail: (1) The current legal and regulatory status as of mid-2026 — the rule was adopted in March 2024, stayed by the Eighth Circuit, and the SEC moved to end its defense of the rule in March 2025 under Acting Chair Mark Uyeda; confirm whether the rule has been formally withdrawn, vacated, or otherwise resolved by August 2026, and any developments since. (2) The original reporting timelines and phased implementation schedule for large accelerated filers, accelerated filers, and non-accelerated filers, including fiscal year alignment and any compliance deadlines that were set or have been revised. (3) Data verification and assurance standards, including the originally phased-in limited assurance and reasonable assurance requirements for large accelerated filers, who would conduct verification, and any escalation of assurance over time. (4) Materiality definition used (financial materiality as defined by the Supreme Court in materiality jurisprudence), and any applicability thresholds such as revenue or market capitalization thresholds. (5) Enforcement mechanisms, including the SEC's role, penalties available under securities laws, and compliance monitoring approaches. (6) Plain-language summary of what the rule would require. (7) Real-world enterprise compliance challenges and cost estimates, citing the SEC's own economic analysis in the 2024 rulemaking (initial and annualized cost estimates in USD), Congressional Research Service analyses, and independent industry estimates from major consulting firms (e.g., Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG), law firms, or industry associations. Provide specific dollar figures and cite all sources by name and document title. Note how cost estimates differ between the SEC's estimates and industry estimates, and any critique of the SEC's cost-benefit analysis. Give a general cross-industry overview rather than sector-specific detail. All sources must be reputable and explicitly cited.

Research the European Union Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) as it stands as of August 2026, for use in a sustainability consulting analysis. Cover in detail: (1) The current legal and regulatory status as of mid-2026 — including the February 2025 EU 'Omnibus' simplification package that delayed and re-scoped the CSRD, the European Commission's subsequent proposals, the final text of any adopted amendments as of August 2026, adoption of the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) and their status including any sector-specific standards, and any delays or changes to the first reporting waves.
